title: Court asked to block Trump's 2nd executive order targeting birthright citizenship
summary: The ACLU is asking a federal court to block President Trump's latest order on birthright citizenship.
story: Trump's 1st bid to end birthright citizenship was rejected by the Supreme Court.

The same legal team that successfully challenged President Donald Trump's first bid to end birthright citizenship is asking a federal judge to clarify that the Supreme Court's ruling also blocks a second executive order attempting to target specific children who Trump says are exempt from becoming Americans at birth.

Trump's second birthright order -- signed last week as a response to the high court's June ruling -- attempts to deny citizenship to children born on U.S. soil to an "alien enemy," or a "foreign government employee," or a parent who "engaged in a commercial transaction" to obtain citizenship or who are born in a territory where citizenship is not conferred by statute.

Attorneys for the American Civil Liberties Union, representing a class of potentially affected immigrant families, filed a motion in federal district court in New Hampshire on Tuesday seeking a declaratory order that the new order effectively defies the Supreme Court.

"Nothing requires this Court to countenance the continued assault on this foundational constitutional principle or issue an endless string of EO-specific injunctions," the attorneys wrote. "The court should make clear that [Trump] may not take away class members' birthright under the auspices of these or any other executive actions."

The Supreme Court did confirm four categories of children born on U.S. soil who would not automatically become citizens:  the children of ambassadors, those born on foreign public ships, those born to enemies occupying American territory and members of Indian tribes. But its 6-3 decision left little room for additional exemptions.

Court precedent "indicated that the four exceptions were a closed set," Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion, "meaning that there can be no additional exceptions recognized based on subsequent circumstances or developments. And the decision has consistently been read that way."
Chief Justice John Roberts' majority opinion explained that the key determinant of citizenship was "fixed by the place of nativity, irrespective of parentage."
The administration argues that the categories specified in Trump's second executive order are acceptable exemptions from birthright citizenship under the legal interpretation presented by Roberts.
The president's executive order is set to take effect on Sept. 6.
The ACLU argued in its motion to the court that none of those specified exemptions appear in the Constitution or federal citizenship law and seeks to block the order.

title: Former US Marine Robert Gilman released after years of detention in Russia
summary: Robert Gilman, a U.S. citizen and former Marine, has been freed from detention in Russia on humanitarian grounds, a State Department spokesperson confirmed Tuesday.
story: Gilman's release came amid concerns about his health.
Robert Gilman, a U.S. citizen and former Marine, has been freed from years of detention in Russia on humanitarian grounds, a State Department spokesperson confirmed Tuesday.

"Thanks to the hard work of President Trump and Special Envoy Witkoff, Mr. Gilman joins over 100 Americans whom the United States has freed during President Trump's second term in office. This Administration will continue to work for the release of all Americans unjustly detained in Russia, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard," the spokesperson said.

Gilman's release came amid severe concerns about his health. According to the organization advocating on behalf of his family, Gilman is on his way to a U.S. military hospital in Texas, where he will be medically and psychologically assessed and treated. His family has flown to Texas, including his mother, who was in Russia attempting to see him at the hospital.

Gilman, now 32 years old, had been detained since 2022. Later that year, he was sentenced to four and a half years in a prison colony after being accused of fighting with a Russian police officer at a train station.
Gilman's family deny the charges and have accused the Russian authorities of wrongfully detaining him for political purposes because he is American.

According to the "Free Robert Gilman" website, Gilman served in the U.S. Marine Corps and also founded "Robert Gilman Just English" to help students in Poland build their English skills. Gilman was in Moldova to teach and was visiting family outside of Moscow when he fell ill and was then accused of kicking a police officer.

Gilman, who was recently designated as a wrongful detainee, was not part of a prisoner exchange, and no other concessions were provided as part of his release, according to the State Department spokesperson.
President Donald Trump said he had discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin about Gilman's release, adding that "Russia asked for no one in return -- No exchange took place."

"Robert will land at Andrews Air Force Base, in Washington, D.C., tonight, where my Representatives, some of whom are on the plane with him, will welcome Robert back to THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA! I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands," Trump wrote in a post on his social media account Tuesday.
Lexie Hudson, Gilman's sister, commented on his release in a press release sent by Global Reach, a nonprofit organization dedicated to bringing home Americans who are wrongly held abroad.
Hudson thanked both Trump and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey.

"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"
"I am looking forward to seeing Robert. I haven't been able to speak with him once since this all began. We will make sure that he gets the treatment and support that he needs."
Sen. Markey celebrated Gilman's release in a post on X while also describing Gilman's debilitating condition.

"Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor -- a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia. We don't yet know the full details of his current condition or the long-term impact on his recovery. I'm grateful that Robert is now on his way back to the United States to receive the life-saving care that he desperately needs," Markey wrote.

Gilman's family members and representatives have said that in addition to the false charges levied against him, Gilman was subjected to torture and harsh physical and mental abuse by Russian prison guards.
Moscow has so far not commented on Gilman's release.

title: What to know about Elon Musk's massive $16.8 billion chip factory
summary: The factory is set to be the largest building in the world, Musk said.
story: The factory is set to be the largest building in the world, Musk said.
Elon Musk plans to build a $16.8 billion chip factory that he says is set to become the largest building in the world.
Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, announced the project as chip manufacturers worldwide ramp up production in response to a surge of demand triggered by advances in artificial intelligence.
The massive plant, known as Terafab, will be located in southeastern Texas, roughly 70 miles outside Houston, according to its website.
"The facility will be an advanced semiconductor fab that will bridge the divide between current global chip supply and the compute demand of the future," the website says.
Here's what to know about the new chip factory:
Why is Elon Musk building a new chip factory?

Semiconductors are a key ingredient in a vast array of products ranging from washing machines to refrigerators to laptops. The growing adoption of AI, meanwhile, has driven up demand for advanced chips.

SpaceX oversees xAI, a Musk-led AI company that offers a chatbot in competition with the likes of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. Those AI ambitions will require data centers equipped with semiconductors.
Tesla-made electric vehicles and humanoid robots will also need chips, the factory's website says.
The combined demand for chips from SpaceX and Tesla is expected to exceed 1 terawatt of compute, a larger amount than the entire global supply currently available, according to the website.
SpaceX and Tesla both rank among the 11 largest companies in the world, as measured by market capitalization. Taken together, they boast a combined value of more than $3 trillion.
What's different about Elon Musk's new chip factory?
The factory will span 100 million square feet of manufacturing space, making it the largest facility of its type in the world, according to its website.
Beyond its size, the website said, the factory will be vertically integrated, meaning it will put each phase of the production process under one roof, including manufacturing, packaging and testing.
The facility will employ 3,000 people, many of whom will be from the local area surrounding the factory site, the website said.
In an effort to mitigate environmental impact, the factory will depend on water from a nearby reservoir rather than local groundwater, the website said.
The plant makes up a a part of Musk's aspiration to build space-bound data centers and other infrastructure in space.

"By building and operating the largest chip manufacturing facility on the planet, we're continuing down a path where future humans can compete over building the largest facilities in the solar system, and eventually the galaxy," the website said.
What's next for Elon Musk's new chip factory?
The multi-billion dollar investment announced by Musk marks the first phase of construction on the plant. A future potential expansion, the website said, could bring "total investment much higher."
In a statement last week, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott applauded the project and hinted at its ever-growing scale.
"Texas is where big ideas grow even bigger," Abbott said.

title: Progressive vs. moderate showdown for Senate seat tops Minnesota primaries
summary: Another Midwestern moderate versus progressive showdown will play out Tuesday in Minnesota, where Rep. Angie Craig and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan are competing.
story: Senate, governor and House races are on the ballot.
Another Midwestern moderate versus progressive showdown will play out Tuesday in Minnesota, where Rep. Angie Craig and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan are competing to replace Sen. Tina Smith.
Flanagan has the backing of national progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Smith, who is retiring.
Craig has the backing of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and top local leaders like Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey.
Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, who is not running for reelection, has notably not endorsed in the race.

This year's midterm election cycle has seen the ascendency of progressive and democratic socialist candidates that has prompted debate among Democrats about whether they can win in a general election and what that means for the party's future. Five House Democratic incumbents have lost their primaries to progressive challengers this year.

Minnesota became the center of outrage over President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies earlier this year when federal immigration agents killed Alex Pretti and Renee Good in separate incidents during Operation Metro Surge. Both Craig and Flanagan have made pushes for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to face legal accountability central to their pitch.

No agents have been charged in the shootings of Pretti and Good and the Hennepin County Attorney's office continues its investigation. Customs and Border Patrol Commissioner Rodney Scott has said his agency is investigating the shootings.

Flanagan has harshly attacked Craig for her vote in favor of the Laken Riley Act, a Trump-backed immigration bill that expands the authorization for the federal government to detain undocumented immigrants charged with crimes. Craig says she regrets that vote.

Like in neighboring Michigan, the issue of support for Israel has also animated the race. Craig has received backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in previous races and appears on its pro-Israel candidate portal, though she says she is not taking its money in this race. Flanagan opposes all offensive weapon sales to Israel and has called Israel's actions in Gaza a "genocide."

Another major issue in the race are the investigations into alleged widespread fraud in the states social services programs that have plagued Walz's tenure and, by extension, Flanagan's. Craig has blamed Flanagan for a lack of oversight and accountability, allegations that Flanagan rejects.

No Republican has won a Senate election in Minnesota since 2002. Sen. Amy Klobuchar won her 2024 race against former NBA player Royce White by 16 points. White is running again this year but will face an uphill battle against NRSC-backed former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya.

In the governor's race, Klobuchar appears poised to clinch the Democratic nomination to succeed Walz. If she wins in November, Walz would appoint a temporary replacement before a special election would be held to fill the term.

On the Republican side, Trump endorsed former MyPillow CEO and prominent election-denier Mike Lindell. He faces current Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth and the businessman Kendall Qualls, who is endorsed by the state Republican Party.
Craig's Senate candidacy creates an opening in the Second Congressional District, which Republicans have long wanted to flip.
The Democratic primary is a hotly contested three-way race between state legislators: flight attendant Kaela Berg, doctor Matt Klein and lawyer Matt Little.
On the Republican side, state Sen. Eric Pratt is running unopposed.

In Minnesota's 1st District, Democrats hope a blue wave could help them oust incumbent Rep. Brad Finstad in a district once held by Walz. The top Democratic candidate is math teacher Jake Johnson, who is a top recruit for Democrats' Red to Blue program.

And one Democrat is hoping a little bit of reality TV star power will help him unseat Rep. Pete Stauber in the deep red Minnesota 8th along the northern border. Actor, businessman and former "Summer House" star Luke Gulbranson is running against Trina Swanson, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party's pick in that district.

title: Darline Graham faces battle for her brother's seat in South Carolina Senate primary
summary: Republican voters in South Carolina return to the polls Tuesday for the second time in two months to decide who will take the place of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
story: The contest will test Lindsey Graham's legacy and Trump's influence.

Republican voters in South Carolina return to the polls on Tuesday for the second time in two months to decide who will take the place of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham after his death in July created a vacancy on the party’s Senate ticket and sparked a rapid-fire campaign season.
Democrats face an uphill battle to try to flip the seat, which the Cook Political Report rates as solidly Republican.
Notable candidates aim to continue Graham's legacy, including his sister
Graham's sister Darline was appointed to the Senate to finish out his term the day after his passing, and then launched a bid for the full term after President Donald Trump endorsed her.

She has faced skepticism from some Republicans who have said they feel that she has been elevated as the party's preferred candidate when voters don't know much about her and thought she would just be a caretaker for the seat.

"There's a little bit of uneasiness about that whole process," John McGrath, the chair of South Carolina's Berkeley County Republican Party, told ABC News in early August. "Because at the end of the day, ultimately the people who are going to decide who the nominee is are the people of South Carolina, not D.C., not the consultants that run these big money [political action committees], organizations."

But Darline Graham, who had a close relationship with her brother and campaigned for him previously, has leaned into her status as a political outsider, saying that allows her to connect with Americans. She has also said she plans to be more focused on domestic issues and affordability than her brother, who heavily focused on national security and foreign affairs, and that she supports doing away with the Senate's legislative filibuster, which her brother supported keeping in place.
"I'm not a politician. I'm not a millionaire. I understand the average struggles of the American family," Graham told viewers during a debate in early August.

Darline Graham has served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, on the South Carolina State Workforce Development Board, and in other state roles. She also previously held roles with Clemson University, the South Carolina Department of Employment and Workforce and the South Carolina Department of Vocational Rehabilitation.
She has maintained that she'd be a staunch Trump supporter in the Senate, including on issues such as the Iran war and voting legislation.
"I completely support the president's agenda. I'm 100% behind him," she said during that same debate.

Chase Meyer, a political science professor at the University of South Carolina, told ABC News that Trump's endorsement of Darline Graham should stand to help her given how voters don't know much about her yet.
"Without that endorsement, it would be hard to tell how well she would do at all in this race," he said.

Darline Graham has not drawn many clear contrasts with other candidates in the race, including two U.S. representatives running for the seat: Ralph Norman and Russell Fry, both conservative stalwarts from South Carolina who have emphasized their support of the president even while running against his endorsed candidate.

Other notable candidates on the ballot include former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, whose tenure was marred by some controversy but who is attempting a political comeback after a stint in Congress; and businessman Mark Lynch, who ran against Lindsey Graham in June and notched around 30% of the vote.
If no candidate gets over 50% of the vote, then the top two vote-getters go to a runoff on Aug. 25.
Democrats eye a new matchup

Whoever wins the primary election or the potential runoff primary will face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November. Andrews, a pediatrician, previously ran in 2022 for the state’s 1st Congressional District and won the Democratic primary for Senate in June.

"No matter who emerges from the primary, my mission remains the same: lowering costs, protecting health care and fighting for South Carolina families," Andrews said in a statement to ABC News. "We have spent more than a year building a statewide grassroots campaign, and we are ready for November."

title: In test of Democratic Party's future, next stop is in battleground Wisconsin
summary: Candidates are vying to win the first open gubernatorial seat since 2010.
story: Candidates are vying to win the first open gubernatorial seat since 2010.

Progressives face another next big test in battleground Wisconsin, where state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, appears to be the front-runner in the turbulent Democratic primary for governor.

In Wisconsin, Hong, a former restaurant owner who represents the capital city of Madison, has led the field of governor candidates in statewide polling, despite some late efforts in the party to unite around an alternative candidate ahead of the Aug. 11 contest.
Candidates are vying to win the first open gubernatorial seat since 2010, replacing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who announced last year that he wouldn't run for reelection.
If Hong wins, it could be another big victory for democratic socialists.

Candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America have won primaries in deep-blue districts in New York City and Colorado. In Michigan, a swing state, progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated a centrist candidate endorsed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the Senate Democratic primary.

Some Democrats are worried Hong could struggle to court independent voters against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, the presumptive GOP nominee backed by President Donald Trump, and could be a drag on other Democrats down the ticket when they hope to retake majorities in the state legislature, Susan Knower, a former Democratic party chair of Sauk County in Wisconsin, told ABC News.
Also complicating matters is that some voters already have cast absentee ballots for Democrats who have bowed out of the race but remain on the ballot.

David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, exited the campaign in July but revived it days later after receiving Evers' endorsement. Crowley trailed behind Hong in the most recent Marquette Law School poll in July.
Crowley has raised more than $775,000 -- more than double what Hong posted during the same period in July, according to a pre-primary campaign finance report.
Knower told ABC News she fears Evers' backing of Crowley might produce the opposite intended effect and boost Hong's prospects as the nominee in what would be a gift to the GOP.
In recent national media appearances, Hong has reversed some past positions she took on social media, including calls to abolish the U.S. Senate and defund the police.
Those previous statements, argued Knower, are "so, so extreme that it'll be easy for [Republicans] to run against her."

In a CNN interview last week, asked if she still wants to "cancel Thanksgiving," something she wrote in a since-deleted post from 2020, Hong said, "Thanksgiving is also a time that's incredibly painful for many people in our communities."
She added: "I think there I wanted to make sure that people understood that there are multiple views, but views can evolve."

While she clarified in an interview with Politico that Thanksgiving is her "favorite holiday," her opponents pounced on the comments. Tiffany said socialists like Hong "want to destroy the traditions and culture that unite us. They want to tear America apart."
Evers criticized Hong over it, saying that her "entire campaign" has been dealing with her past social media posts -- prompting Hong to push back.

"We have the most developed platform with detailed plans on over 100 different policy points and she would love to talk about them whenever people are done asking about 7-year-old tweets," Hong's campaign said in a statement.

In a hypothetical matchup with Tiffany, a Hong victory would indicate that democratic socialism can prevail in a purple state while a loss would greatly hurt their progress, according to Anthony Chergosky, a professor at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse.

"If Hong were to lose, it would be a clear opportunity for the center-left faction of the Democratic Party to try to regain control of the party and to go into 2028 aiming to discredit the electoral viability of democratic socialism," he said.
Either way, Chergosky added: "the recriminations would be epic."
In battle for control of Congress, two competitive U.S. House races
While Tiffany has cast the gubernatorial election as a choice between "chaos" and "common sense," some Republicans have leaned into that messaging in the state's congressional races.
With Tiffany's bid for governor, the congressman's seat in the state's ruby-red 7th Congressional District is up for grabs.

Michael Alfonso, 26, is one of five GOP candidates running for the nomination. He is the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who held the seat for eight years before stepping down in 2019. Alfonso won a coveted endorsement from Trump, but has faced some criticism from Republicans over his age and what they say is a lack of experience.
Alfonso said in a recent televised debate that he is still working as an accountant for his local parish in Hayward, Wisconsin.
Alfonso, like other Republicans across the state, has said socialism is "infecting America's youth."
On the Democratic side, former state Rep. Fred Clark, business owner Chris Armstrong and attorney Ginger Murray are running for the nomination.
And as Democrats hope to retake the House majority, they are looking to unseat Republicans in Wisconsin's 1st and 3rd Congressional Districts.

Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse, is widely considered the front-runner in a three-way Democratic primary in the 1st District. He is largely campaigning on access to healthcare in his bid against GOP incumbent Rep. Bryan Steil.

In the western and central parts of the state, Democrat Rebecca Cooke is mounting a third bid to unseat Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a U.S. Navy SEAL veteran in the highly competitive 3rd District.

Cooke nearly ousted Van Orden in the 2024 general election, but lost by a nearly 3-point margin. In June, Trump stumped for Van Orden and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visited a farm with him.

But anti-establishment fervor has also seeped into the Democratic primary. Cooke, backed by the campaign arm of the House Democrats, is fending off a challenge from progressive Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire City Council president.

"I think we have seen local elements of the party become emboldened to push back against the national party institutions because the national party has become so dysfunctional and unpopular," Chergosky said of Democrats.

title: A year into Trump’s unprecedented deployment, National Guard is entrenched in DC
summary: The deployment, dubbed “Make DC Safe and Beautiful,” quickly has expanded to include some 4,000 troops from states and territories across the country.
story: The deployment is expected to cost $1.4 billion through the end of Trump's term.

On Aug. 3 last year, the assault and attempted carjacking of Edward Coristine, a 20-year-old programmer known online as “Big Balls” who had worked for Elon Musk’s now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, became a flashpoint for President Donald Trump’s argument that Washington, D.C., had spiraled out of control.

Eight days later, Trump mobilized roughly 800 National Guard troops to the capital, an extraordinary use of military personnel on U.S. soil. He cast the deployment in dire terms, describing a city overwhelmed by violence and disorder and promising that federal intervention would restore control, even as violent crime in Washington had fallen to its lowest level in 30 years, according to the Department of Justice.

The deployment, dubbed “Make DC Safe and Beautiful,” quickly expanded. Some 4,000 troops from states and territories across the country are now deployed to the capital, down from a summer surge for America's 250th anniversary that pushed the force to roughly 5,000. That number is expected to decline further in the coming weeks, with the mission typically hovering between 2,500 and 3,000 troops.
But even as the force shrinks from its summer peak, the deployment is expected to remain a fixture in D.C. through the remainder of Trump’s term, ABC News was first to report.

The mission is unprecedented in its scale and duration. The deployment is projected to cost an additional $1.4 billion, a staggering price tag even as its effectiveness remains murky. Two soldiers were also killed in an attack near the White House last year. Meanwhile, the Guard is juggling competing demands, with thousands of troops deployed to the Middle East amid the war with Iran and others serving on missions around the world.

The sustained presence represents a sharp departure from how presidents have historically used military forces at home. Domestic deployments have generally been reserved for relatively brief moments of extraordinary unrest, major security threats or natural disasters.

In 1794, President George Washington led a force of roughly 13,000 militiamen from Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey and Pennsylvania to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion. More recently, roughly 20,000 National Guard troops poured into Washington, D.C., following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, when a mob sought to keep Trump in power after his 2020 election loss.

The Guard is also routinely called up for natural disasters and major public events, largely because it can quickly provide thousands of personnel for basic but labor-intensive tasks such as clearing debris after a hurricane, distributing food and water or helping manage crowds and traffic.

Washington was initially only one piece of a broader push by the administration to deploy troops to American cities. Forces were also sent to Los Angeles and Chicago, though those missions became tied up in legal challenges and troops were eventually withdrawn. The president has substantially broader authority in Washington, D.C., where the National Guard operates under a unique legal framework and ultimately answers to the president.

But the Guard is principally built and trained to fight wars abroad. Today, some 15,000 guardsmen are deployed overseas, according to service data, including thousands in the Middle East amid the ongoing war with Iran. Guard units are also serving across Africa and regularly participate in major exercises in the Pacific aimed at preparing for a potential conflict with China.
At the same time, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic, governors and presidents have increasingly turned to the Guard for missions at home.

Brig. Gen. Leland Blanchard II, the interim commander of the D.C. National Guard, told reporters that units deployed to D.C. continue to carve out time for military training, including marksmanship and medical care, and in some cases may train more frequently than they otherwise would. Some of that training, he said, can also complement the skills troops use on the mission.

In Washington, the National Guard has settled into what is becoming a lengthy deployment, even as the troops carrying out the mission rotate with relative regularity. Much of their time is spent patrolling tourist corridors and downtown transit hubs, areas where crime is generally low. Blanchard says putting guardsmen in those relatively safe areas allows local police to concentrate more officers in parts of the city where crime is higher.

But sustaining that rotation has presented its own challenges. The Guard at times has struggled to find fresh units for the mission, according to people familiar with the situation, in part because Democratic-led states have been reluctant to participate in a deployment strictly associated with the Trump administration.

That effectively takes a large portion of the National Guard off the table, narrowing the pool of available units at a time when the force is also balancing deployments and other commitments overseas. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer threatened to pull her troops from D.C. who were there supporting July 4th events in the city if they were used for Trump’s broader security mission, though in practice, detangling the two is virtually impossible.

Blanchard told reporters that guardsmen have responded to some 800 medical emergencies, including administering Narcan 325 times as well as ancillary things like reuniting lost children with their parents, but the administration has not provided a clear accounting of whether those services could still have been done with civil workers or police officers.

“If you actually want to improve public safety in the District of Columbia, give the District of Columbia Police Department $100 million to go hire competent, qualified, appropriately trained police,” Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, said.
“Don't drag these poor men and women from around the country who have no idea what they're doing in D.C. and, most of them, are not trained for policing anyway, to stand here and wander around.”

An analysis from the Niskanen Center estimated the government spends roughly $607 per Guardsman each day, compared with about $384 for a D.C. police officer. The group found no reduction in violent crime attributable to the Guard deployment, though its presence coincided with a decline in property crime.
Guard units have slowly begun expanding into less visible parts of the capital where crime is more prevalent, a shift that could accelerate as the deployment enters its second year.
“We want to get after that and continue to expand the mission,” Blanchard told ABC News.

The Pentagon is also making increasingly long-term arrangements for the troops. The Trump administration recently signed a $292 million contract to move Guard members into apartments around the region, replacing the costly hotels where troops have been housed at government expense. Blanchard said the move is expected to save roughly $90 million through 2029.

But keeping the Guard in Washington, D.C., through the remainder of Trump’s term will still come with a hefty price tag. The deployment is projected to cost an additional $1.4 billion through 2029, according to Pentagon information provided to Congress and reviewed by ABC News.

The figure serves as the first public accounting from the administration on the mission’s cost, but it's unclear what the mission has cost up to this point. Previously, the Congressional Budget Office estimated its deployment in D.C. costs about $55 million per month, accounting for just under 3,000 troops.

The troops sent to D.C. have overwhelmingly come from Republican-led states. Just under 700 members of the D.C. National Guard are currently serving on the mission, according to Guard data, leaving most of the force to be supplied by governors elsewhere.

South Carolina has kept troops in the capital for virtually the entire year and currently has nearly 500 there. Georgia has roughly 800 Guardsmen deployed and Florida nearly 400. Louisiana, West Virginia and Mississippi are among the other Republican-led states that have maintained a sustained presence.

“South Carolina has a long history of answering the call when our country needs our National Guard,” South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, a Republican, said in a statement to ABC News. “They represent our state with professionalism and dedication, and we know they will continue to do so wherever they are called to serve.”
From the beginning, Army leaders were acutely aware that the political stakes of the deployment extended well beyond what troops were actually being asked to do.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll was on vacation when the mission began and hurried back to Washington as troops mobilized. Officials familiar with the discussions said optics quickly became a major concern. Commanders understood that virtually any encounter involving a guardsman could be filmed and turned into a national controversy, potentially damaging an institution that continues to enjoy broad public confidence.

In 1970, Ohio National Guard members of the 1st Battalion, 145th Infantry Regiment, and 2nd Squadron, 107th Cavalry Regiment, opened fire into a crowd at Kent State University, killing four unarmed students and wounding nine others during protests against President Richard Nixon’s expansion of the Vietnam War into Cambodia.

The killings became an enduring cautionary tale about putting troops in direct contact with Americans exercising their right to protest and further inflamed antiwar sentiment at a time when the military was already struggling to attract its next generation of officers. Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC) enrollment plunged in the early 1970s, leaving the Pentagon with far fewer prospective officers than it needed.

But officials explained they did not need to imagine another Kent State to understand the risks in Washington. Driscoll and others involved in the mission worried that something far less dramatic could derail it, such as an accidental weapon discharge, an isolated confrontation with a protester or a guardsman caught on camera behaving poorly. Until the U.S. and Israel launched the war with Iran in February, the Guard’s presence in D.C. was the Pentagon’s highest-profile mission.

For most of the past year, those fears have not materialized. The mission’s most serious episode instead came in November, when two West Virginia National Guard members were shot just blocks from the White House.
Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom, 20, died from her injuries. U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe, 24, was critically wounded and is still recovering, according to his family.
Rahmanullah Lakanwal, a 30-year-old Afghan national accused in the attack, has pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department said in June that it was determining whether to seek the death penalty.

title: Netanyahu rejects Board of Peace 15-point peace plan until Hamas 'truly disarmed'
summary: Netanyahu made the remarks at a Cabinet meeting Sunday.
story: Netanyahu made the remarks at a Cabinet meeting Sunday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Israel would reject the 15-point proposal for peace in Gaza put forward by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at the start of a cabinet meeting on Sunday, speaking in Hebrew. "The IDF will not make any withdrawal until Hamas is truly disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens."
Trump in July announced an agreement for Hamas to disarm and for the Israel Defense Forces to withdraw from the Gaza Strip as part of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire signed last year.

"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people," Trump said in a social media post on July 30, referencing the newly formed multinational organization established by the U.S. president to oversee the 20-point peace plan in Gaza, announced in September.
"At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks," Trump added.

Trump's 20-point plan led to a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, as well as the exchange of Israeli hostages and Palestinian detainees. The plan also calls for Hamas to surrender its weapons and dismantle its military infrastructure, including a vast tunnel network, and relinquish power to a new technocratic Palestinian government in return for an Israeli troop withdrawal, humanitarian aid for Gaza's population, and an international effort to rebuild the war-ravaged Palestinian territory.

Hamas said in a statement Sunday after Netanyahu's remarks that it "affirms its commitment" to Trump's 15-point plan for the second phase of the ceasefire agreement with Israel in the Gaza Strip "and establishing a clear timetable for their implementation."

"We call upon the mediators, guarantors, and the Peace Council to assume their responsibilities, ensure the commitment of all parties to what has been agreed upon, and prevent any violations or breaches that could disrupt the implementation process or undermine the ceasefire agreement," the Hamas statement continued, in part.
Hamas will "continue to engage positively and responsibly with efforts aimed at completing the implementation of the agreement," the statement further said.
Earlier in July, Hamas announced it had dissolved its government in the strip to make way for the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza as part of phase two of the plan.

"Regarding the Gaza Strip: First of all, I want to clarify the main thing. As long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria," Netanyahu further said Sunday.

"The IDF will not make any withdrawal until Hamas disarms. And when I say disarming Hamas, I mean the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu said.

While Netanyahu called Trump "our greatest friend in the White House" and said he "greatly appreciate[s]" him, the prime minister added, "now we are talking to the Americans about this issue. They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us."

"Contrary to all those who preach to us, we do what needs to be done for the security of Israel and we can and know how to stand our ground even against our best friends when necessary," Netanyahu added.
"The existence of Israel and the security of all Israeli citizens is non-negotiable. We stand firm on these interests," Netanyahu said Sunday.
ABC News' Diaa Ostaz contributed to this report.

title: Ocasio-Cortez says Democrats are 'unifying,' focused on 'working people'
summary: Instead of divisions, Dems should focus on "our plan to improve people's lives."
story: Instead of divisions, Dems should focus on "our plan to improve people's lives."

In the wake of progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed's victory over centrist Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Senate primary on Tuesday, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said the party is experiencing "a time of renewal" and is "unifying" and focused on winning in November.

"We understand that our priority is the working class of this country, and we have to make the case that we're here to make people's lives better," Ocasio-Cortez told ABC News' "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl. "The Republican Party right now is jacking up prices, making housing impossible to afford, and we are focused on everything from healthcare to your grocery bill and making it more affordable for, for working people."
Ocasio-Cortez endorsed El-Sayed in July, campaigned with him in the state and appeared with him in ads.

El-Sayed survived millions in super PAC spending aimed at branding him too extreme for a race that could determine who controls the Senate in the next Congress, ultimately winning with less than 50% of the vote. His opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, had the backing of the Democratic establishment, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and retiring Sen. Gary Peters -- both of whom have since coalesced around El-Sayed.

Some moderate Democrats have raised alarms over democratic socialist candidates ousting longtime incumbents in solidly blue districts from New York to Colorado. After the New York primary, centrist Democrats led by Reps. Tom Suozzi and Adam Gray signed a letter declaring, "We are capitalist, not socialist." Democratic group Third Way pledged $15 million to counter democratic socialism ahead of the 2028 elections, calling it a "mortal danger."
Ocasio-Cortez responded: "I don't think that we should be worried about what somebody somewhere believes. I think we should be focused on what our plan to improve people's lives are."

Asked whether Twitch streamer Hasan Piker -- who endorsed and campaigned for El-Sayed but has faced backlash over controversial comments -- should have a continued role in the progressive movement, Ocasio-Cortez pushed back on the premise, calling it part of a broader tactical debate among party consultants.
She argued Democrats can't afford to be selective about which platforms they engage with if they want to win back young voters, a demographic she said the party lost last election.

"Much hay was made about the fact that we lost young men in the last election, and many of the same consultants that are wringing their hands today were the same ones talking about how we need to go on Joe Rogan and we need to be not, not so, you know, willing to engage in cancel culture," she said.
She also pointed to there being a "generational tidal wave" of younger voters taking part in elections.

"Millennials are not punk kids anymore," Ocasio-Cortez said. "We're grown adults with mortgages and kids, and that generation is starting to be decisive at the polls, and there is anger at being ignored, sidelined, having our economic futures mortgaged by the generations that came before us on everything from the economy to climate, and we're taking the reins."

Ocasio-Cortez has endorsed sparingly compared to other lawmakers on the left, though nearly all her picks have won their primaries. Notably, she hasn't endorsed insurgent House candidates challenging Democratic incumbents.

Responding to progressives who have called her strategy too cautious, she noted the contrast with 2018 when she unseated an incumbent without institutional support: "I wasn't endorsed by anybody when I was running ... I don't think I was endorsed by a single elected official when I was running for office."

She added that "politics is a workplace" on why she in part has not endorsed in races against fellow members of the House, while noting that she endorsed challengers to incumbents in the New York State Assembly.
"I don't work in state government, which gives me a greater freedom to be able to do that."

Pressed on past statements from figures like Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate and democratic socialist Francesca Hong, who previously called to abolish prisons and police, Ocasio-Cortez said she hasn't endorsed in that race and that "all politics are local,” but noted Hong has since clarified some of her positions.
Ocasio-Cortez also invoked New York City Council Member Chi Ossé's framing: "'Woke 1 was crazy,'" in reference to policy positions taken in the past by members of the left.
Asked whether the left went too far after 2020, she called the pandemic a distinct period but said those debates were "fruitful."

"The doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place," she said. "Of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today, and I'm grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they're campaigning on in this moment."
Ocasio-Cortez, a member of the New York City Democratic Socialists of America chapter, was asked to distinguish socialism from communism.

"One prevailing one is democracy, and I believe that democratic socialists are fundamentally pro-democracy, and we believe in the ballot box. We believe in respecting the outcomes of elections and governing democratically."

Confronted with parts of the national DSA platform -- including defunding the Department of Defense, abolishing police and prisons and abolishing the Senate -- she said "no" when asked if she aligns with those positions.

"I think that people are less interested in these academic debates, and they're more interested in how we're going to bring their bills down and make sure that they can afford to see a doctor," she said.
Asked about a New Hampshire poll showing her as Democrats' leading choice and whether she'd run for president, Ocasio-Cortez didn't rule it out.
"I haven't ruled out the possibility, and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there." She said her focus remains on the midterms, not "our individual aspirations or plans."
Asked whether a Senate run against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was also on the table, she gave a similarly open-ended answer: "I think that anything is possible at this juncture."

title: El-Sayed spoke with Obama as Michigan Democrats look to unite
summary: El-Sayed says he hopes the former president will campaign with him.
story: El-Sayed says he hopes the former president will campaign with him.

BRIDGEWATER, N.J. -- BRIDGEWATER, N.J. (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, said Sunday he has spoken with Barack Obama and hopes the former president campaigns with him as the party tries to unite after a bitter primary that exposed deep rifts between its progressive and moderate wings.
El-Sayed said his Friday conversation with Obama was “really warm and inspiring." The candidate did not provide details.
“I was grateful for his advice. It was very warm, very inviting, and I know that he knows the critical role that Michigan is going to play,” El-Sayed told NBC’s “Meet the Press."

Asked if he would like to see Obama come to Michigan to drum up support for Democrats before the midterm elections in November, El-Sayed said he “really” hoped so and that Obama “knows a lot about winning Michigan” after carrying the state in the 2008 and 2012 presidential races.
An Obama spokesperson confirmed the call.

The discussion came the same day that a group of Michigan nominees and other notable national Democrats tried to present a united front at a rally in Detroit. The crowd cheered loudest for El-Sayed, a former public health official who last week narrowly beat establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a contentious and closely watched primary. A Democratic victory in the fall is crucial to the party's chances of regaining a Senate majority.
Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is not seeking reelection in the perennial swing state, which Republican Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden carried in 2020.

El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost the Senate race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in 2024 and has tried to capitalize on lingering tensions within the Democratic Party.
Rogers has released a video message attempting to appeal to Democrats who feel their party may be moving too far to the left with El-Sayed. “You have a home with us," Rogers says in the video.

During an interview Sunday with CNN's “State of the Union,” El-Sayed acknowledged that "we aired our differences” in the heated primary. But he said the internal divisions are "so much smaller than the similarities that we share.”
“You’re seeing folks come together,” El-Sayed said, before adding of moderate Democrats, “We might see the world differently. But we also recognize the responsibility to come together.”

title: Former Trump Defense Secretary Esper calls Iran's demands 'ridiculous'
summary: Former Trump Defense Secretary Esper calls Iran's criteria for reopening the Strait of Hormuz "ridiculous" and will prevent the negotiation process from moving forward.
story: Esper said the U.S. should reject Iran's terms "out of hand."

Former Secretary of Defense Mark Esper on Sunday called the latest Iranian criteria for reopening the Strait of Hormuz a "ridiculous" set of demands that will prevent the negotiation process from moving forward.

"They've put forward demands of the United States, which, frankly, are ridiculous and should be rejected out of hand, Esper, who served as secretary of Defense during President Donald Trump's first term, told ABC News' "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl. "Demands such as the withdrawal of all U.S. forces from the region, reimbursement for the costs of the war, the fact that we would end our blockade, we would end sanctions. So it's gone beyond the pale."

Esper said the new set of requirements Iran has outlined to reopen the critical waterway and allow the resumption to prewar levels of shipping shows that Iranian leadership is confident in their negotiating position and the leverage they hold by controlling the strait.
"It shows that they believe that they have the upper hand, they believe they are winning, and they are already. So that's what we're up against right now," Esper said.

"These demands they've now raised last night show that they are emboldened, that they feel confident about their position in the world, and at the same time they are flexing their muscles by using their proxies."
Esper also commented on the severity of the U.S. shortage of some munitions amid the ongoing war in Iran and the administration's efforts to ramp up production to reduce the impact of the shortage.

"The administration is trying hard in multiple ways," Esper said, "but when you're talking about taking two years to build a Patriot missile, whatever we do now is not going to help in the short term, but nonetheless needs to be done for strategic reasons."

A U.S. official, who would not discuss numerical estimates, told ABC News last week that the U.S. stockpiles of ballistic missile interceptors "are extremely low." Those reduced stockpiles are one constraint as Trump has weighed different military options in the conflict.
Trump on Thursday acknowledged that "we need more all the time" but "we have certain types of munitions that are very powerful [of which] we have unlimited, virtually unlimited supply."
"We have others where it's a little bit tighter, and we're getting them in on a daily basis," the president said.
It was unclear which munitions Trump was referring to.
Esper said the problem goes back decades and was exacerbated by Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden.

"It is a serious situation that goes back to the end of the Cold War and the decisions we made between then, and then with the onset of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars," Esper said, "and frankly, it accelerated during the Biden administration when we were expending munitions or giving munitions to Ukraine."

title: Deadline passes for embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller to drop off ballot
summary: The deadline has officially passed for embattled Republican Max Miller to drop off the ballot for reelection in Ohio's 7th Congressional District.
story: Miller has denied domestic abuse allegations against him.

The deadline officially passed Monday afternoon for embattled Republican Max Miller to drop off the ballot for reelection in Ohio's 7th Congressional District, and he will remain in the race, according to a spokesperson for the Ohio Secretary of State's office.

"Congressman Miller has represented Ohio’s 7th District for two successful terms, and he will fight for the opportunity to continue representing them in the next Congress," Abigail Angelos, a spokeswoman for Miller, said in a statement on his decision to stay in the race.
"He is invested in every way possible and intends to move forward with the work he started back in 2023," Angelos said.

Miller has faced numerous calls to step down and drop his reelection bid amid allegations of domestic abuse made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller has denied the allegations.
Last week, President Donald Trump called Miller and raised concerns about his reelection bid, sources told ABC News.

In an interview with CNN the next day, Miller said Trump told him, "'Maxie, it's going to be a tough race,' and, 'I don't know if you're going to be able to pull this one out.'" But the congressman remained defiant, telling the network: "I am never going to give up."
Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, in an interview on NewsNation on Sunday, indicated Miller would continue to receive the backing of the national party.
"We're going to support our nominees," Gruters said.
Miller's Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter, commented on his decision to remain in the race in a statement to ABC News.

"As I've said before, if the accusations against Max Miller are proven true, he should be in prison, not in Congress," Poindexter said. "It's unfortunate that Miller has chosen to keep putting his ex-wife and her family through this nightmare in the public spotlight. But let me be perfectly clear. I got into this campaign to fight for my neighbors and for working people across this district. That continues to be my north star."

"Our campaign's doors are wide open to anyone -- Democrat, Republican, or anything in between -- who believes their representative should serve with honor and work for Ohioans, not for special interests and not for themselves," Poindexter said. "In November, we will win this race, and the people of the 7th District will finally have a representative who fights for them."

Police reports obtained by ABC News show that Emily Moreno alleged multiple incidents of physical violence during their marriage and divorce proceedings. The police reports obtained by ABC News also shows Emily Moreno told the police that her daughter received physical injuries while in Miller's care. Miller denies abusing his wife or daughter. He was never charged with a crime and the Department of Children and Family Services did not find evidence to substantiate allegations of child abuse, according to records released in court filings.

title: Tiffany Haddish avoids additional jail time after pleading guilty in Georgia traffic case
summary: Actor and comedian Tiffany Haddish has pleaded guilty to a charge stemming from a 2022 traffic arrest in Georgia
story: Actor and comedian Tiffany Haddish has pleaded guilty to a charge stemming from a 2022 traffic arrest in Georgia

FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. -- Actor and comedian Tiffany Haddish avoided additional jail time Tuesday when she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor alcohol-related driving charge that stemmed from her 2022 arrest in Georgia after someone called 911 about a driver asleep at the wheel at a traffic light.

Other charges were dropped. After entering the plea by video, Haddish was placed on 12 months' probation and told to avoid drugs and alcohol and complete a substance abuse evaluation. She was credited for the brief time she spent in jail following her arrest.

Haddish’s films include the comedy “Girls Trip,” “Night School,” “Like a Boss” and “The Kitchen.” She wrote the New York Times best seller “The Last Black Unicorn,” which earned a Grammy nomination. In 2018, Haddish won an Emmy for her appearance on “Saturday Night Live” and a Grammy in 2021 for her special “Black Mitzvah.”

At around 2:30 a.m. on Jan. 14, 2022, someone called 911 to report seeing a person who appeared to be asleep in the driver's seat of a white Ford Explorer with their foot on the brake in Peachtree City, about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Atlanta, according to a court filing. An officer spotted an SUV that matched the description given by the caller and stopped Haddish as she pulled into a neighborhood, according to a police report.

Haddish's lawyers in May asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing that waiting more than four years for the case to be resolved had caused personal and professional difficulties and violated her right to a speedy trial. Fayette County State Court Judge Jason Thompson rejected her arguments.

The judge found that Haddish and her attorneys had requested some of the delays, including a request for a delay so she could attend a fashion show in Morocco and a request to leave a hearing early to catch a flight. He wrote that she also did not show any evidence of having missed specific performing opportunities or of actual financial harm because of the delay.

Haddish also was arrested in November 2023 in Beverly Hills, California, on suspicion of driving under the influence after police received a call and said Haddish appeared to be slumped over the wheel of a vehicle while the engine was still running.

Haddish reached a plea deal with prosecutors in that case in February 2024, pleading no contest to a vehicle code violation, and the two misdemeanor DUI charges against her were dropped, according to the Los Angeles Times.

title: Britain's Andy Green sets another speed record, this time for fastest run in a hydrogen-powered car
summary: The only person to break the sound barrier in a car has earned another world record, this time in a show of force for hydrogen power
story: The only person to break the sound barrier in a car has earned another world record, this time in a show of force for hydrogen power
WENDOVER, Utah -- The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.

British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph (653.908 kph) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.

The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 32-foot (9.75-meter) car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.

To be clear, Tuesday’s feat didn’t come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and drove it to an outright record of 763.035 mph (1,227.985 kph), breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.

In 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car — 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) — at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future.”

In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 185.5 mph (298.5 kph). He had a 10-mile (16-kilometer) straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.

A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.

Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrier.
Green did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power will shake up the clean-energy industry.
The company's chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.

Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.

title: Flights grounded in Chicago, power knocked out as severe weather pounds Illinois, Indiana
summary: Severe weather has cut power in the Chicago area and northwestern Indiana
story: Severe weather has cut power in the Chicago area and northwestern Indiana
CHICAGO -- Severe weather cut power Tuesday in the Chicago area and northwestern Indiana as perilous storms pummeled the region, darkening the sky and carrying extreme wind gusts across state lines.

Tornado warning sirens blared in Illinois and Indiana, and all flights were stopped by late morning at Chicago's two major airports. There were numerous reports of wind gusts of 80 mph (128 kph) or more at personal weather stations, with trees blown down.
“These are dangerous storms!” the National Weather Service said by late morning.
More than 575,000 customers lost electricity in Illinois and Indiana, according to poweroutage.us. Lake County, Indiana, was especially hit hard.

title: Over 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war in Ukraine are still held, UN estimates
summary: The United Nations estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during its war in Ukraine are still being held
story: The United Nations estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during its war in Ukraine are still being held

UNITED NATIONS -- The United Nations estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during its war in Ukraine are still being “deprived of their liberty,” many held incommunicado and on grounds that don't comply with international law.

“Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment" of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the U.N. assistant secretary-general for human rights.

She spoke at an informal meeting of the U.N. Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022. The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine have escalated attacks in the four-year conflict.

Since the invasion, Julio said, U.N. human rights staff have interviewed 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees following their release. The U.N. has not been able to visit detention facilities in Russia, and its estimated figure of those held does not break down how many are adults or children.

More than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said. They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services.

The Geneva-based human rights office “has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity, and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention,” Julio said.

The U.N. Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a “political prisoner” of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds that held out for months at the Azovstal steel plant in the besieged city of Mariupol before turning themselves over to the Russians in May 2022.

Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council.

He said he was tortured, beaten harder and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States.
“Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army,” said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military.
He said the Russians tried to break the prisoners mentally and force them to confess to falsified crimes through tortures including freezing, beatings, electrocution and sexual abuse, he said.

“Two of my friends were beaten to death in detention centers in the Donetsk region,” Garsiya said. “Two of my friends died because of the conditions they were put in in Russian prisons and were returned in plastic bags to the homeland.”
For Umerova, her captivity began when she tried to enter Russia from Georgia to visit her seriously ill father in Crimea, which is part of Ukraine but has been occupied by Russia since 2014.

She said she was placed in detention on “fabricated charges.” But unlike many others, she was able to contact an attorney. In the third month, she said, her attorney obtained her release through a court order.

“But as soon as the prison gates opened, a bag was put over my head and I was taken away again.” In six months, she said she was moved to seven different facilities, calling it “a carousel of repression.”

What happened to her, Umerova said, is part of a system Russia uses to unlawfully detain, isolate, torture and fabricate charges against civilians. She named half a dozen women in Russian prisons today and said at least 84 women have faced criminal prosecution.

U.N. human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general.

About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said. But U.N. monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, “the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022.”

Russia’s deputy U.N. Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced “torture and degradation, and moral and physical abuse.”

She called the Security Council meeting part of “a disinformation campaign against Russia,” funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, "is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians.”

Ukraine’s deputy U.N. Ambassador Volodymyr Pavlichenko said he was struck that during Monday’s meeting, Russia was not ready to discuss the return of POWs — “including their POWs” — and all civilian detainees including abducted children.

title: Former US Marine held in Russia for more than 4 years has been released, his advocates say
summary: A former U.S. Marine from Massachusetts who has been held in Russia for more than four years on disputed charges has been released
story: A former U.S. Marine from Massachusetts who has been held in Russia for more than four years on disputed charges has been released

WASHINGTON -- Russia has released an American military veteran who spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges under abusive conditions and was said to be gravely ill and at risk of dying, a group advocating for him said Tuesday. Robert Gilman was on his way to a U.S. military hospital in Texas, where he will be medically and psychologically assessed and treated, said Eric ‌Lebson, chief strategy officer of Global Reach, a group that’s been working to free him and other American detainees abroad. Gilman’s family has flown to Texas to be with him, including his mother, who was in Russia attempting to see him at the hospital. Gilman, a 32-year-old teacher detained since 2022, was initially handed a 3 1/2-year sentence in 2022 when he was convicted of beating a police officer after being taken off a train for causing a disturbance. He later was convicted of attacking a prison inspector during a cell check, beating an investigator and assaulting a guard, and he was sentenced in October 2024 to eight years and one month. His sentence was extended last year to 10 years after he was found guilty of assaulting prison guards. Before he was flown out of Russia, he had been in “a dissociative stupor” for 47 days due to the abuse he has suffered in prison, Lebson said. Gilman had been moved from a prison to a civilian hospital, where he was hooked up to a feeding tube and handcuffed to a bed.

Hospital reports conveyed Gilman’s condition “as dire and life-threatening,” pushing the U.S. government into action and leading to “a unilateral humanitarian release” by Russian officials, Lebson said. U.S. Sen. Edward Markey had called on Russia and the U.S. to work together to get the Massachusetts resident released. Gilman was among at least eight Americans who remained in Russian custody after a series of high-profile prisoner exchanges with the U.S. in recent years..

title: Groups sue Trump administration over targeting of the International Criminal Court
summary: Human Rights Watch and three other advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration to challenge its campaign against the International Criminal Court
story: Human Rights Watch and three other advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration to challenge its campaign against the International Criminal Court

UNITED NATIONS -- Human Rights Watch and three other advocacy groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday to challenge its campaign against the International Criminal Court, arguing that sanctions against ICC judges and prosecutors are undermining the ability to prosecute people responsible for humanity’s worst crimes.

The complaint — filed in the Southern District of New York — says that President Donald Trump's executive order last year targeting the Hague-based criminal court and the U.S. sanctions issued against a U.N. human rights expert and three Palestinian rights groups represent a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice and should be struck down," according to a press release.

The lawsuit is the latest example of organizations pushing back on what they call the Trump administration’s efforts to undermine international law and prevent efforts to combat impunity by governments around the world.

“The fact that so many leading human rights and humanitarian organizations have come together to challenge Trump’s unlawful executive order demonstrates the widespread harm it is causing across civil society groups dedicated to bringing those responsible for grave crimes to justice,” said Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP, the lead counsel representing the plaintiffs.

The groups assert that the financial and legal penalties against the ICC have forced them to “curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.”
Other organizations joining the lawsuit are the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights and the Open Society Institute.

Efforts to retain the global tribunal's power come as the ICC faces enormous pressure, both internally and from its more than 120 member states. Among those sanctioned by the U.S. last year was Karim Khan, who was the ICC’s chief prosecutor until he was removed from the post last month, nearly two years after sexual misconduct allegations against him first emerged, as detailed in stories by The Associated Press.

The Trump administration had issued those sanctions against Khan and a dozen other ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.
Since then, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced that the U.S. was launching a “sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty.”

In a video message last month, Rubio said the U.S. would pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Countries that “enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella” will be called upon to reject the court’s jurisdiction over U.S. citizens, he added.
Several countries, including U.S.-allied Venezuela, announced they would withdraw from the court shortly after Rubio's statements and Khan's removal.

title: FBI teams with the NCAA to help athletes avoid sexual exploitation
summary: The FBI is teaming with the NCAA to start a program to combat sexual exploitation of college athletes whose private images are increasingly found and targeted online in an era when they use their name, image and likeness to enhance their own marketability
story: The FBI is teaming with the NCAA to start a program to combat sexual exploitation of college athletes whose private images are increasingly found and targeted online in an era when they use their name, image and likeness to enhance their own marketability

INDIANAPOLIS -- The FBI is teaming with the NCAA to start a program to combat sexual exploitation of college athletes whose private images are increasingly found and targeted online in an era when they use their name, image and likeness to enhance their own marketability.

The FBI, which unveiled the collaboration Monday, said bad actors typically target athletes through phishing, and also by password and PIN targeting and by portraying themselves as social media customer service representatives with urgent requests to reset passwords.

“Athletes have large social media followings, expended further by NIL activities that not only increases the exposure for targeting, it increases the leverage vendors believe they hold to exposure them," said Shohini Sinha, assistant director of the FBI Victim Services Division. "There is a pressure to protect the clean image of their school, team and themselves.”

The FBI said hackers can steal images, then post or sell them, which can lead to sextortion, in which athletes can be harassed, stalked or even have the content that's stolen from them posted on their own social media pages.
Neither the NCAA nor the FBI had specific numbers of athletes who were victimized by sextortion plots. Their partnership will go toward educating athletes.

“If we can play even a small role in preventing these crimes or getting justice or appropriate support for the people impacted by them, we will do everything we can to help," NCAA Vice President of Enforcement Jon Duncan said.

title: Pentagon official asks Asian allies to invest more in defense to deter aggression
summary: A Pentagon official has urged Asian allies to invest more in their defense to deter regional aggression
story: A Pentagon official has urged Asian allies to invest more in their defense to deter regional aggression

MANILA, Philippines -- A Pentagon official on Monday asked allies in Asia to invest more in their defense and help deter aggression in the region and said the United States remains committed to do the same with “partners, not protectorates.”

Elbridge Colby, an undersecretary of defense, made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop in Southeast Asia, where he will also visit Indonesia, Thailand and Cambodia. He renewed Washington’s assurances that the U.S. is not backing away from Asia despite its current preoccupation with the Iran war and the Middle East.

“America is definitely not disengaging from Asia — to the contrary. Our vital national interests dictate our enduring presence here,” Colby told an audience that included foreign diplomats, generals, business executives and journalists.
“We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in, to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most,” the Pentagon’s top policy adviser said. “We see Asia as of paramount importance.”

Colby stayed away from the usual U.S. tirade against China's growing aggression in the region, including in the disputed South China Sea. Washington has often expressed alarm over Beijing’s increasingly hostile actions against Philippine coast guard and naval forces in recent years.

Washington has repeatedly warned that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines, its oldest treaty ally in Asia, if Filipino forces, ships or aircraft come under armed attack, including in the South China Sea.

China and the Philippines, along with Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan, have been locked in territorial standoffs in the disputed waters, a key global trade route, for decades. Beijing virtually claims the entire waterway and has rejected a 2016 ruling in an arbitration case initiated by the Philippines that invalidated its expansive claims.

Colby repeated a vow by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a speech at the Shangri-La defense conference in Singapore in May that the U.S. will build and sustain a strong defense in the Western Pacific "that ensures aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive and war deemed irrational.”
