title: Jessica Alba rocks animal-print bikini as she shares glimpse into summer with Danny Ramirez
summary: Jessica Alba's August Instagram carousel showcases a tiger-print bikini selfie, golf outings, family beach time, and moments with Danny Ramirez.
story: Fox News contributor Tammy Bruce joins Rachel Campos-Duffy to recap this week’s pop culture news on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’
Jessica Alba is packing plenty into the final stretch of summer.
The 45-year-old actress shared a series of photos highlighting how she has spent August so far, from bikini days and time with her family to golf outings and moments with boyfriend Danny Ramirez.
"August so far 🍒👙🌺💗," Alba captioned the Instagram carousel.
JESSICA ALBA STUNS IN RED CORSET AND LACE MINI DRESS AS SHE CELEBRATES HER 45TH BIRTHDAY
Jessica Alba showed off an animal-print bikini while sharing highlights from her summer on social media. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)
She opened the post with a close-up selfie in an animal-print string bikini, posing indoors with the ocean visible through the windows behind her.
Alba accessorized the tiger-striped two-piece with layered gold necklaces, hoop earrings and narrow burgundy sunglasses. Her hair was pulled back as she looked directly into the camera.
The "Fantastic Four" actress also traded her swimwear for the golf course during another outing.
Alba posed alongside a friend while the pair sat on the grass wearing coordinating black sleeveless golf dresses with white collars.
Jessica Alba hit the golf course with a friend while sharing highlights from her August activities. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)
She completed her look with a black baseball cap and sunglasses while flashing a peace sign at the camera. Her friend paired the matching style with a wide-brimmed straw hat and white sunglasses.
Family time also made its way into Alba’s summer recap.
In one playful beach photo, Alba’s eldest daughter, Honor, 18, stretched out on top of her mother as the pair relaxed on a board in the sand.

The Honest Company founder appeared to be wearing a patterned bikini while Honor wore a green-and-white striped string bikini and a baseball cap. The mother-daughter duo relaxed on the beach with lush greenery and towering cliffs in the background.
MOLLY SIMS FLAUNTS TONED ABS IN MISMATCHED BIKINI DURING PERFECT BEACH DAY WITH HER KIDS
Honor is Alba’s eldest child with her former husband, Cash Warren. The former couple also share daughter Haven and son Hayes.

Alba included another glimpse of her relationship with Ramirez, sharing a candid photo of the couple laughing together at an outdoor table. Alba wore her hair up with gold under-eye patches and a patterned cover-up, while Ramirez sported a black T-shirt and baseball cap as they held matching bowls.
Fresh fruit and a row of limes were spread across the table in front of them as the two smiled at each other.
Jessica Alba shared a candid moment with boyfriend Danny Ramirez as the couple enjoyed time together this summer. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)
Alba and Ramirez first sparked romance rumors in July 2025 before confirming their relationship later that year when they attended the Baby2Baby Gala together.
The couple have since become more public about their relationship, with Alba referring to Ramirez as "my love" in a birthday post and thanking him "for loving me through every chapter."
Last month, Alba shared multiple bikini photos from a vacation with Ramirez in Tuscany, where the two were photographed relaxing by the water, paddleboarding and spending time together on a boat.
Alba included another beach moment in the summer roundup.
In a video included in the post, Alba was seen from behind walking barefoot from the sand into the ocean in a white bikini as gentle waves rolled toward shore beneath an overcast sky.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Jessica Alba headed into the ocean in a white bikini while sharing a glimpse at her summer by the water. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)
The actress has previously spoken about how her understanding of love has changed over time.

"Over time, I’ve learned to embrace every version of how love can show up," Alba told Elle in May. "Love shows up in so many different ways, and it’s not always grand gestures. Sometimes it’s just holding space."
Alba said her perspective has moved beyond the picture-perfect version of romance often portrayed on screen.

title: Brad Pitt admits he began drinking again after years of sobriety
summary: Brad Pitt tells Esquire he got "back off the wagon" after seven years sober and describes the one period he says he understood suicide as relief.
story: Jon Voight spoke to Fox News Digital while promoting his film "Reagan," and weighed in on the family drama between his daughter Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt.
After seven years of sobriety, Brad Pitt started drinking again.
The startling confession came as Pitt reflected on his darkest moments, the lasting scars of grief and the complicated reality of struggling despite having "won the lottery" in life.
"I was sober for seven years. And then I got back off the wagon," Pitt told Esquire for the September cover story.
COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH
Brad Pitt revealed he started drinking again after seven years of sobriety in a candid new interview. (Samir Hussein/WireImage))

The actor said he approached drinking differently after giving up his sobriety, describing his consumption as more limited than before. "In a more restrained manner," he clarified. "I got overconfident a couple times, went, ‘Yep, nope, not good for me. Not in big quantities.’"

Pitt’s candid admission came as he reflected on the harder chapters of his life and acknowledged that fame and success had not insulated him from struggle. The "F1" star has been dealing with "family stuff" since 2016, when he began the divorce process from his ex-wife, Angelina Jolie.
Pitt’s reflections took a darker turn as he recalled a period when the pain became nearly unbearable.

"I was never suicidal in any way. It just was not my makeup," he told the outlet. "In fact, if I have any afflictions, it’s probably being a congenital optimist. Which has helped many times, and it’s also gotten me – I’ve walked foolishly head-on into a Mack truck because of my optimism. Or, as my forever-funny friend David Fincher will say, 'Yeah, you see the glass as half full, but it’s half full of urine.' Anyway, I’ve never been suicidal except for one little period."
Brad Pitt reflected on sobriety, grief and the difficult years dealing with "family stuff." (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"And in that one little period, I just thought – I just couldn’t – just didn’t see a way out," Pitt continued. "The pain was so oppressive that – I wasn’t going to act on this, but I could feel – I could feel the cold steel of the bullet in my head, and it felt like relief. And I thought, Oh, okay, now I understand – I understand suicide, in the sense that it’s just relief. It’s just looking for relief from the pain. But I also think we have incredible survival instincts. And for me, that immediately kicked in, but it was just... "
The Oscar winner tempered his candid admission by acknowledging the extraordinary hand he had been dealt in life.
Brad Pitt said fame and success did not shield him from personal struggles. (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)
"Yeah. Like, listen: This s--t ain’t easy," he said. "And you’re talking to a guy who won the lottery."
Pitt also reflected on the lasting impact of grief, describing the pain it left behind alongside an unexpected sense of beauty.
"Grief, if you survive it, leaves a gaping hole, but it also leaves profound beauty," he said. "It’s an aching beauty, but it’s beauty."

Brad Pitt poses for the cover of Esquire magazine. (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)

Pitt first gained major attention with his memorable supporting turn in 1991’s "Thelma & Louise," before becoming a leading man in films including "A River Runs Through It," "Legends of the Fall" and "Se7en."
His signature films include "Fight Club," "Ocean’s Eleven," "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button," "Moneyball" and "Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood."
Brad Pitt smiling in a scene from the film 'Thelma & Louise', 1991. (Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer/Getty Images)

Pitt has also built an influential career behind the camera through his production company, Plan B Entertainment. As a producer, he won the best picture Oscar for "12 Years a Slave," adding to a résumé that extends well beyond acting.
Now in his 60s, Pitt looked back on the previous decade with a sense of urgency.
"God, I want my fifties back," he said. "I would do more. Your fifties are just – man, anything that’s on your mind, go. Go attack it. Go attack it now."

title: Ben Jones, 'Dukes of Hazzard' actor and former congressman, dead at 84
summary: Ben Jones, who played mechanic Cooter Davenport on "The Dukes of Hazzard," died from a heart attack at age 84, his wife announced.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
"The Dukes of Hazzard" star Ben Jones has died. He was 84.
The actor appeared as "good ol' boy" mechanic Cooter Davenport in the beloved series from 1979 to 1985.

Jones had a "massive heart attack" at his home Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media. The couple had been married since 1992.
Rappahannock County Sheriff Connie Compton also confirmed his death.
Ben Jones died at age 84 after a heart attack, according to his wife. (CBS via Getty Images)

Viator wrote on Facebook, "I lost the love of my life today. Ben passed from a massive heart attack. He was home resting in his favorite chair waiting for the Braves to come on and whoop the Yankees."
"Ben had the most amazing rich full life. He loved and was loved by so many. He will be missed. I love him so so much," she finished off her post.
Viator shared the news along with an image of Ben holding a dog.
Jones was born in Edgecombe County, North Carolina on August 30, 1941.
‘KNOTS LANDING’ STAR DONNA MILLS SAYS REFUSING TO POSE NUDE COST HER PLAYBOY COVER

Cast members from "The Dukes of Hazzard" pose for a group photo in Los Angeles on Jan. 1. Front row, from left: Rick Hurst, John Schneider, Catherine Bach, Tom Wopat and James Best, with basset hound Sandy. Back row, from left: Sorrell Booke, Denver Pyle and Ben Jones. (CBS via Getty Images)
He got his start on stage, before making his film debut in 1972 for "Together For Days" as Douglas. He also appeared in "Moonrunners" in 1975 as Fred and "The Lincoln Conspiracy" in 1977.
On the TV front, Jones made his television debut in 1976, playing a thief in an episode of "Movin’ On."
He also appeared in the 1977 series "Nashville 99," and "The Magical World of Disney" in 1978.
Jones landed the role of Cooter Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard" in the seventies.
‘DALLAS' STAR LINDA GRAY REVEALS THE BIZARRE WAY LARRY HAGMAN AVOIDED KISSING SCENES
Ben Jones played Cooter Davenport on "Dukes of Hazzard." (Rick Diamond/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
He played Davenport for more than 140 episodes from 1979 to 1985.
He reprised his role as Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!" in 1997 and "The Dukes of Hazzard: Hazzard in Hollywood" in 2000.
His final TV appearance was in "Surface" in 2005, and his final film he appeared in was the 2021 movie "Unbreakable."
In addition to his acting career, Jones also had a political career.
ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG

James Best as Rosco P. Coltrane, Rick Hurst as Deputy Cletus Hogg, Tom Wopat as Luke Duke, Catherine Bach as Daisy Duke, John Schneider as Bo Duke and Ben Jones as Cooter Davenport pose together in the made-for-television movie ‘The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!’ air date April 25, 1997. (CBS via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Jones served two terms in the House of Representatives.
He served as a U.S. House of Representatives member from Georgia’s fourth district from 1989 until 1993.
Jones’ "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star Tom Wopat shared a statement to Fox News Digital, and also shared it on his Instagram on Sunday.
The Dukes of Hazzard" cast members Tom Wopat with co-stars Catherine Bach and John Schneider in 1981. (CBS via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Wopat, who played Lucas K. "Luke" Duke, said: "’The Dukes of Hazzard’ lost another integral part of their cast today. Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed… Denver Pyle frequently said to Ben, ‘I’m not your Uncle Jesse!’ But I feel like we lost a Duke cousin today."

Whey Jennings, grandson of country music legend Waylon Jennings, is also grieving the loss of his dear friend and musical supporter. The two shared the stage on multiple occasions, but their bond extended well beyond performing together. Jones also helped finance Jennings’ first recorded live album, playing a meaningful role in the singer-songwriter’s career.
Whey Jennings (right), Waylon Jennings' grandson, is seen here with Ben Jones (center) and his wife Alma Viator. (Courtesy of Whey Jennings)

"Wow, this one hurts," Jennings told Fox News Digital. "I'll never forget all you have done for me, brother. It's been an honor to share the stage with you so many times. Thank you for believing in me. You have been a true friend when I needed one most, and I'm gonna miss you so much. I love you, Ben. Alma, I love you very much. Big hugs and prayers."
The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones previously told the Richmond Times-Dispatch in 2001.
"The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win," Jones said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Prince William was 'fuming' over request for Kate Middleton to spell her name differently: book
summary: King Charles III and Queen Camilla allegedly asked Kate Middleton to change her name spelling over royal crest concerns, leaving Prince William fuming.
story: Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," tells Fox News Digital that the Princess of Wales’ modern approach, family values and "soft power" make her a vital asset to the royal family and the UK.

Prince William was reportedly "fuming" after King Charles III and Queen Camilla suggested that Kate Middleton change the spelling of her first name when she joined the royal family, according to a new book.

"Charles and Camilla each had a royal monogram that consisted of interlocking C’s beneath a crown, and they expressed concern that a third royal cypher with a C was overkill," Christopher Andersen wrote in his biography "Kate! The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen." "Would Kate mind if she changed the spelling of her full name from ‘Catherine’ to ‘Katherine.’"

Andersen added, "Offended by yet another command from on high essentially aimed at placating Camilla, a fuming William replied on his wife’s behalf. The request was nothing less than ‘insulting,’ he told his father, not only to Kate but to her entire family."
KATE MIDDLETON IS 'INDISPENSABLE' TO ROYAL FAMILY AS SLIMMED-DOWN MONARCHY FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE: EXPERT
Prince William was "fuming" after then-Prince Charles asked if Kate Middleton would change her name from Catherine to Katherine, according to a new book. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they don't comment on books.

"The entire nature of Charles and Camilla's request — that Catherine was adding too many C's to the royal crests — shows just how much image and branding means to members of the royal family. The monarchy really is a giant game of one-upmanship," Andersen told Fox News Digital, adding that from the very beginning of their relationship "William has gone to war for Kate."
William’s top concern has always been for the Princess of Wales’ "safety," but he also came out "guns blazing" in her defense after topless photos of her sunbathing were published in France in 2012.

"He angrily ordered Palace lawyers to sue and even wanted to see those involved prosecuted criminally under French privacy laws," Andersen said. "When they started a family, it was William who made sure that Kate was not forced to take on too heavy a royal workload if it meant that she would have to spend too much time away from their children."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

But, he said the king and Camilla "expected her to go along because she has always been a nice, cooperative team player … but didn't take into account the fact that she personally prefers to be known as Catherine and feels very strongly about the name her parents gave her."
While most of the world knows her by her nickname, Kate, her real name is Catherine.
The princess is "genuinely fond" of Charles and assumed that he got the "absurd" idea from someone else, Andersen explained, adding that she didn’t hold any ill will toward him.
Prince William has "gone to war for Kate" since the beginning of their relationship, royal author Christopher Andersen said. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
"Besides, it wasn't long before they were having to deal with their simultaneous cancer diagnoses, which put everything else in stark perspective," he added.
KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
And although Middleton comes off as "kind and compassionate," she still has a "will of steel," he said.

"Kate is very secure about who she is and how she wants to be perceived by the outside world," Andersen said. "Changing her formal given name for such a bizarre, almost comical reason was a bridge too far."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard called the issue a "nonstarter" and a "lost cause," telling Fox News Digital that Charles and Camilla were thinking with a "business head" since she was known to the world as Kate anyway.
"Although a hopeless endeavour, I can see both sides of the coin," she admitted, explaining that William was not only offended for his wife but for his in-laws as well.
PRINCE WILLIAM REFUSES TO QUIT HOBBY THAT TERRIFIES KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERTS
King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Kate Middleton pose for a photograph at Buckingham Palace in 2023. (Getty Images)
But "the concerns were brushed aside. It wasn’t important enough to cause a fight. They had bigger fish to fry."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner called it a possible "volatile moment" between Camilla and the princess as she joined the family, "but nowadays, William was there to protect her. Since then, Kate has managed to stay one step behind when Charles and Camilla are around so as not to outstage them."
KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT
He noted, however, that more recently the 44-year-old is "building a stronger brand in her own right as William tries to take on the reins of Kingmanship."
"If true, it’s idiotic," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital of the story. "The idea is simply stupid. And why? Because her name began with C and theirs did!"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Andersen also felt the incident "speaks volumes about how conscious the royals are of all the bells and whistles — not just the gold coaches, the castles, and the crown jewels, but things as small as the letters in their crests and coats of arms. It may seem trivial to the rest of us, but to them things like this mean everything."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

"If you wish to attend the Cheap Trick / X show on Sept. 5, do nothing and your tickets will be valid. We look forward to seeing you," it added.
"If you wish to get a refund, please contact your point of purchase and we hope to see you at another show in the future."

Jett's concert in Louisville was scheduled to take place on the opening day of the four-day Bourbon & Beyond festival at the Highland Festival Grounds at the Kentucky Exposition Center. The festival's lineup includes Foo Fighters, Queens of the Stone Age, Mumford & Sons, Chris Stapleton, Kacey Musgraves and others.
Jett rose to international stardom after founding Joan Jett & the Blackhearts in 1979.  (Reuters)
Jett first rose to fame in the 1970s as a founding member of the all-female rock band The Runaways. She later found international success after she founded Joan Jett & the Blackhearts in 1979.

The band released 10 albums between 1981 and 2013, scoring major hits including "I Love Rock ’n Roll," "Bad Reputation" and "I Hate Myself for Loving You." Joan Jett and the Blackhearts were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2015.
In 2022, Joan Jett & the Blackhearts released their first acoustic album, "Changeup," followed by their six-song EP "Mindsets" in 2023.

Joan Jett & the Blackhearts have stayed active on the road since they first formed. In recent years, they have toured alongside artists including Def Leppard, Mötley Crüe, Bryan Adams, Alanis Morissette and Billy Idol. The band completed their first U.K. headline tour in 16 years in July.

"Highlander" star Christopher Lambert suffered a medical scare after collapsing at Steel City Con in Philadelphia during a meet and greet over the weekend.

The French actor was subsequently taken to a local hospital by ambulance, according to TMZ.

story: "Free Bert" star Bert Kreischer reflects on his weight-loss journey, sobriety and a series of life-changing events that gave him a new perspective on mortality.
John Goodman is turning heads with his dramatic transformation.
The 74-year-old actor appeared nearly unrecognizable in a new photo with fellow actor David DeLuise after the two unexpectedly crossed paths at a grocery store.
DeLuise, known for playing Jerry Russo on Disney Channel's "Wizards of Waverly Place," shared the snapshot on Instagram Thursday, showing himself smiling alongside a noticeably slimmer Goodman.

"He was my childhood!! Legend!" DeLuise wrote in the caption. "I love that I get to say that to someone ;), if you know you know."
Goodman's latest appearance comes after the "Roseanne" star spent years shifting his lifestyle and shedding a significant amount of weight.

The veteran actor previously revealed that he was approaching 400 pounds at his heaviest and had struggled for years with losing weight, only to gain it back.
In 2010, Goodman revealed that he had lost more than 100 pounds after cutting sugar from his diet and committing to regular exercise, including working out six days a week.

"I dug it. Yeah. Nobody’s going to get hurt, but it’s just hitting the mitts and trying to learn," he told The Rolling Stone in 2023. "I never got good enough where I would trust myself to spar because once I get whacked in the face, I don’t know if I wouldn’t lose it."

title: 'Dallas' star Linda Gray reveals the bizarre way Larry Hagman avoided kissing scenes
summary: Linda Gray, who starred as Sue Ellen Ewing, shares wild stories from the "Dallas" set, including Patrick Duffy's surprise ambush and Larry Hagman's on-set pranks.
story: The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.
Linda Gray is ready to kiss and tell.

The actress, who played Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, famously troubled wife of villain J.R. Ewing on "Dallas," is teaming up with Julien's Auctions for "Ladies of the '80s," which goes live Aug. 12.

The sale gives bidders the chance to own costumes, props, personal archives and other rare memorabilia from some of the decade's most beloved television stars. It features two of Gray's original "Dallas" scripts from the episodes surrounding the infamous "Who Shot J.R.?" saga.
ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG
"Dallas" aired from April 2, 1978, to May 3, 1991. At its peak in the 1980s, it was one of the biggest shows on television, (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)
Ahead of the auction, Gray looked back on her "Dallas" years, including the less-than-romantic kissing scenes she shared with her on-screen husband, Larry Hagman, who died in 2012 at 81.

"The first time we kissed, he had a mouthful of peanut butter," the actress told Fox News Digital. "I thought, 'Oh no.' And I had to keep going with this kiss. The camera didn't know what was going on. But here I was, kissing him with peanut butter. I almost killed him. I was like, 'You are so bad and very inappropriate, Larry.' And he didn't care. He just kept laughing. He thought that was funny."
Linda Gray told Fox News Digital that Larry Hagman wasn't a fan of filming kissing scenes. He'd often pull silly pranks to ease the awkwardness and keep everyone laughing. (CBS/Getty Images)

"And then it was onions," said the 85-year-old. "It was kissing him with peanut butter, onions, whatever he could find in a jar. That wasn't some romantic thing. On camera, it looked pretty good, but that was not my reality."
WATCH: CHRISTOPHER ATKINS LOOKS BACK AT ‘THE BLUE LAGOON’ AND ‘DALLAS’
Gray later discovered that Hagman wasn't a fan of on-screen kisses. Rather than endure the awkward moments, he turned them into practical jokes.
Larry Hagman died on Nov. 23, 2012, at the age of 81 in Dallas. (Gregg DeGuire/WireImage)

"He had told me quite honestly that he didn't like kissing scenes," said Gray. "And I thought, 'Well, we're going to be kissing a lot!' So when there was a kissing scene, Larry cringed, just cringed. He did not like it. But I think the pranks, psychologically, were his way of getting over the anxiety of having to kiss me on camera."
The "Dallas" set was notorious for its practical jokes, and everyone got caught in the crossfire.

Linda Gray (right, seen here with Larry Hagman) is offering treasures from her personal collection in Julien's Auctions' "Ladies of the '80s," featuring screen-used scripts, director's clapperboards, cast photos, awards, and more from her iconic career. Bidding is open now, with the live online auction taking place on Aug. 12, 2026. (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"It was a daily prank, if you can imagine," said Gray. "And you never knew who it was going to come from. But it was mainly Larry. Larry was the prankster. I remember there was one episode where Sue Ellen was in the hospital. I was attached to all kinds of tubes and things on my wrists, arms and nose — all this hospital stuff. Larry came in, and he was supposed to talk to Sue Ellen. And Sue Ellen was out of it. She wasn't speaking, which was great for me."
Linda Gray's personalized director's chair, used while directing episodes of "Dallas," is estimated to sell for $800–$1,200. (Julien's Auctions)

"So Larry sits beside my bed and starts telling Sue Ellen how much he loves her," she shared. "Very soap opera dialogue. He's going, 'Oh, Sue Ellen!' and I'm lying there with my eyes closed, my eyes rolling underneath my eyelids. Then the door opens again. I thought, 'Who is in this scene that I didn't know about?' It's Patrick Duffy. He stands next to Larry and says, 'I did not know this was in the scene. Would it help if we sang that old song we used to sing?' Larry says, 'Yes.' And then the two of them started singing this very inappropriate song. I can't even repeat the words to you."
An original drawing created by Tony Bennett for Linda Gray is estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)

"I just burst out laughing," she continued. "The tube came flying out of my nose. I was totally blindsided. I thought I had ruined the scene, but everyone just started laughing hysterically. That was just how it was every day."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

From left: Patrick Duffy, Linda Gray and Larry Hagman pose during the 18th annual Screen Actors Guild Awards broadcast at The Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on Jan. 29, 2012. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)
Hagman's practical jokes were one thing. Facing Texas women in real life was another altogether.

"I was at a Dallas hotel for an event," she recalled. "I went to the ladies' room to put on lipstick. Next to me was this lovely lady with a little Judith Leiber bag. She opened it to put on her lipstick. I glanced down, and there was a gun in her purse. That was all she had in it: a gun and lipstick. I thought, 'Oh boy, I'm in Texas. Who carries a gun around?' So I said, 'Excuse me, is that a gun?' Really stupid, I know. She said, 'Of course, darling. This is Texas!'"

From left: Charlene Tilton, Linda Gray, Larry Hagman, Patrick Duffy and Sheree J. Wilson won the TV Land Pop Culture Award for "Dallas." An award presented to Gray is estimated to sell for $500–$700. (L. Cohen/WireImage)

"I had never been to Dallas in my life," she reflected. "I remember landing in Texas. Everything was beige and flat. I thought, 'I've got to know the women here.' And where do the wealthy women of Texas go? Neiman Marcus, of course, to get their hair done. And that's what I did. I remember seeing big, big hair. It was unlike anything I saw in California. These women dressed a certain way. Their shoes were always very stylish. And apparently, they carried guns in their tiny evening bags."
In "Dallas," Linda Gray starred as Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, resilient and unforgettable wife of J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) on the hit CBS series Dallas. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)
Gray got a crash course in Texas high society over one unforgettable lunch.

"One woman invited me to lunch, and she wore a special outfit just for it," said Gray. "I didn't have any friends in California who would do that. We're having lunch, and then she looks at her watch. She says, 'Oh, I'm so sorry. I have to go home. I have to fluff and fold.' I'm thinking, 'She has to do laundry? Fluff her towels and fold them?' No. She had to fluff her hair, put on her makeup and turn into the woman her husband expected."
Two of Linda Gray's original *Dallas* scripts from the iconic "Who Shot J.R.?" storyline are estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)
If learning Texas customs was intimidating, keeping the show's biggest twist under wraps was downright terrifying.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Linda Gray arrives at the Larry Hagman and Linda Gray VIP Preview Party at Julien's Auction on June 1, 2011, in Beverly Hills. (Tibrina Hobson/WireImage)

The "Dallas" Season 3 finale ended with one of television's most famous cliffhangers: J.R. was shot by an unseen gunman, leaving viewers to wait eight months to learn not only who pulled the trigger but whether he survived.

Gray recalled that the writers were searching for a jaw-dropping way to end the season with a bang when one of them blurted out, "Let's just shoot the bastard." After a brief silence, everyone agreed: "What a great idea. We'll shoot him."

Linda Gray is seen here as Sue Ellen Ewing in a scene from "Dallas." The Ewing family returned to primetime in 2012 when "Dallas" was revived on TNT. After three seasons, the reboot concluded in 2014. (United Archives via Getty Images)
As "Who Shot J.R.?" became a worldwide obsession, Gray found herself fielding the question everywhere she went, including during an interview with David Hartman.

In the "Dallas" Season 3 finale, "A House Divided," J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) is gunned down by a mysterious assailant, setting off the legendary "Who Shot J.R.?" cliffhanger. The mystery captivated millions of viewers and became one of the biggest pop culture moments in television history. (© Lorimar Film Entertainment/Courtesy Everett Collection)

"I was not very smart, but I said, 'Yes, I do,'" Gray recalled when asked whether she knew the shooter's identity. "'I know, and one of my children knows.' After that, I thought, 'Oh my God, I just opened Pandora's box. I thought everyone was going to call my house and one of my kids would answer the phone and reveal who it was. And then it would be all over.'"
The moment the interview ended, Gray said she rushed to call home.

"I remember telling my kids, 'Somebody's going to call you, and they're going to ask you who shot J.R. You cannot answer.' My heart was racing because it all could have been ruined. But nobody called, thank God."

summary: "Nation's Dumbest" contestant Hilaria Baldwin reveals the one simple thing she's learned that has kept her marriage to Alec Baldwin strong after more than a decade.

title: Tears for Fears star admits he fell in love with another woman before his wife died
summary: Roland Orzabal reveals in his memoir "Welcome to Your Life" that he fell in love with Emily Rath before his wife Caroline died of alcohol-related illness.
story: Matthew Nelson and Gunnar Nelson, the sons of late entertainer Ricky Nelson, have written a memoir, "What Happened to Your Hair?: How We Played Loud... Loved Proud... and Never Backed Down... Together."

Tears for Fears star Roland Orzabal is opening up about the painful final years of his marriage, revealing that he fell in love with another woman before his first wife, Caroline, died after a long battle with an alcohol-related illness.

The "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" singer, who has written a new memoir, "Welcome to Your Life," admitted he reached his breaking point after spending years watching his wife’s condition deteriorate. Orzabal described that while walking away may have seemed cruel, he eventually saw "a clear way forward."

"Why was it important to be so candid? Well, because it’s the truth," the 64-year-old told Fox News Digital. "I didn’t want to write something false. And also, I always felt that somewhere out there is someone who’s going through what you went through."
'YOU'RE SO VAIN' SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON'S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE

From left: Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith of Tears For Fears circa 1985 in New York City. Tears for Fears are best known for a string of ’80s hits, including "Everybody Wants to Rule the World," "Shout," "Head Over Heels" and "Mad World." (Robin Platzer/IMAGES/Getty Images)
"I’d spent years and years with Caroline in this state," Orzabal reflected. "It wasn’t just a year or six months. And yes, I had enough. I was shown a clear way forward."

In October 2016, Orzabal met writer and photographer Emily Rath while Tears for Fears were in Colorado to perform at Red Rocks. He wrote that his immediate reaction when he noticed her was, "That’s my wife."

"I’ve been around the world many times and had seen and met many attractive women, but I’d never heard those words before," he wrote. "They didn’t make sense, either, because I was already married, and this woman looked nothing like Caroline."
"Welcome to Your Life: Love, Death & Tears For Fears – An Iconic Musician's Journey Through Grief, Addiction, and Recovery" by Roland Orzabal is available now. (Dey Street Books)
Rath was 30 when she met the then-55-year-old Orzabal. "Ouch," he wrote. "If only I was half my age and she was older."

After exchanging numbers, the pair developed what Orzabal initially described as a "friendship between two creatives." Looking back, however, he acknowledged, "The truth is, I was falling in love with Emily before Caroline had died."
By then, Orzabal had spent decades with Caroline, whom he had known since they were teenagers.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Roland Orzabal's first wife Caroline. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal)
Orzabal was around 14 years old when he first met Caroline Johnston. They married in Bath, England, in 1982, when the singer had just turned 21 and Caroline was 20. They had two sons.

Before Caroline’s physical and mental health deteriorated, the marriage had already endured significant strain. In the book, Orzabal describes a passionate but volatile relationship marked by frequent arguments. As his career took off, he spent long periods away and admits becoming increasingly "selfish," "hedonistic" and absorbed in his rock star persona.

By the mid-1990s, the marriage was in serious trouble. The couple discussed separation and sought marriage counseling. Orzabal says he was determined to keep his family together while acknowledging "the pain that I put Caroline through." Despite the turmoil, they stayed together.
British musician Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears plays guitar during a performance at the Aragon Ballroom in Chicago on June 23, 1985. (Paul Natkin/Getty Images)

Things changed in the late 2000s, when the couple settled into what Orzabal describes as a predictable, day-to-day life where heavy nightly drinking became routine. Around 2011, friends began noticing a change in Caroline’s behavior.

"It was a slow process," Orzabal recalled to Fox News Digital. "She would say it’s menopause. 'It’s the menopause. I’m not eating because of the menopause. I’m weird because of the menopause. I’m depressed because of the menopause.' And she was always very emphatic, hard to argue with."
Roland Orzabal formed Tears for Fears with Curt Smith in 1981. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal)

"I went along with this for many, many years until it was obvious that menopause was over, but the symptoms continued and got worse," he said. "It got worse and worse. We went to see several doctors, and they all said, 'It’s alcohol.' But even then I was in denial because I was a wine drinker. I thought, 'It isn’t doing me any harm, so why is it doing harm to her?'"
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Roland Orzabal married his first wife, Caroline Johnston, in 1982. The wedding took place around the same time his band Tears for Fears released their debut single "Mad World." (Pam Springsteen)
"To be honest with you, it wasn’t until the autopsy that I realized the truth," Orzabal admitted. "Terrible."

According to Orzabal, Caroline eventually struggled to eat solid food even as she continued drinking. She spent increasing amounts of time on the sofa, became anxious, stopped regularly cooking for their sons and alienated friends. Orzabal writes that her condition escalated to "seizures and hospitalizations," "bizarre ideation" and loss of normal bodily control. He described watching helplessly as she "slowly melted away."
According to the book, Roland Orzabal wrote, "Please Be Happy" about Caroline’s depression and deteriorating condition. (Pam Springsteen)

Orzabal writes that Caroline’s drinking became increasingly secretive, and he later discovered that she had been hiding bottles of vodka. He recalled seeing her jaundiced with "deathly red marks" on her face.
Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears performs at Koninklijk Circus in Brussels, Belgium, on April 21, 1985. (Gie Knaeps/Getty Images)

"How much of a carer are you? Is that your natural bent?" Orzabal told Fox News Digital. "I would say with me, it probably wasn’t, but I did it anyway. And I think what it did was it would make me very angry inside, which wasn’t good. I had people talk to me about just leaving, which I would never have done. But I think in hindsight, it’s stupid to say now, but maybe I should have done something about it earlier or left. Sounds harsh."
Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith of Tears for Fears arrive at the German Radio Award 2022 ceremony in Hamburg, Germany, on Sept. 8, 2022. (dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images)
"I think the problem was that, one minute, she’d be fine," said Orzabal. "We would have a decent conversation. And then the next minute. She was doolally — not making sense, demented."
Orzabal wrote that as his feelings for Rath developed, he found himself confronting a choice about his future.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Roland Orzabal and his first wife, Caroline Johnston, had two children together: sons Pascal and Raoul. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"I was at a crossroads, a tipping point, if you like," wrote Orzabal. "A tipping point that would redefine my life. With all the things that were going on with Caroline, with all the visits to psychiatrists, to neurologists, to hepatologists, I was falling in love with a young, healthy woman who I believed loved me too and was the opposite of what I had left at home.
Tears for Fears at the Shepherd’s Bush Empire 2022. (Emily Rath Orzabal)

"... I had a talk with myself, out loud, pacing the room like some crazy man. I knew what was going to happen to Caroline: She would once again be committed and the whole process, the whole nightmare, would start again. And where would it end? I could choose the scenario, the illness, the misery and the frustration, or I could choose an alternative and leave her madness behind. ... I could choose life, or I could choose death. God strike me down, cancel me, whatever, but I chose life."
Orzabal told Fox News Digital that imagining a life beyond his wife’s illness left him with an agonizing sense of guilt.
Singer Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears performs onstage during The Darker Waves Festival in Huntington Beach, California, on Nov. 18, 2023. (Scott Dudelson/WireImage)

"If you choose life at this moment, you were cruel," he said. "But I think it was the final straw because Caroline had already spent three months in a psych ward. I’d been there virtually every day going to visit her. And then, all of a sudden, that night I saw an alternative life for myself, which is hard to do — hard to take. But I did."
In 2017, Orzabal’s first wife of 35 years died. She was 54.
"I felt belief and disbelief," he said. "I couldn’t take it in because you have to go into action. I had to speak to my sons, my family. You’re clearing up the mess that death leaves."
WATCH: NELSON TWINS REFLECT ON FAMILY LEGACY AND THE TRUE COST OF FAME
In 2019, Orzabal said he entered InnerBalance, a rehabilitation center in Colorado, for treatment of his Ambien addiction. He said he began to forgive himself there.

"There’s this madness that comes with grief," he explained. "There’s the negotiation. 'What if I did this?' 'What if I did that?' And then, what happens when you no longer have that person to negotiate with? You no longer have that person to get angry. That’s all gone, and you are only left with the feeling."
Roland Orzabal's first wife, Caroline, died in July 2017 at the age of 54. According to multiple reports, she developed alcohol-related dementia. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal.)

"I left out a lot of details, especially when it came to Caroline," he continued. "It was a lot worse, but I wanted to be respectful of those who’ve passed on. I wanted to respect her name. She’s my sons’ mother. So no, I couldn’t put the gruesome details at all. Even though it sounds bad, it’s much worse."
Roland Orzabal and Emily Rath on their wedding day. (Tara Marolda)
Orzabal and Rath married in 2020. They had a daughter, Eula, in 2025.

"Emily has been an amazing support system for me," said Orzabal. "It depends on your belief system - I think that if you believe in the soul, then [Caroline] would completely understand. When I think about the person she was ... she would understand."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Scott Eastwood says his father sent Kevin Costner home from set while filming 'A Perfect World'
summary: Scott Eastwood reveals on "Armchair Expert" how Clint Eastwood calmly sent Kevin Costner home from the "Perfect World" set after a trailer standoff.
story: The actor bought his dad a Silverado truck for Christmas once he found success as an actor.
Scott Eastwood is getting candid about how his father once asked a well-known actor to leave a movie set.

During a recent interview on the "Armchair Expert" podcast, the 40-year-old actor shared that everybody has "a lot of respect" for his father, Clint Eastwood, on set and that he "didn't raise his voice ever" while on set.

He then shared a "legendary story" about when his father worked with Kevin Costner and how he reacted when the actor wouldn't leave his trailer, noting "I’m sort of going to paraphrase it, and I’ll probably tell it a little wrong."

"Kevin Costner sort of going through maybe, the Kevin Costner rise to fame and maybe got a big ego, you know, blah blah blah, but they were doing 'Perfect World,'" he said. "Apparently, he didn't want to come out of his trailer for some reason."
Scott Eastwood said his dad never raised his voice while on set. (Aitor Rosas Sune/WWD via Getty Images)
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

"So he sent him home, and I guess they just went to Kevin and said, 'Hey, you're going to go home for the day,'" Scott explained. "He said, 'What do you mean I'm in the scene?' You know, 'Well, I guess you're not anymore. Clint changed that.'"
After he was asked to leave the set that day, Scott noted, "I think the next day he was on set ready to go."

"I think I was lucky in some ways because I got to see it growing up and got to see like how it's bulls---," he said on an episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience," in June of certain behaviors on modern movie sets.

While Eastwood said he got a peek at bad behavior on set when he was younger and visiting his iconic dad on set, the "Wrath of Man" star said his father "did a really good job of protecting" him and his siblings from the pitfalls that come with child stardom.

title: Dangerous drug-resistant fungus spreads across US, reaching 27 states
summary: Thousands of Candida auris cases have been reported across 27 states in 2026, with the drug-resistant fungus posing deadly risks in healthcare settings.
story: Fox News medical contributor Dr. Marc Siegel unpacks a deadly fungus spreading throughout the U.S.
Thousands of cases of a potentially deadly, drug-resistant fungus have been reported across 27 states so far this year, according to provisional CDC data.
As of the week ending July 25, a total of 3,437 clinical cases of Candida auris (C. auris) had been documented in the U.S. so far in 2026.

California accounts for 873 cases — roughly one-quarter of the country’s total. Other states with high numbers include Texas (433), Tennessee (283), Ohio (279), Georgia (193), Louisiana (179), Illinois (171), Arizona (171), Michigan (146), Virginia (132) and Pennsylvania (121), per the CDC.
EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO AVOID DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE AS NYC OUTBREAK KILLS 5
The remaining states have fewer than 100 cases each.
Candida auris is a type of yeast that can cause serious infections, primarily in hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare settings.
Thousands of cases of a potentially deadly, drug-resistant fungus have been reported across 27 states so far this year, according to provisional CDC data. (iStock)

The fungus, which can survive on surfaces for prolonged periods, is "highly transmissible between patients through contact with contaminated surfaces or objects," the CDC states. It can spread through contaminated items such as bedrails, doorknobs and shared medical equipment.
C. auris can also be spread by people who carry the fungus but do not show symptoms, known as "colonization."
California accounts for 873 cases — roughly one-quarter of the country’s total.
Clinical cases do not necessarily represent infections. The CDC defines a clinical case as detection of C. auris in a specimen collected during the normal course of medical care.
Some clinical specimens can come from sites where the presence of C. auris may represent colonization rather than a true infection.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The health effects of the fungus can range from colonization without symptoms to potentially deadly invasive infections, including bloodstream infections.

Those most at risk of infection include patients with severe underlying medical conditions. In particular, those who use breathing tubes, feeding tubes, IVs or catheters are more vulnerable, as are those who are hospitalized frequently or for long periods of time.
As of the week ending July 25, a total of 3,437 clinical cases of Candida auris (C. auris) had been documented in the U.S. so far in 2026. (iStock)
People without those risk factors are unlikely to become colonized with C. auris or develop an infection.
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst and clinical professor of medicine at NYU Langone, said he considers C. auris an "emerging problem of great concern."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It is resistant to multiple antifungal drugs, and it tends to spread in hospital settings, including on equipment being used on immunocompromised and semi-immunocompromised patients, such as ventilators and catheters," he previously told Fox News Digital.
"Unfortunately, symptoms such as fever, chills and aches may be ubiquitous, and it can be mistaken for other infections."

Those most at risk of infection include patients with severe underlying medical conditions. In particular, those who use breathing tubes, feeding tubes, IVs or catheters are more vulnerable, as are those who are hospitalized frequently or for long periods of time. (iStock)

Invasive C. auris infections have been associated with mortality rates of 30% to 72%, although most affected patients are already seriously ill. This can make it difficult to determine how often the fungus is a direct cause of death.
Candida auris can be difficult to treat because it is often resistant to antifungal medications, leading the CDC to classify the fungus as an "urgent antimicrobial-resistance threat."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

More than 90% of U.S. samples are resistant to fluconazole, a common antifungal treatment. Echinocandins, another family of antifungals, are currently the main treatment option for C. auris, although some strains are resistant to all three main classes of antifungals.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Major research" is ongoing to develop new treatments, according to Siegel.

"This is part of a much larger problem of emerging antibiotic resistance in the U.S. and around the world," the physician previously cautioned. "At the same time, sterilization and disinfection measures in hospitals can be very helpful."
Fox News Digital's Angelica Stabile contributed reporting.

title: Cut off by your adult child? Psychology researcher reveals what parents should do next
summary: Dr. Richard Blake shares steps that may help repair parent-child estrangement, from stabilizing mental health to avoiding moralized language.
story: While every relationship is different and there are no guarantees, Texas-based psychology researcher Dr. Richard Blake says the majority of estrangements do come to an end – but willingness to change and find common ground is key.
Family estrangement has become increasingly common in the U.S. — but experts stress that reconciliation may still be possible after relatives have cut ties.

A 2025 YouGov poll found that 38% of U.S. adults were estranged from at least one close family member, including 16% who were estranged from a parent and 10% from a child. Among parents estranged from their children, 70% said they would consider reconciling.

Research also suggests that many parent-child estrangements eventually experience a period of renewed contact. In one nationally representative study published in the Journal of Marriage and Family, 81% of adult children who experienced estrangement from their mothers later became unestranged, as did 69% of those estranged from their fathers.
5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

While every relationship is different and there are no guarantees, Texas-based psychology researcher Dr. Richard Blake stated that the majority of estrangements do come to an end – but willingness to change and find common ground is key.
Family estrangement has become increasingly common in the U.S. — but experts stress that reconciliation may still be possible after relatives have cut ties. (iStock)

In many cases, parent-child estrangements are a cycle — "they'll re-engage, then they'll fall out again," Blake said. "One of the key things from the research is that adult children will reach out and if they see nothing has changed, they'll estrange again."
In an interview with Fox News Digital, the psychology researcher shared the following steps that may increase the likelihood of repairing a fractured relationship.
No. 1: Aim for stability first
Estrangement from an adult child can be seen as a form of "ambiguous loss" — a situation in which someone is gone, but there is still hope they could return, according to Blake.

He compared the situation to having a child missing in action: "You don't know if he's dead or alive and you kind of have to grieve, but you don't really know if you should be grieving, because there's hope."
SECOND LADY USHA VANCE GETS CANDID ABOUT NEW BABY, JUGGLING FOUR CHILDREN AND MOTHERHOOD

Research supports the significant emotional toll of estrangement. In a 2025 study of older parents, being cut off from an adult child was associated with poorer well-being and a reduced sense of purpose, as well as greater depressive symptoms.
Before attempting a reconciliation with an estranged parent or adult child, Blake said the first priority should be stabilizing oneself.
"What I tend to recommend first is to get that person stable, have healthy habits and build a community," he advised. "Good mental health practices are really important."
No. 2: Listen and validate

When communication with an estranged family member is possible, Blake recommends repeating back what the other person has said and acknowledging how they experienced the conflict before offering a different perspective.

"Listen to the other person and then actually repeat back what they said as you understood it, and validate that – like, ‘Oh, I can see why you felt like that. I see why you interpreted it in that way,’" Blake said.
The majority of estrangements do come to an end – but willingness to change and find common ground is key, an expert said. (iStock)

It’s important to resist the impulse to immediately correct, contradict or defend, and to acknowledge the other person's experience without necessarily agreeing with every aspect of their account, according to the expert.
After listening, parents should be open-minded about making some changes as needed, Blake said.

"I really tell our parents … if you're 100% perfect, great … but most parents have done something wrong, something that they want to change. And if they want a relationship with their child, they are going to have to change some things."
No. 3: Pause before reacting to accusations or labels
Certain labels used during family disputes can make compromise more difficult, Blake noted, an issue he refers to as "moralized language."

"I talk about these therapy words that get thrown at parents … abuse, toxic boundaries, narcissists, gaslighting, all those things," he said. "In the research, when you use moralized language like that, compromise becomes far more difficult."
"I don't think anyone can promise, ‘I can get your kids back.’"
To parents on the receiving end of this type of terminology, Blake’s first recommendation is not to immediately react.
"I tell adult parents to pause before they really react, because it's understandably going to make them very angry."
Taking time before responding can help keep the conversation from escalating and allow both sides to focus on the underlying conflict rather than reacting in the moment.
No. 4: Focus on specific behaviors and events
After pausing, Blake recommends asking the other person to explain specifically what they mean, going beyond broad labels to the behaviors underlying the complaint.
"Okay, you've used the word toxic – can you describe the behavior or behaviors that you consider to be toxic?" he asked as an example.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Blake distinguished between describing a person’s behavior and its impact on you, and assigning that person a sweeping label.
"If someone says, ‘When you criticize my weight, I left dinner feeling really, really upset,’ that's a fact. That's the person's interpretation," he said.
Taking time before responding can help keep the conversation from escalating and allow both sides to focus on the underlying conflict rather than reacting in the moment. (iStock)
"But if you say, ‘You're toxic because you always criticize me,’ it’s very difficult to come back from that. So it sort of inflames the situation."
That approach shifts the conversation away from judgments about character and toward concrete actions and events that can actually be discussed.
No. 5: Use ‘I’ statements; avoid ‘always’ and ‘never’
When continued communication is appropriate, Blake suggested using language that focuses on a person’s own experience of a conflict rather than beginning with an accusation.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"First, I would start by using ‘I’ statements, rather than ‘you,’" he advised. "It'd be like, ‘When you said this, I felt like this. When this happened, I did this.’"
This allows the person to discuss their own reaction to a specific interaction rather than beginning with an accusation.
When continued communication is appropriate, the expert suggested using language that focuses on a person’s own experience of a conflict rather than beginning with an accusation. (iStock)
Blake also recommends avoiding absolutes, such as "you always..." or "you never..." when trying to resolve a conflict.
In cases involving abuse, threats or other safety concerns, however, reconciliation or continued communication may not always be appropriate, he noted.
No guarantees
Although Blake maintains there is always hope for a reconciliation, he acknowledged that there is no single guaranteed formula for restoring a fractured relationship.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While there are many people who are "selling" reconciliation services, Blake cautioned, "I don't think anyone can promise, ‘I can get your kids back.’"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The goal is to create better conditions for reconciliation, not to promise that specific actions can achieve it, he noted.
Ultimately, Blake’s advice is for the person to focus on things within their control, such as embracing healthy habits, aiming for stability and building a community.

title: Fauci said ‘no red flags’ for pregnant women days after raising theoretical vaccine miscarriage risk: text
summary: Newly released messages highlight differences between Fauci’s private discussions and his later public comments on COVID vaccination during pregnancy.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., releasing texts from Dr. Anthony Fauci's government iPhone on 'The Story.'

Former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Dr. Anthony Fauci privately raised a theoretical risk of first-trimester miscarriage tied to reactions from COVID-19 mRNA vaccines — then publicly said thousands of vaccinated pregnant women had shown "no red flags."

Newly released text messages from Fauci’s government-issued phone, made public by Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and Rand Paul, R-Ky., show the contrast between his private discussion and later public reassurances.

In a Jan. 25, 2021 exchange with then-CDC Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky and Dr. Vivek Murthy, Fauci discussed fever and other immune reactions some people had experienced after a second mRNA vaccine dose.
That reaction, Fauci wrote, "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester," according to the messages.
FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS
Anthony Fauci is sworn in before testifying at a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Walensky responded that it was "definitely a good point, esp after dose two," while Murthy called Fauci’s observation "a really good point."
On Feb. 3, 2021, Fauci said more than 10,000 pregnant women had received COVID-19 vaccines without any concerning safety signals being detected, CNBC reported at the time.
"The FDA … have found, thus far … no red flags about that, about pregnant women," Fauci said during an interview with the Journal of the American Medical Association.
One week later, Fauci repeated the reassurance.

During a Feb. 10 White House briefing, Fauci said approximately 20,000 pregnant women had been vaccinated and that officials had seen "no red flags," Politico, The Daily Mail and The New York Post reported at the time.
FAUCI IN THE CONGRESSIONAL WRINGER: A TEST FOR TRUMP'S NEWLY-MINTED ATTORNEY GENERAL
Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines are prepared in syringes at Borinquen Health Care Center on May 29, 2025, in Miami, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"Since the [Emergency Use Authorization] and under the [Emergency Use Authorization], approximately 20,000 pregnant women have been vaccinated with no red flags, as we say, and this is being monitored by the CDC and the FDA," Fauci said.

The public comments came shortly after Fauci had privately raised the theoretical possibility that fever and cytokine-related reactions after a second vaccine dose could be associated with first-trimester miscarriage.
The messages do not show that officials had found an increased miscarriage risk, only that they were discussing a theoretical concern while pregnancy data was still limited.

Months later, Fauci continued to emphasize the lack of adverse safety signals, saying "tens and tens and tens of thousands" of pregnant women had been followed after vaccination and there was "no indication whatsoever" of increased adverse outcomes compared with unvaccinated pregnant women, according to an article published Aug. 30, 2021 by What to Expect.
FLORIDA AG JAMES UTHMEIER SAYS FAUCI PROBE COULD UNCOVER GROUNDS FOR CRIMINAL LIABILITY DESPITE PARDON

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., arrives for a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing at the Dirksen Senate Office Building on April 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The newly released texts show a contrast between officials’ private concerns and public reassurances.
"The text chain released today could have an immediate impact [on] public health and the principle of informed consent," Johnson's press release read.
Fauci, Walensky and Murthy could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

title: Fauci texts suggest officials were ‘too slow to pivot' amid pandemic, says Dr Marc Siegel
summary: Dr. Marc Siegel, senior medical analyst, says newly released Anthony Fauci text messages reveal he was "too dogmatic" and too slow to pivot on COVID-19 vaccine guidance.
story: In a Monday evening interview, the Fox News senior medical analyst suggested the former White House chief medical adviser was at times too "dogmatic" and slow to adapt as the science evolved.
Newly released text messages from Dr. Anthony Fauci have sparked fresh questions about his handling of evolving COVID-19 evidence, according to Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst.

The texts are part of an initial batch of communications from Fauci's government-issued cellphone released Monday by Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and Rand Paul, R-Ky. The messages shed light on private discussions between Fauci and other top health officials as they navigated evolving questions around the coronavirus pandemic.
In a Monday evening interview, Siegel suggested the former White House chief medical adviser was at times too "dogmatic" and slow to adapt as the science evolved.
EXPOSED FAUCI DIARY SHOWS HE ESTIMATED COVID-19 DEATH RATE TO BE MUCH LOWER THAN WHAT HE TOLD CONGRESS
Siegel said Fauci was a "top immunologist" and "top vaccinologist."
"And I respect that a lot," he said, adding that he felt Fauci then ventured beyond those areas of expertise.
Newly released text messages from Dr. Anthony Fauci have sparked fresh questions about his handling of evolving COVID-19 evidence during the pandemic. (Getty Images)

"The other issue is flexibility. I have a feeling about Dr. Fauci that he's too dogmatic," Siegel told Fox News Digital, adding that Fauci would "stick to some idea he has and [follow] it through regardless of contradictory or changing evidence."
Siegel said he believed Fauci veered into territory beyond his medical training and knowledge, on issues including lockdowns, school closures and masking.
LEGACY MEDIA COVERS ANTHONY FAUCI DIARY BY CRITICIZING DONALD TRUMP INSTEAD OF FAUCI'S DISHONESTY
"So it's not surprising that he would, for lack of a better word, flip-flop on those areas," he said.
Regarding the newly released texts, Siegel said, "it looks like he was trying to guide other public officials and leaders from the television camera, and that's not what you should be doing."
Questions around pregnancy guidance
Among the issues addressed in the newly released messages is COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy.
Siegel emphasized that he remains a strong supporter of vaccines, including mRNA technology.
"I'm a big fan of the COVID vaccines and of the mRNA COVID vaccines," the doctor said. "I think they're getting a bad rap right now."
Among the issues addressed in the newly released messages is COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy. (iStock)
Pregnancy presented a complicated risk calculation because COVID-19 itself posed dangers to expectant mothers, Siegel noted.
Early in the pandemic, he said, recommending vaccination during pregnancy was reasonable based on what was known at the time.
But as the virus changed and vaccines became less protective, Siegel said he believes the public discussion should have changed with it.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"As the vaccine changed and the virus mutated, and as the vaccine became less protective, that needed to be entered into the public debate about the vaccine — and Dr. Fauci wasn't fast enough to do that," Siegel said.
Siegel also pointed to a study that raised questions at the time about a potential link between a second vaccine dose and early miscarriage.
"I don't think that Dr. Fauci and others may have been quick enough to consider that," he said.

"As the vaccine changed and the virus mutated, and as the vaccine became less protective, that needed to be entered into the public debate about the vaccine — and Dr. Fauci wasn't fast enough to do that," said Dr. Siegel. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

While subsequent research has continued to support vaccination during pregnancy — Siegel said "the accumulation of data right now favors the vaccine throughout pregnancy" — he questioned whether contradictory evidence received sufficient consideration as it emerged.
"It's a little eyebrow-raising to me that it appears he was trying to dismiss a study" suggesting miscarriage could be a concern, Siegel said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
More broadly, such decisions should rest with patients and their doctors, while emphasizing that the underlying medical data was "not suppressed," according to the doctor.

"I don't like when the government superimposes their views, especially if they're incorrect or if they are ill-informed, but I still think it should be between the patient and the doctor," said Siegel.
‘The mandates continued'
Siegel argued that another problem came when policies failed to adjust quickly enough to changing evidence about the vaccines' effectiveness.
"I think the problem was that the mandates continued," he said. "We were too slow to pivot on this vaccine, and that led to a lot of public distrust."
Siegel emphasized that he remains a strong supporter of vaccines, including mRNA technology. (iStock)
Asked whether he saw a meaningful difference between what Fauci was discussing privately and what Americans were hearing publicly, Siegel said there was "more than I would like."
"There's a difference between public and private discourse here," he said. "There should be none."
"Where was the evolution of guidance and thought and staying within your lane as more and more information came out?"
As additional messages are released, Siegel said he will be watching how Fauci's guidance evolved alongside the evidence.

"I'm looking at one thing: Where was the evolution of guidance and thought and staying within your lane as more and more information came out?" he said. "Or did this develop more and more into dogma and megalomania? I don't know. That's what I'm disturbed about."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
At the same time, Siegel cautioned against judging pandemic-era communications without considering what scientists knew at the time.
"To be fair to Dr. Fauci, things need to remain in context," he said. "When did this happen? What was going on at the time? What did we know and what did we not know?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Added Siegel, "We were learning on the job. We were learning as we went. We knew nothing about this thing, and it just blew over us."
That uncertainty, he said, made a willingness to change course all the more important.
"Humility is the best way to go — not dogma."

title: 3 things to avoid in middle age could mean 13 more years without dementia, study finds
summary: NYU Langone Health research reveals how avoiding high blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking in midlife could add nearly 13 dementia-free years.
story: Older adults who walked at a significantly faster speed than their peers were about half as likely to develop cognitive impairment, according to Dr. Joe Verghese, MD, neurologist at Stony Brook Medicine.
Middle-aged adults who manage to avoid high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking can gain nearly 13 additional years of life free from dementia, according to new research led by NYU Langone Health.
The study, published in the journal Neurology Open Access, analyzed long-term health data to determine how midlife cardiovascular wellness shapes brain function decades later.
Minimizing these three common vascular threats between ages 48 and 68 dramatically postpones mental decline, according to the research.
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

"Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade," said Dr. Josef Coresh, the study’s senior investigator and founding director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone, in a press release.
Identifying actionable ways to stall memory loss is vital, he said, pointing out that roughly 42% of Americans are projected to develop dementia after turning 55.

Maintaining normal blood pressure, avoiding diabetes and refraining from smoking between ages 48 and 68 is associated with nearly 13 additional years of dementia-free life, the study suggested. (iStock)

The reviewed data came from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, an ongoing trial that began in 1986. It included a cohort of more than 12,000 dementia-free participants whose average age was 56.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
After screening subjects for smoking habits, elevated blood pressure and diabetes, researchers tracked their health trajectories for an average of 26 years.
By the end of the observation window, 3,008 participants had developed dementia, while 5,238 died without cognitive impairment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study revealed a significant gap based on midlife health: Participants who avoided all three risk factors averaged 30 dementia-free years following their baseline exams. In contrast, those with all three conditions averaged just 17 years before developing dementia or dying.

Experts emphasize that targeted cardiovascular prevention efforts starting in midlife are essential to preserve brain health, particularly with 42% of Americans at risk for developing dementia after age 55. (FG Trade / Getty Images)
Demographic trends were reported across sex and race. Female participants had longer periods of cognitive health than male participants, regardless of health risks.
Among subjects with all three risk factors, women survived an average of 18.1 years without dementia, compared to 16.6 years for men.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
White participants with all three risk factors averaged 19.6 dementia-free years, while Black participants facing the same health profile averaged 16.0 years.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"These results suggest that vascular risk reduction may benefit all groups, but that certain populations, such as Black adults, may especially benefit from targeted prevention efforts," Coresh said, expressing hope that the data will motivate people to quit smoking and monitor cardiovascular health starting in their late 40s.

Women consistently experienced more years of cognitive health than men across all risk levels, averaging 18.1 dementia-free years with all three risk factors present compared to 16.6 years for men. (iStock)
The authors noted several limitations to their findings, including that the observational design cannot prove direct cause and effect.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Additionally, health status was recorded during a single visit, and some potential midlife lifestyle changes were unreported.

title: Trouble sleeping? Your neighborhood could be partly to blame, experts say
summary: A study of 200,000 Google Street View images reveals how neighborhood greenery, safety and enclosure levels may influence sleep duration and insomnia.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
Where you live in your neighborhood could significantly affect your sleep, according to experts and recent research on urban landscapes.

Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
Factors such as cohabitating with family members, pets or high-noise environments frequently disrupt sleep patterns, she said.
POPULAR SMOOTHIE INGREDIENT MAY REDUCE ONE KEY HEALTH BENEFIT, STUDY SUGGESTS
"If you live in noisy environments, the fact is that it is going to be noisy, and you do have to make some adjustments," Palinski-Wade told Fox News Digital.
She suggested that individuals living near busy city streets consider using a white noise machine because it "can cancel out some of that environmental noise."
Simple adjustments like using white noise machines, installing blackout curtains and keeping bedroom doors closed can effectively reduce environmental sleep disruptions. (iStock)
Beyond the immediate bedroom environment, the visual characteristics of one’s neighborhood can subconsciously influence sleep patterns, research shows.

A study led by Professor Daisuke Matsushita of the Graduate School of Human Life and Ecology at Osaka Metropolitan University in Japan analyzed more than 200,000 Google Street View images, using artificial intelligence to assess streetscape features.
WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS
"Based on the technique used in this study, cities could potentially measure perceived safety, beauty, liveliness and enclosure, as well as pollution and noise," Matsushita stated in a press release.

The study examined 1,089 working adults residing on lower apartment floors in Tokyo. Individuals living in neighborhoods with a stronger perceived sense of safety tended to experience longer sleep durations, the researchers found.
"Cities could potentially measure perceived safety, beauty, liveliness and enclosure, as well as pollution and noise."
Visual elements like trees and other greenery, and high "enclosure" rates (tall vertical buildings with few open spaces) aligned with longer sleep and fewer insomnia symptoms.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Alternatively, highly walkable environments with abundant sidewalks and traffic signs were linked to a lower sense of safety and shorter periods of sleep, possibly due to increased foot traffic and crowdedness, the study found.
Artificial intelligence analysis of Tokyo streetscapes revealed that neighborhoods perceived as safer were linked to longer sleep durations among residents. (iStock)
"We hope that opening up this new perspective creates further possibilities for designing healthier neighborhoods," Matsushita said.
Palinski-Wade recommends using blackout curtains to "shut out some of that light pollution and get more restful sleep."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Environmental factors inside the home, including room temperature and whether bedroom doors are left open or closed, can also impact how much outside noise gets into the bedroom.
The findings do not necessarily suggest that people need to relocate, the researchers noted.
Household interruptions, pet disruptions and ambient noise levels can significantly interfere with sleep quality, the researchers said. (iStock)
The study relies on self-reported sleep data from working adults in Tokyo, which may be subject to imperfect memory, and only represents a specific group of people.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Because the research focused strictly on residents living on the lower floors of apartment buildings in a single city, the findings may not apply to people living on higher floors or in rural and suburban settings.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The simplest thing you really can do is try to set yourself on a schedule where you go to sleep, and you wake up at the same time each night," Palinski-Wade advised, noting that maintaining this consistency on days off or weekends has the biggest impact on sleep quality and quantity.
