title: Bride cautions others before wedding day about risky beauty treatments: 'Pain wasn't worth it'
summary: A young bride's eyes swelled shut with yellow discharge hours after getting eyelash extensions for her wedding — landing her in a hospital emergency room.
story: 'The Five' co-hosts discuss the growing trend of young couples opting for courthouse weddings instead of more extravagant ceremonies.
A bride-to-be who wanted to look "like a princess" on her wedding day ended up looking far worse than that after a severe allergic reaction to a fake eyelash treatment.
Polly Bibby, 26, an illustrator, decided to try classic eyelash extensions ahead of her big day compared to her usual minimal makeup look.
She had a patch test done, she said, according to Kennedy News & Media — and since she suffered no reaction, she went ahead with the procedure in early July, before her wedding day.
DOCTORS WARN OF ‘LOOKSMAXXING’ DANGERS AFTER INFLUENCER’S LIVESTREAM EMERGENCY
After getting the treatment done — which cost her about $88, she said — she was initially happy with her "dressier" appearance.
Just a few hours after the appointment, however, her eyes became watery and sore. She shrugged it off as symptoms of hay fever.
Polly Bibby, pictured, was left with red, raw and swollen eyes after suffering an allergic reaction to eyelash extensions. (Kennedy News & Media)

But when her eyes started to sting and then stick together due to a yellow discharge, alarm bells began going off. She called an urgent care medical line and was advised to head to the nearest hospital emergency room.

A shocking photo shows her red, raw and swollen eyes. After being seen by a nurse in the eye unit at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Hinchingbrooke, Cambridge, it was confirmed she'd suffered an allergic reaction to the eyelash extensions.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO 'OZEMPIC EARS' AND OTHER COSMETIC COMPLAINTS, SURGEONS SAY
She was given a course of antibiotics and antihistamines, and told to wait three days for the swelling to go down before getting the false lashes removed.

"To keep the eyes safe, [artificial] lashes should be applied by an experienced aesthetician in a sanitary setting, with chemicals that are safe for your skin," said Rebecca J. Taylor, M.D., a board-certified ophthalmologist in Nashville, in a statement on the American Academy of Ophthalmology website.
"The procedure does come with risks, namely trauma to or infection of the eyelid or cornea; allergic reaction to the glue; and permanent or temporary loss of eyelashes."
Many brides opt for special beauty treatments for their wedding day. But one suffered a severe allergic reaction to an eyelash extension procedure. (iStock)
Infection can also result, Taylor said, from inadequate hygiene in the salon or damage to the eye during application.
Even though her skin is now slowly healing, Bibby of Cambridgeshire, in the United Kingdom, feared her eyes would still be red by the time she said "I do" to her to 29-year-old fiancé, Benjamin May.
She said she's been sharing her experience to warn other brides about getting certain treatments so close to their big day.
"I just didn't look like myself."

"I don't wear that much makeup," she told Kennedy News & Media. "Getting married is the biggest day of your life, so I just wanted to test out different makeup and actually feel like a princess for the day."
She said it was a trial for her wedding, as she'd "never had my eyelashes done before."

About four or five hours after the appointment, her partner looked at her eyes, she said, and thought they were a little red.

"By that evening, they had gone red, raw and were stinging. The only way I can describe [how I looked] is the man from 'The Goonies' with the big puffy eyes called Sloth. I just didn't look like myself. I looked like a different person."

Bibby, shown here in both images, was given a course of antibiotics and antihistamines and told to wait three days for the swelling to go down before having her false lashes removed. (Kennedy News & Media)
She said her eyes were "burning," and "it got to the point where I was losing my vision and I couldn't see at all."
Every time she blinked, she said, her "eyes were sticking together as I had discharge building up [in] my eyes ... a sticky yellow discharge pretty similar to when babies have conjunctivitis."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
She said the medical staff who treated her were "quite taken back and shocked by it."
During the removal of the false lashes, she said it felt like "acid was being poured onto her face."
"I didn't realize it would happen to me."
She said, "I was screaming, crying and tensing up. My eyes are still red, scabby and very 'rashy.' The eyelids themselves are really swollen, and I've still got quite blurry vision."

She also said, "When people joke around and say things [can] go wrong [on your wedding day] — I didn't realize it would happen to me."
"I won't be getting eyelash extensions for the big day," said Bibby (not pictured) ahead of her big day, after suffering an allergic reaction. (iStock)
Ahead of her wedding, she said, "I won't be getting eyelash extensions for the big day. Going through that pain was not worth it. If I knew in hindsight, I'd just use mascara."

She added, "I'd hate for anyone else to go through this."

title: Fitness expert reveals one simple exercise for a stronger core — and it’s not a situp
summary: A certified yoga instructor explains how boat pose challenges the entire core as an integrated system, offering more stability benefits than a situp.
story: While traditional abdominal exercises can be effective, one yoga pose may offer added benefits. Boat pose, or Navasana, forms the body into a "V" and challenges multiple muscles involved in core stability.
Strengthening the core improves balance and stability, which supports movement and physical performance, experts say.

While traditional abdominal exercises can be effective, one yoga pose may offer added benefits. Boat pose, or Navasana, forms the body into a "V" and challenges multiple muscles involved in core stability.
Melissa Leach, a certified yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach in Philadelphia, said a strong core provides a foundation for both exercise and everyday movement.
FITNESS EXPERTS REVEALS SIMPLE RULE TO GET IN SHAPE WITHOUT DREADING THE GYM: 'JUST MOVE'
"Ab exercises help support that by strengthening key muscles such as the obliques, lower back and deep stabilizers like the transverse abdominis," she told Fox News Digital.
A yoga instructor demonstrates a boat pose. (Yoga-Go)
"Together, these muscles work to stabilize your spine, creating a strong foundation for movement and allowing you to transfer force more efficiently between your upper and lower body."
Many routine activities, from carrying groceries to getting up from a chair, engage the core muscles to stabilize the trunk, maintain balance and support controlled movement.
PEOPLE ARE USING VIBRATION PLATES FOR WEIGHT LOSS: DO THEY WORK?
A strong core can also help reduce the risk of lower back pain by improving stability in the spine and ensuring control during lifting and other physically demanding movements, the expert said.
"While injury risk isn’t determined by core strength alone, a well-conditioned core provides a stable foundation for movement in everyday life," she noted.
Many routine activities, from carrying groceries to getting up from a chair, engage the core muscles to stabilize the trunk, maintain balance and support controlled movement. (iStock)
Core benefits

Boat pose challenges the ab muscles while also engaging the hip flexors, glutes and back, according to Leach. This helps to build functional core strength rather than just targeting a single muscle group.

Compared to the traditional situp, which is carried out in "one plane of motion," the boat pose requires the entire core to "work together to keep you balanced and lifted, which places greater demands on core stability, balance and control," Leach said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Whether you're holding the pose or moving dynamically, you're training the muscles that stabilize your spine and pelvis, rather than primarily strengthening the muscles required for trunk flexion, as a situp does," she went on.
"Both have their place, but boat pose challenges the core to work as an integrated system rather than focusing on one movement pattern."
Compared to the traditional situp, which is carried out in "one plane of motion," the boat pose engages the entire core. (iStock)
The pose develops both stability and muscular endurance, according to Leach.

"The position requires your deep core muscles, the ones that support your spine and pelvis, to stay engaged throughout," she said. "Over time, this can translate into better posture, a stronger lower back and a core that supports everyday movement."
How to do a boat pose
Leach shared the following steps for performing the boat pose safely and with proper form.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Sit down on a mat or the floor with the knees bent and feet flat on the ground.
Lean back slightly onto the sit bones, keeping the lower back straight.
Lift the feet off the ground, keeping the shins parallel with the floor. If possible, extend the legs upward for the full pose.
Reach the arms forward, keeping them parallel to the ground.
Engage the core muscles and balance.
A yoga instructor demonstrates an active boat pose. (Yoga-Go)
Those looking to make the exercise more dynamic can move in and out of the pose rather than holding it, the expert said.
Lie flat on your back on the floor or a mat.
Use the core muscles to lift the legs and upper body off the mat, reaching the final "V" shape of the boat pose.
Extend the body back down to the floor or mat and repeat.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For beginners, Leach recommended some modifications.
Keep the legs bent in a half boat pose instead of straight, which can reduce core strain and effort.Hold the backs of your thighs lightly to provide support and help with balance.
Keep the legs bent in a half boat pose instead of straight, which can reduce core strain and effort.
Hold the backs of your thighs lightly to provide support and help with balance.
A boat pose with legs bent can reduce core strain, the expert said. (iStock)
Those who struggle with balance and maintaining a straight spine can sit on a folded blanket or cushion to help tilt the pelvis forward, Leach suggested.
Another option is to sit with the back a few inches from the wall "for reassurance," she said, "while still allowing enough space for you to perform the crunching movement without hitting your head."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For seniors or anyone with limited core strength, Leach recommends trying a chair-supported version. Sit toward the front edge of a sturdy chair, hold the sides for support, and lean back slightly while lifting one or both feet a few inches off the floor.
"This builds the same engagement without the demand of balancing unsupported, and you can progress to the floor version once you feel steadier," she advised.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Biden's battle with advancing cancer renews focus on prostate disease
summary: Hunter Biden revealed in a BBC interview that Joe Biden's prostate cancer has metastasized into his bones, calling it very painful and debilitating.
story: Fox News contributor Karl Rove and former Biden 2020 campaign surrogate Kevin Walling discuss former President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer diagnosis and allegations of a cover-up by the Democratic Party on ‘The Story.’
Former President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread further since his diagnosis last year, his son Hunter Biden revealed in a BBC interview that aired Friday.
"The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," Hunter told BBC Newsnight, describing his father’s condition as "very painful" and "very debilitating in many respects."
"It’s really sad to watch," Hunter said. "The only thing that I’d say about my dad about his health right now is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good."
JOE BIDEN'S CANCER HAS SPREAD FURTHER, LEAVING HIM IN 'VERY PAINFUL' CONDITION, HUNTER REVEALS
Former President Biden, 83, announced his diagnosis in May 2025, after news that a "small nodule" had been found in his prostate during a routine exam.

"While this represents a more aggressive form of the disease, the cancer appears to be hormone-sensitive, which allows for effective management," his office said at the time. "The president and his family are reviewing treatment options with his physicians."
Former President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread further since his diagnosis last year, his son Hunter Biden revealed. (Getty Images)

Biden later underwent hormone therapy and radiation treatment, completing a course of radiation at Penn Medicine Radiation Oncology in Philadelphia in October 2025, according to the former president's spokesperson.
In addition to hormone therapy, common treatment options for prostate cancer include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and radiopharmaceutical treatments.
Fox News Digital reached out to Biden's office for comment.
What to know about prostate cancer

Prostate cancer is a disease found in men that develops in the prostate gland. Cases have been on the rise in recent years, with overall incidence increasing about 3% annually from 2014 through 2021, according to the American Cancer Society (ACS).
Rates of advanced-stage prostate cancer rose about 5% per year during that period.
NEW BLOOD TEST DETECTS 90% OF AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER CASES, BEATING CURRENT SCREENINGS
About 333,830 new cases of prostate cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the U.S. in 2026, and about 36,320 men are expected to die from the disease, according to the American Cancer Society.
One in eight men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, the same source stated.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Older men are at a higher risk of the disease, with six in 10 cases diagnosed in patients 65 and older. The average age at diagnosis is 67, with men under 40 rarely affected.
Prostate cancer is the second-most common cancer in men, behind only skin cancer, the ACS noted.
Signs and symptoms
Among men who undergo routine prostate cancer screening, the disease is usually caught early before symptoms emerge, per the ACS.
Typical early symptoms include problems urinating, a weak or slow urinary stream or an increased need to urinate. Some men may also notice blood in the urine or bodily fluids.
Biden, 83, announced his diagnosis in May 2025, after news that a "small nodule" had been found in the former president's prostate during a routine exam. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin, File)
More advanced symptoms may occur after the disease has spread. Those may include pain in the hips, back (spine), chest (ribs) or other areas, the ACS stated.
Men may also suffer from erectile dysfunction, weight loss, extreme fatigue, weakness in the legs or feet, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Screening recommendations

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) states that men aged 55 to 69 years should have the option to undergo periodic prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening to monitor for prostate cancer.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Before deciding whether to be screened, men should have an opportunity to discuss the potential benefits and harms of screening with their clinician and to incorporate their values and preferences in the decision," the USPSTF states.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force states that men aged 55 to 69 years should have the option to undergo periodic prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening to monitor for prostate cancer. (iStock)

While screening offers a "small potential benefit" of reducing the chances of dying from the disease, the agency noted that some men may experience negative effects, including false-positive results, overdiagnosis and overtreatment, and treatment complications.
Alternative prostate cancer screening methods are currently being researched, including one that uses a non-invasive urine test, as Fox News Digital recently reported.
Survival rates
For localized prostate cancers, where the disease is contained within the prostate, the five-year survival rate is at least 99%, according to the ACS.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For regional cases, where the disease has spread only to "nearby structures or lymph nodes," the five-year survival rate is also 99% or greater.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
If the cancer has spread to other areas of the body, the five-year survival rate drops to 37%.
Actual survival rates may vary based on the patient's age, overall health, how the cancer has progressed post-diagnosis, the disease's response to treatment and other factors, the ACS noted.

title: Common marriage habit could quietly kill your sex life, expert warns
summary: A clinical sexologist reveals the everyday habits that quietly kill intimacy and explains how couples can work together to reignite desire.
story: Dr. Anna Elton dives into research on sexual frequency, why partners benefit from agreeing on a comfortable routine and how open communication can help prevent one person from feeling neglected.

Sexual desire can change over the course of a marriage, particularly with age and major life changes. And research suggests certain lifestyle and relationship factors may also contribute to a lower libido.
But changes in desire or frequency do not necessarily mean a couple’s sex life is unhealthy, according to experts.
Dr. Anna Elton, a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said there is "no medically prescribed number that defines a healthy sex life."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA
"What's healthy is whether both partners feel connected, satisfied and respected in their intimate relationship," she told Fox News Digital.
"For some couples, that may mean several times a week, while for others it may be once or twice a month. The healthiest benchmark is mutual fulfillment."
There is no set benchmark for how often married couples should have sex, as long as both partners feel fulfilled, an expert said. (iStock)
Rather than comparing their sex lives to those of others, Elton encouraged couples to define what is healthy for their own relationship.

"Talk about what feels satisfying, how much time can pass before one or both of you starts feeling disconnected and what your warning signs are," she said. "Once you've agreed on that range, make a commitment to maintain it together."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Elton advised couples not to let too much time pass without "intentionally reconnecting" because prolonged disconnection can take a toll on the relationship.

"If we simply wait until the mood is perfect or the stars align, work, children and everyday responsibilities usually get in the way," she said. "Healthy relationships require intention. Both partners should share responsibility for initiating connection and creating the conditions where desire can develop."
The expert advised couples not to let too much time pass without "intentionally reconnecting" because prolonged disconnection can take a toll on the relationship. (iStock)

For many couples, building careers, raising children, caring for aging parents, managing finances and juggling other responsibilities can demand more of their attention, and they may not realize that the relationship itself has become a low priority.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"As a result, couples begin living parallel lives," Elton told Fox News Digital. "Conversations revolve around schedules, errands, bills and the kids. Intentional time together becomes less frequent. Affection, physical touch, flirting and playfulness become less frequent, replaced by stress, conflict and growing resentment.
"For many couples, those changes are among the earliest signs that the relationship is no longer being intentionally nurtured, and sexual intimacy declines soon afterward."
Less affection, physical touch, flirting and playfulness is an early sign that the relationship could be in danger. (iStock)

Elton countered that many couples she's worked with continued to have sex regularly to "keep the peace or avoid conflict." While their sex life appeared healthy from the outside, the couples felt "emotionally disconnected and unfulfilled."
"Physical intimacy and emotional closeness go hand in hand," she said. "If we want to improve our sex lives, we have to focus on the connection itself."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If one or both partners consistently feel rejected, lonely or resentful or avoid conversations about intimacy altogether, it's time to seek help."

If sex becomes painful or erectile difficulties arise or if hormonal concerns, trauma, depression, anxiety or persistent differences in desire are creating distress, couples should address these issues with a professional as early as possible, the expert advised.

If sex becomes painful or erectile difficulties arise – or if hormonal concerns, trauma, depression, anxiety or persistent differences in desire are creating distress – couples should address these issues with a professional as early as possible, the expert advised. (iStock)
One of the most common concerns Elton sees in her practice is differences in sexual desire, which she confirmed is "completely normal."
The key is to approach intimacy "as a team" because research has shown this leads to maintaining "stronger desire" over time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Being responsive means staying curious about your partner's experience," she said. "Instead of pressuring or withdrawing, couples communicate openly, respect each other's boundaries and work together to find an approach to intimacy that feels satisfying for both people."

Couples should also broaden their definition of intimacy, Elton suggested, as general affection, physical touch, flirting, emotional closeness and intentional time together can "help partners feel more connected and create the conditions where sexual desire naturally returns."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Beachgoers warned after deadly 'flesh-eating' bacteria kills 5 in southern state
summary: Five deaths in Louisiana from Vibrio vulnificus mark a sharp rise, as all nine cases involved open wounds exposed to warm seawater this year.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel shares how to stay protected from the 'flesh-eating' bacteria vibrio vulnificus on 'Fox News Live.'
A potentially deadly "flesh-eating" bacteria has killed five people in Louisiana this year, a sharp rise from the state’s typical death toll.
Health officials are warning beachgoers to take extra precautions before heading into the water.

Vibrio vulnificus is part of a wider group of Vibrio bacteria. Found primarily in warm, coastal waters, it can cause serious, potentially life-threatening infections when contaminated seawater enters an open wound, according to the CDC.
DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER
Infections can also occur when someone eats raw or undercooked shellfish, especially oysters.

The Louisiana Department of Health has reported nine cases and five deaths so far this year. All nine cases were linked to people entering seawater with open wounds, and all of the infected patients had existing medical conditions, officials said.
A potentially deadly "flesh-eating" bacteria has killed five people in Louisiana this year, a sharp rise from the state’s typical death toll. (iStock)
In previous years, the state has averaged seven cases and one death.
Vibrio bacteria are found in higher numbers from May to October, when water temperatures are warmer, the health department noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Although infections are rare, Vibrio vulnificus can cause an illness called vibriosis, often marked by vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, as well as potentially severe skin infections.

"People with severe infections may require intensive care or limb amputation," Louisiana health officials warned. "About one in five people with Vibrio vulnificus infection dies, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill."
Vibrio bacteria are found in higher numbers from May to October, when water temperatures are warmer, the health department noted. (Allison Joyce / AFP via Getty Images)
Initial signs and symptoms of a Vibrio skin infection include fever, redness, pain, swelling, warmth, discoloration and discharge, per the CDC.
While healthy people generally experience only mild symptoms, those who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease can face serious health risks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
If Vibrio vulnificus enters the bloodstream, it can cause advanced illness marked by fever, chills, septic shock and blistering skin lesions.

Some severe cases can cause an infection called necrotizing fasciitis, which is when the flesh around an open wound dies, the CDC cautions. This rare side effect has led to Vibrio vulnificus being described as "flesh-eating bacteria."
Diagnosis and treatment
The bacterial infection is diagnosed by testing cultures obtained from stool, wounds or blood, according to health officials.
For mild infections, the CDC recommends increasing fluid intake to prevent dehydration.
Those with severe or prolonged infections should receive antibiotics to improve survival rates.
Those with severe or prolonged infections should receive antibiotics to improve survival rates. (iStock)
For patients with infected wounds, surgery may be necessary to remove dead tissue.
About one in five people will die from the infection, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill, the CDC states.
Prevention tips
Health officials caution against entering warm saltwater or brackish water if any fresh cuts, scrapes or wounds are present.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
It’s also recommended to avoid consuming raw oysters and other raw shellfish, and to avoid cross-contamination of other foods with raw seafood or its juices.
Protective gloves should be worn when handling raw shellfish.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Those with liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV or thalassemia (a group of hereditary blood disorders) — as well as those who are taking immune-suppressing medications — are at a higher risk of complications and should take extra precautions, the CDC warns.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Organ harvesting began while patients still showed ‘signs of life,’ federal investigation finds
summary: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. says Network for Hope pressured medical personnel to proceed with organ procurement despite patients showing signs of life.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel interviews Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on the ethics of the organ donation industry and what his agency is doing about unsafe practices on 'Special Report.'

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has begun the decertification of Network for Hope, the federally designated organ procurement organization serving Kentucky and parts of Indiana, Ohio and West Virginia, following federal reviews that uncovered serious patient safety failures.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services initiated the decertification action after investigations revealed persistent safety issues, including instances where the organ harvesting process was initiated on patients who still showed active signs of life.

Appearing on America's Newsroom, Dr. Marc Siegel, a senior medical analyst for Fox News, described details from his interview with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. regarding the department's actions against the nonprofit organization.
EATING TOO MUCH PROTEIN COULD BACKFIRE, EXPERTS WARN AFTER LONGEVITY REVIEW
"Health and Human Services Secretary Kennedy is bringing to light horror stories about the dark corners of organ harvesting," Siegel said.
"The department is now pulling the accreditation of Kentucky's Network for Hope, the main organ procurement organization in the state."

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. affirmed strong support for ethical organ donation, drawing on his family's personal experience after his nephew saved lives as a donor. (Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Network for Hope's chief executive officer stated that the organization plans to appeal the federal decision, maintaining that it remains fully compliant with organ procurement and transportation network policies.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS
Siegel said he spoke with Secretary Kennedy about the case of TJ Hoover, a prospective donor who reportedly nearly had his organs removed by Network for Hope while still alive.
"Even after those signs of life, Kennedy says the organ procurement process continued until the physician refused to proceed," the doctor said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
HHS' Health Resources and Services Administration examined 351 cases at Network for Hope between 2021 and 2024 in which organ donation was authorized but ultimately not completed.
Federal investigations revealed multiple instances where organ harvesting procedures were initiated on patients who still showed active neurological function and signs of life. (Getty Images)
The review identified 103 cases with concerning features, including 73 patients with what HHS described as "neurological signs incompatible with organ donation."

"HHS says it uncovered 73 separate instances where the process of harvesting an organ should have been stopped sooner," Siegel said. "The investigation revealed that the nonprofit pressured medical personnel to proceed despite patients showing active signs of live and neurological function."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

According to federal officials, investigators found evidence of inadequate neurological assessments, poor coordination with hospital care teams, questionable consent practices and improper classification of causes of death.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Thirty percent of the procedures that they were performing had something wrong with them," Siegel added. "If there's a bad organization that's willing to do things that are unethical, they're going to get away with things at any place where they operate."
Network for Hope’s chief executive officer announced plans to appeal the federal decision, maintaining that the organization complies with all procurement safety policies. (iStock)
Despite the agency's findings, Siegel noted that Kennedy remains supportive of organ donation when conducted under proper standards, pointing to personal experience with his own family.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Kennedy says he strongly supports organ donation when it's done ethically and properly," Siegel said. "His own nephew, Michael Hines, saved multiple lives by donating his organs after his death at age 20."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Eating too much protein could backfire, experts warn after longevity review
summary: Excess protein may strain the body in sedentary people, but adding exercise and plant-based protein sources could unlock compounding longevity benefits.
story: Instead of restricting foods, dietitian Tanya Freirich recommends building a balanced plate with vegetables, protein and starch, and swapping some animal protein for beans, lentils, nuts or seeds to support better health.

A recent scientific review challenged the idea that consuming more protein necessarily leads to better health, suggesting that the optimal amount depends on factors such as age, activity level and overall health.

After reviewing more than 350 studies, researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison concluded that while higher protein intake can support muscle growth and other health benefits, consuming more than the body needs may offer little advantage.
In fact, it could even reduce longevity in some sedentary adults, particularly when protein comes from certain sources or amino acid profiles, they concluded.
LIVING LONGER COULD HINGE ON ONE SURPRISING DIETARY CHANGE, STUDY REVIEW SUGGESTS
For those wondering how to adjust their own diets in light of these findings, the answer lies in personalization, activity level and food sources, according to experts.
"We are hearing conflicting things from doctors ... and influencers," Tanya Freirich, a registered dietitian nutritionist in Charlotte, North Carolina, told Fox News Digital.
People who are active can still benefit from higher protein intake, the expert said. (iStock)
"The message lately has been to increase your protein," said the expert, who was not involved in the research.
"However, we do know that excess protein is associated with negative effects. It can put a strain on your kidney health, and it can interfere with bone and calcium homeostasis."
POPULAR SMOOTHIE INGREDIENT MAY REDUCE ONE KEY HEALTH BENEFIT, STUDY SUGGESTS
For sedentary individuals, cutting back on excess protein isn’t the only option, according to Freirich. Increasing physical activity can also help the body use nutrients more effectively.
"If you are moving your body — strength training, building muscle or doing sports — you probably do need a little bit more protein," she noted.
"Everyone should think about their personal situation and discuss it with healthcare providers to figure out the best route for them."

"Now, let's say you were a super active person and unfortunately had an injury and have gone down to a very sedentary level — you should modify your protein because your body is not utilizing it in the same way."
Exercise may also support longevity in ways that go beyond nutrition, Freirich noted, by helping people stay active and independent.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Adding exercise is always a good idea because it is associated with having fewer falls, having more joy in life and protecting you from injury," she said.

The recent analysis suggests that high-protein diets could have negative effects on longevity in sedentary individuals whose bodies are not actively using the extra nutrients to build or repair muscle. (iStock)
For those looking to rebalance their nutrition without doing a total overhaul, Freirich offered the following five tips.
No. 1: Focus on plate proportions: Aim for 50% of your plate to consist of vegetables, 25% protein and 25% starches or whole grains.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

No. 2: Do the quick math: A general guideline is to consume 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for adults with lower activity levels, while those who are more physically active may benefit from about 1.0 gram per kilogram per day.
No. 3: Eat the rainbow: Incorporate fruits and vegetables across various colors to ensure a diverse intake of vitamins and micro-nutrients.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

No. 4: Switch to plant proteins: Shift a portion of animal protein toward plant-based alternatives like lentils, beans, chickpeas and seeds. "A lot of people who were on protein-restricted diets and saw better health outcomes were eating a lot of their proteins from plants," Freirich noted.

No. 5: Stick to whole foods: Unprocessed foods support natural satiety signals. "Moving away from really processed foods to more unprocessed foods actually helps your body regulate a lot better," Freirich advised.
Swapping animal proteins for plant-based sources like beans, lentils and seeds provides alternative amino acid profiles alongside fiber, the nutritionist said. (iStock)
Ultimately, dietary choices shouldn't be governed by a single headline or study, according to the expert.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Research is ever-evolving," Freirich said. "Everyone should think about their personal situation and discuss it with healthcare providers to figure out the best route for them."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: FDA approves first-ever mRNA flu vaccine for millions of older Americans
summary: A new mRNA flu vaccine showed a 27% reduction in flu cases in a clinical trial, but its path to FDA approval faced an early regulatory setback.
story: An experimental pancreatic cancer vaccine shows promise in its first human trial, generating an immune response in 90% of high-risk patients.
The FDA has approved the nation's first flu vaccine made with mRNA technology, the manufacturer, Moderna, announced on Thursday.
The vaccine, which is based on the same messenger RNA platform used in COVID-19 shots, has been fully approved for adults ages 50-64 ahead of the 2026-2027 flu season.
For adults 65 and older, the vaccine received accelerated approval, which allows the vaccine to be used while Moderna completes an additional study to confirm its effectiveness in seniors.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
Experts say mRNA vaccines can be updated more quickly to protect against changes in circulating flu strains.
The approval was based on a phase 3 clinical trial including around 40,000 participants, in which the new vaccine was found to effect a 27% reduction in flu cases compared to a standard flu vaccine.
The FDA has approved the nation's first flu vaccine made with mRNA technology, the manufacturer, Moderna, announced on Thursday. (iStock)
No major safety concerns were identified in the trial, according to the announcement.
It was found to have more short-term side effects than conventional flu shots – including arm pain, fatigue, headache and fever – although these were noted to be generally mild and temporary.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"This is not a universal vaccine, but is geared for rapid turnaround once the yearly strains have been identified," said Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst.
"It’s similar to the COVID vaccine and was found to be 25% to 30% more effective than the current flu vaccine," he added. "It’s geared to protect the elderly."
Experts say mRNA vaccines can be updated more quickly to protect against changes in circulating flu strains. (iStock)

Older adults face the biggest risk of severe influenza. During the 2024-2025 season, people 65 and older accounted for 57% of flu-related hospitalizations and 71% of deaths, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
An estimated 51 million Americans contracted the flu during the 2024-2025 season, with the virus linked to around 710,000 hospitalizations and 45,000 deaths, per the above source.
Looking ahead, the approval could pave the way for combination vaccines that protect against multiple respiratory viruses at once, according to Moderna. (Reuters/Brian Snyder)

Earlier this year, the new mRNA vaccine faced a regulatory setback when the FDA initially refused to review Moderna's application, citing concerns about the design of its clinical trial, the Associated Press reported.
Moderna disputed the decision, and the FDA later agreed to move forward with the review.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
In June, an independent FDA advisory committee agreed that the vaccine's benefits outweighed its risks, paving the way for its approval.

Looking ahead, the approval could pave the way for combination vaccines that protect against multiple respiratory viruses at once, according to Moderna.
The company said it is pursuing a combined flu/COVID vaccine, with the goal of giving people one seasonal shot.

title: FDA widens cyclospora outbreak investigation to six more states as confirmed cases top 6,000
summary: The FDA says 6,358 cyclospora cases are now linked to contaminated iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, with 278 hospitalizations and two deaths.
story: Panelists debate whether more government is really the answer to controlling the outbreak.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its investigation of the cyclospora outbreak on Wednesday, announcing that there are thousands of confirmed cases across more than a dozen states.

The intestinal illness was first reported in July among people who developed severe diarrhea after eating shredded lettuce at Taco Bell. Health authorities later traced the outbreak to contaminated lettuce supplied to the fast-food restaurant by Taylor Farms de Mexico.
"Due to the additional interview data, the outbreak now includes people who reported exposure to Taco Bell or recalled Taylor Farms de Mexico iceberg lettuce," the FDA said in a news release.

According to the FDA, 6,358 cases have now been reported across 15 states. Six states — Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina — were added since the administration’s previous update on July 24.
CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
A crop of lettuce is watered in Bakersfield, California, in 2021. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The FDA said the outbreak began on June 22, nearly a month before Taylor Farms de Mexico voluntarily recalled all lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 17.
Since then, cyclosporiasis has been linked to 278 hospitalizations and two deaths in Michigan, according to the FDA.

"We also expect to continue to see the number of confirmed cases rise, despite the recall, due to the fact that it can take as long as six weeks for CDC and state officials to determine if a sick person is part of this outbreak," the FDA said.
A massive surge in cyclospora cases means people may be mistaking this parasitic foodborne infection for a standard summer stomach bug. (iStock)
SENATE CONFIRMS NEW CDC DIRECTOR AS DIARRHEA-CAUSING PARASITE OUTBREAK SWEEPS US

Cyclospora is a single-celled parasite that can cause stomach cramps, nausea, fatigue, weight loss and other health problems, though some infected people remain asymptomatic, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Symptoms usually begin about one week after being infected and can last for a few days to a month, according to the CDC. Symptoms can also appear to go away before returning one or more times.
Man sits on a bed and holds his stomach while home alone. Cyclospora can cause stomach cramps, as well as a number of other symptoms. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FDA again urged consumers and retailers to throw away contaminated lettuce, including Marketside-branded products sold in grocery stores across 27 states in early July.
Health officials also recommend sanitizing any surfaces that came into contact with the lettuce and contacting a doctor if symptoms develop after eating it.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Popular smoothie ingredient may reduce one key health benefit, study suggests
summary: A viral video claims bananas degrade blueberry benefits in smoothies, based on recent research, but dietitians argue that fruit shouldn't be villainized.
story: Registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein weighs in on claims that bananas reduce the health benefits of berries in smoothies, noting that the current research shouldn't be overstated.
Bananas are a smoothie staple, but a viral social media video has raised questions about whether they could reduce the nutritional benefits of other ingredients, such as blueberries.

In a July appearance on the "Mel Robbins Podcast," Dr. Rhonda Patrick, a biomedical scientist and founder of FoundMyFitness, demonstrated how she likes to make her smoothies, which do not include bananas.

Bananas contain polyphenol oxidase (PPO), an enzyme that can break down polyphenols, which are beneficial for gut, heart and brain health, according to Patrick, who is based in San Diego. PPO is also responsible for turning cut fruit brown.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Recent studies suggest that when a banana is added to a blueberry smoothie, fewer beneficial polyphenols are absorbed from the berries.
Bananas contain polyphenol oxidase (PPO), an enzyme that can break down polyphenols in fruits like blueberries, which are beneficial for gut, heart and brain health. (iStock)

Instead, Patrick uses avocado to give the smoothie the same creamy texture with 95% less sugar, she said. Avocado also adds more vitamins and monounsaturated fat, which can increase absorption of carotenoids, like lutein and zeaxanthin, from kale in the smoothie.
This opinion sparked debate in the online nutrition community, with some dietitians and nutritionists arguing that bananas should not be villainized based on a small body of research.
STUDY FINDS SPECIAL TOMATO DRINK MAY REDUCE INFLAMMATION IN ADULTS WITH OBESITY
The study Patrick referenced, which was published in the journal Food & Function in 2023, analyzed food absorption in eight healthy men.

On separate days, participants drank either a banana smoothie (high in an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase), drank a mixed berry smoothie (low in the enzyme) or took flavan-3-ol capsules (dietary supplements that contain concentrated plant compounds) with milk.
Study results revealed that the banana smoothie produced a peak concentration of polyphenols that were about 84% lower than the flavan-3-ol capsules. (iStock)
Blood tests showed that people absorbed about 84% fewer beneficial plant compounds after drinking the banana smoothie than after taking the flavan-3-ol capsules.
While researchers didn't test a banana-blueberry smoothie, the results suggest that bananas could reduce the benefits of foods high in flavan-3-ols.
LIVING LONGER COULD HINGE ON SURPRISING DIETARY CHANGE, STUDY REVIEW SUGGESTS
Los Angeles-based registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein, author of the upcoming book "Beyond the Shot," said the findings are "interesting," but don't tell the whole story.
"It doesn't mean the smoothie loses all of its health benefits," she said. "You're still getting fiber from the banana, and many other beneficial nutrients from polyphenol-rich fruits."

Muhlstein pointed out that the study included only eight participants and has not yet been replicated. She also noted that researchers used a standardized cocoa-derived flavanol supplement instead of whole fruits, such as berries, which may be absorbed differently by the body.
While researchers didn't test a banana-blueberry smoothie, the results suggest that bananas could reduce the benefits of foods high in flavan-3-ols. (iStock)

In a follow-up post on Instagram, responding to the backlash from the original post, Patrick said, "You can add bananas to your blueberry smoothies. However, you should know that you are going to degrade some of the polyphenols in those blueberries."

"Bananas are nutritious, I eat them, and this is not a reason to stop," she added in the caption. "But if your goal is to preserve as many of the berry polyphenols as possible, the chemistry matters."
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Not every beneficial compound in blueberries will be eliminated by bananas, Patrick wrote, as the fruit contains many other polyphenols, including anthocyanins.
"This was a small study that should be replicated," she said. "But the magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie."
"The magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie."
New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco agreed that the findings don't mean everyone should avoid bananas.
Unlike well-established advice to limit processed meats and added sugar, the guidance on bananas is more nuanced and doesn't apply to everyone, she told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
As nutrition advice spreads on social media, DeCicco said it's important to remember that everyone's health needs are different and to consult a doctor before following online recommendations.

The broader issue, she noted, is that Americans aren’t eating enough nutrient-rich foods, like bananas and berries, and are instead consuming more processed foods that have been linked to chronic disease.
"It doesn't need to be so complicated all the time," a nutritionist said. "If you're eating a banana instead of french fries, that's good." (iStock)

"That’s why Americans are fatter and sicker than they've ever been, so I think focus on that more," DeCicco advised. "It doesn't need to be so complicated all the time … If you're eating a banana instead of french fries, that's good."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Nutrition should be individualized, DeCicco said. Someone who eats mostly fast-food should focus on replacing processed foods with fruits and vegetables, while someone with a more advanced nutrition plan may benefit from limiting high-carb, high-sugar fruits like bananas.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
For those trying to lose weight and balance blood sugar, choosing fruits that are lower in sugar and higher in fiber may help with these outcomes.
"It really [depends] on where you're coming from and what your health journey is," DeCicco said.
Those who are looking to maximize their polyphenol intake can use frozen zucchini, avocado or Greek yogurt in place of banana in a smoothie, nutritionists say. (iStock)
Those looking to maximize polyphenol intake can swap bananas for frozen zucchini, avocado or Greek yogurt in smoothies for the same creamy texture, Muhlstein added.

title: Viagra could do more than advertised as study reveals surprising health superpower
summary: Sildenafil, Viagra's active ingredient, may restrict cancer metastasis by limiting cancer cells' cholesterol access, a new study has found.
story: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence and potentially new diagnoses.
Viagra could do more than give men a boost in the bedroom, as new research suggests it may have benefits for cancer patients.
The prescription medication, which is manufactured and distributed by Viatris, is commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction by increasing blood flow during sexual stimulation.

It was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
A new study published by the American Association for Cancer Research found that the pill may have properties that can prevent cancer from spreading.

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, led by Dr. Yarden Ariav in the lab of professor Ayelet Erez, found that Viagra’s active ingredient — sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor — may restrict cancer metastasis, or the formation of new tumors.
Viagra’s active ingredient, sildenafil, may restrict cancer cells from spreading, a new study suggests. (Getty Images)

The team, which included scientists at the U.S. National Cancer Institute, analyzed human and mouse cancer cells, genetic experiments and 20 years of health data from 5 million members of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest nonprofit healthcare provider and health insurer. They also examined how genes, proteins, fats, cholesterol and cellular energy interact.

The analysis revealed that sildenafil limits the cancer cell’s ability to make use of cholesterol, which is an important mechanism in how the cell breaks away from the primary tumor and migrates throughout the body, according to a press release from the American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Sildenafil was found to block an enzyme called phosphodiesterase type 5, or PDE5, and increase the signaling molecule called cGMP, which dilates blood vessels – the feature that has made Viagra a successful treatment for erectile dysfunction.

According to the researchers, cGMP also binds to a protein that transports cholesterol within cells, reducing the cholesterol available for essential cellular functions. Cancer cells are "particularly vulnerable to this reduction in cholesterol supply," they noted.

Viagra was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials. (Alex Segre/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Based on their findings, the researchers suggested that combining Viagra-related drugs with statins, which lower cholesterol, could help slow the spread of cancer by reducing tumor cells' access to both existing and newly produced cholesterol.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We have uncovered a new biological pathway that links a well-known signaling molecule to cholesterol regulation within cells and shown how this pathway can be harnessed to interfere with the ability of cancer cells to form metastases," Erez, senior researcher and dean of Weizmann’s Miriam and Aaron Gutwirth Medical School, commented in a statement.

Combining drugs from the Viagra family with statins – a class of drugs responsible for reducing cholesterol production in the body – may be even more effective in restricting the spread of cancer, the researchers suggested. (iStock)

"Beyond their therapeutic promise, our findings highlight that cancer biology is shaped not only by mutations in tumor cells, but also by the patient’s metabolic state and by medications they are already taking for other conditions."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The researcher added that this study "underscores the importance of treating the whole patient – not just the cancer – when tailoring the most effective therapy."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study’s use of mouse models could pose a limitation to the final implications, as cancer treatment may not always translate similarly to humans, the researchers acknowledged.
The human evidence is also observational, which reveals an association instead of a proven cause and effect.
Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors and the medication's manufacturer for comment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 5 reasons more Americans are cutting off their own parents, according to psychologist
summary: The spotlight on NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers' family estrangement has sparked renewed interest in why relatives become estranged. A psychologist breaks down five common contributing factors.
story: Dr. Richard L. Blake, a British psychologist and author based in Austin, Texas, shared five factors that he believes commonly contribute to fractured family relationships.
Cutting off family members is becoming more and more common, leading experts to consider the drivers of the division.

NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers' years-long estrangement from members of his family — which reportedly ended recently after a reconciliation with his parents — has renewed public interest in why some relatives become permanently divided.
A 2025 YouGov survey found that 38% of U.S. adults are estranged from at least one family member, including siblings, parents, children or grandparents.
'DOORMAT MOM' CUT OFF BY DAUGHTER AMID ESTRANGEMENT TREND: ‘COMPLETELY BLINDSIDED’

Based on his research and work in the field of family estrangement, Dr. Richard L. Blake, a British psychologist and author based in Austin, Texas, shared the following five factors that he believes commonly contribute to fractured family relationships.
No. 1: Political and value differences

A longstanding study of more than 2,000 mother-adult child relationships found that "value dissimilarity" was a strong predictor of estrangement, suggesting that differing beliefs may play a large role in family rifts.
Cutting off family members is becoming more and more common, leading experts to consider the drivers of the division. (iStock)
"That could be political values, that could be gender ideology," Blake told Fox News Digital.

"There were people more likely to cut off someone for having a different opinion than for people who have done serious violent crimes," he said. "So certainly, political differences are a big problem."
No. 2: Social media influence

Heavy social media use has been linked to poorer parent-child relationships. A study of nearly 9,800 teens found that spending more than two hours a day on social media was linked to significantly greater odds of negative relationships with one or both parents.
Blake believes social media may also normalize family estrangement by exposing users to viral "no contact" stories and encouraging what he described as "word-of-mouth mimicry."
SECOND LADY USHA VANCE GETS CANDID ABOUT NEW BABY, JUGGLING FOUR CHILDREN AND MOTHERHOOD

"Someone might see a video on TikTok — 'I cut off my parents, and I'm much happier now. They were toxic narcissistic boundary crossers. And now I'm great,'" he said. "And people mimic that. Or they think, 'Oh, this person's getting a lot of attention.'"
Although he acknowledged that there are no long-term studies that have definitively documented an increase, "that doesn't mean absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence."

A long-standing study of more than 2,000 mother-adult child relationships found that "value dissimilarity" was a strong predictor of estrangement, suggesting that differing beliefs may play a large role in family rifts. (iStock)
According to Blake, society has shifted away from what he described as a "dignity culture" toward one that places greater value on "victim culture."

"So now it's a race to the bottom," he said. "If you don't have enough victim status because of the way you were born, you can create a victim status by suggesting your parents abused you or neglected you … and therefore you have value, a reason to cut them off."
No. 3: ‘Therapy culture'
The expert also pointed to what he described as "therapy culture," claiming that changing attitudes toward trauma and abuse have influenced how some people view relationships with their parents.

"Another justification is, ‘I cut off my parents to protect my mental health’ — and this is a sort of false belief," he told Fox News Digital. "There is this huge bias that if you're struggling in your adult life, it must be because your parents did something they shouldn't or didn't do something."
An expert argued that family relationships remain one of the strongest protective factors for mental health. (iStock)
Blake argued that family relationships remain one of the strongest protective factors for mental health.
"Families are one of the most evidence-based buffers against mental illness," he said. "There’s this myth that families are not important."
The psychologist pointed to a well-known Minnesota study of adopted twins, which found that twins often resembled their biological parents more than the adoptive parents who raised them.
BECKHAM FAMILY FEUD: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT BROOKLYN'S WIFE, BILLIONAIRE HEIRESS NICOLA PELTZ

He also cited a 2024 study led by German sociologist Karsten Hank, which found that adults estranged from parents or siblings reported lower life satisfaction and more depressive symptoms than those who maintained family relationships.

"So it seems like it's certainly a health event for parents who get cut off, and it's probably a negative health event for the kids or the adult children who are doing the cutoff," he said. "It's this lie they're getting sold on social media: ‘Cut off your parents and your mental health will be better.’"
No. 4: Communication breakdowns
The way families communicate during conflict can determine whether disagreements escalate into long-term estrangement, according to Blake.
It’s important to listen first, he said, noting that "hostage negotiation" can be useful in these scenarios.
"Perhaps we should be learning from our grandparents more than the therapists."

"[That means] listening to the other person and then repeating back what they said as you understood it and validating that … and then waiting until that person's really finished before you give your side of it."
Blake also raised the issue of "moralized language," or "therapy words" that get thrown at parents — "such as abuse, toxic, boundaries, narcissists, gaslighting."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"When you use moralized language like that, compromise becomes far more difficult," he said.

"So I tell parents to pause before they really react ... and then say back, ‘Okay, you've used the word toxic. Can you describe the behavior or behaviors that you consider to be toxic?’ Then you're dealing with facts and events, rather than who’s a better person or who's the worst person."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The psychologist also recommends starting with "I" statements rather than using the word "you," and also avoid using the words "always" and "never."
No. 5: Outside influences
Finally, Blake said that outside influences — including romantic partners and evolving parenting philosophies — can also contribute to family estrangement.
Heavy social media use has been linked to poorer parent-child relationships. (iStock)
Those outside influences may differ by gender, he noted, with romantic partners often playing a larger role for men.

As an example, Blake pointed to public figures such as Brooklyn Beckham and Prince Harry, suggesting that romantic partners can sometimes influence how people view their relationships with family members.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Conflicting parenting philosophies may also strain family relationships, as adult children and grandparents sometimes disagree over how children should be raised, according to Blake.
"Parenting styles are obviously different, and they've changed a lot over the last few years," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If you look at the outcomes of the gentle parenting or the permissive parenting that we've slipped into, we have the most mentally ill generation in history, the least fit for adulthood," Blake suggested. "Perhaps we should be learning from our grandparents more than the therapists."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Vulnerable Dem's campaign pitch clashes with 'radical' voting record on top culture war issue
summary: Sarah Trone Garriott's Iowa legislature votes on bathroom policy and girls' sports clash with her new campaign video opposing men in women's locker rooms.
story: Concerned Women for America spokesperson Macy Petty Charles and assistant United States attorney Julie Hamill discuss the Supreme Court's decision allowing states to ban transgender athletes from competing in girls' sports on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic candidate for Congress in Iowa's 3rd Congressional District, is trying to reassure voters that she doesn’t support men having access to women’s locker rooms — a stance she believes her opponents have tried to obfuscate.

"I’m a mom with two kids in Iowa public schools. Their education and safety literally keep me up at night. So, when my opponent cherry-picks and twists my record, I have to set it straight," Trone Garriott said in a recent campaign video.
"I oppose letting men in women’s locker rooms," she added.
WASHINGTON MOTHER SAYS SHE FOUND ADULT MALE SHOWERING IN WOMEN'S LOCKER ROOM DURING CHILDREN'S SWIM MEET

State Sen. and candidate for Iowa’s 3rd congressional district Sarah Trone Garriott speaks during the Polk County Democrats’ spring dinner on April 7, 2026, in Des Moines. (Cody Scanlan/USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

However, Trone Garriott's voting record from her time in the Iowa legislature is clashing with her assertions, complicating the picture for her as she attempts to flip one of the country’s most competitive House seats and topple incumbent Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Even before Trone Garriott captured the Democratic nomination to run in the district earlier this year, Republicans have sought to highlight parts of her record that seem to show she has championed positions farther left than the campaign she’s currently running.
Many have bashed a Muslim prayer she offered up on the Iowa Senate floor and how, as a Lutheran minister, she officiated a satanic wedding.
However, it was Trone Garriott’s stance on bathroom policy that Vice President J.D. Vance zeroed in on in a campaign speech for Nunn earlier this year.
"His opponent voted to push biological males in girls’ sports as early as kindergarten. She was voting against banning gender transition surgeries for minors," Vance said.

Vance, like other Republican critics, referred to two key votes Trone Garriott cast in the Iowa Senate: one, passed in 2023, prohibits elementary and secondary schools from letting someone enter a bathroom "that does not correspond with the person’s biological sex." A second bill, which became law in 2022, sets the eligibility rules for school and college sports teams based on biological sex.
LUTHERAN MINISTER AND HOUSE CANDIDATE UNDER FIRE AFTER RECOUNTING HER PART IN SATANIST COUPLE'S WEDDING

State Senator Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democrat from Iowa and U.S. congressional candidate, works behind the counter at the West Des Moines United Methodist stand during the Iowa State Fair in Des Moines, Iowa, US, on Wednesday, Aug. 13, 2025. (Scott Morgan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Trone Garriott voted against both of them.

Her votes seem consistent with previous statements she made in 2023 where she indicated bathroom policies and sports policies looking to restrict participants were based on racial and gender tensions.

"It’s very threatening of the idea of the white, male powerful figure because it muddies the waters and makes things ambiguous and confusing," Trone Garriott said in an address with the United Methodist Church, speaking on politics and faith.

"We see all sorts of responses happening in legislation and in community conflict — a lot more emphasis on really funding and supporting the private schools, the parents’ rights. And within that, the parents’ rights piece is used to enact book bans, sports bans about who can play and who can compete; it’s really couched in a language of there’s a threat to women. And white men are responsible to protect women against threats."

Her campaign did not address how her previous votes and statements align with her current campaign positions, or whether those positions have changed. But in a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Trone Garriott said she stood by her campaign video.

"Sarah does not want men in women’s locker rooms. As a parent, there is nothing more important than the safety of our children, that’s why she will always stand up for a parent’s right to decide what’s best for their children," Zach Schenkman, the spokesperson, said.
PROGRESSIVE TALARICO KNIFES BIDEN'S OPEN BORDER, TRIES MODERATING STANCE ON KEY ISSUES IN TEXAS SENATE RACE

State Senator Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democrat from Iowa and US congressional candidate, during a primary election night event at The Loft DSM in Des Moines, Iowa, US, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. ((Photographer: Scott Morgan/Bloomberg via Getty Images))
In her campaign video, Trone Garriott said she believed too much political attention had been given to the topic.
"Politicians have become too extreme on these issues. I’ll always put kids and families first," Trone Garriott said.
At least one Republican strategist isn't buying the switch in position.

"Even Sarah Trone Garriott's handlers realize her radical record and insane history of woke statements is completely unelectable in Iowa. No amount of false ads or consultant lies will hide the truth about the Wicked Witch of Woke and her sinister trans-for-all obsession," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC) said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Nunn, the district’s current representative, last won re-election in a 51.8% to 47.9% victory over Democratic challenger Lanon Baccam in 2024. With the Democratic nomination in tow, Trone Garriott will face off against Nunn in the Nov. 3 general election.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump’s sly plane switch raises eyebrows over safety of passengers left behind on board
summary: Trump secretly switched to a military jet in Turkey over an Iranian missile threat, leaving journalists and White House staff aboard the decoy aircraft.
story: Senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich provides details on President Donald Trump's decision to switch planes to evade a potential threat from Iran.

Reports of President Donald Trump’s secret move to a military jet during last month’s NATO summit in Turkey has put a rare security trade-off in focus: As officials apparently sought to shield Trump from a credible Iranian threat, White House staff, Secret Service agents, U.S. Military members and journalists remained aboard the decoy aircraft.

The White House did not return Fox News’ request for comment on whether officials assessed a separate risk to those left aboard the plane, which could have included Secretary of State Marco Rubio. It's not clear what, if any, protective measures were in place.
Air Force One is the call sign of the plane the U.S. president is traveling aboard, not the name of a specific aircraft.

The Washington Post first reported that Trump secretly switched to a military jet after appearing to board the older Air Force One in Turkey. Journalists and White House staff traveling with the president for the trip abroad remained on the aircraft that flew to the United Kingdom. Trump later rejoined the group before continuing home, according to the report.

U.S. President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the NATO leaders summit at the Bestepe Presidential Compound in Ankara, Turkey, July 8, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
TRUMP USED CATERING TRUCK, AIR FORCE ONE DECOY TO EVADE IRAN THREAT: REPORT

In a separate follow-up to that article, the Wall Street Journal reported that Israeli intelligence briefed the Trump administration on a threat to use shoulder-fired missiles against Air Force One. It also noted that Rubio was among top aides who remained aboard the older aircraft.

Former Secret Service agent Bill Gage told Fox News that the people aboard the aircraft "probably did face an elevated risk." But he described the reported operation as a calculated response to the threat environment surrounding Trump.
"Any travel with him should be considered a risk," Gage said. "I think some members of the government at the highest levels made a calculated risk to not tell anyone on the fake AF1."

The key distinction in the reporting is that the threat was allegedly aimed at the aircraft believed to be carrying Trump, rather than at the older jet itself. The secret slip-away by the president left all passengers on the plane as potential collateral of any attacks, with no public accounting of if there were additional protections in place for them in the heightened threat environment.

Reporters traveling on the older Air Force One from Turkey to the United Kingdom recount being asked to close their window shades as the plane took off. Asked later that day whether he knew why reporters were asked to close the shades, Trump replied: "You’re probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with."
"I’m number one on their list, before you," he told a reporter. "But if I go, you go right? So perhaps some day you want to change professions."
This photo shows the press boarding the Air Force One aircraft from Ankara, while a catering truck is located at the front of the plane. (Pool)
TRUMP SAYS HE'S IRAN'S 'NO. 1' TARGET AS RENEWED CONFLICT RAISES ASSASSINATION FEARS

Gage told Fox News Digital that the reported operation was likely kept to a very small circle because of the security sensitivity. "Very few people would have been told about this plan ahead of time."
He said the decision to actually move Trump to a different jet suggested officials were acting on serious intelligence.

"Overall, the threat must have been substantial and corroborated to conduct the switch/ruse. The highest levels of the government and intelligence agencies (CIA/NSA etc.) would have been involved in analyzing the threat and developing countermeasures."

Robert "Bobby" McDonald, a former senior Secret Service official, said deceptive presidential movements — sometimes referred to as "shell games" — are unusual but a part of the Secret Service playbook when credible intelligence demands extraordinary measures.
McDonald said the Air Force, rather than the Secret Service, is responsible for protecting presidential aircraft and said he believed both planes were likely being monitored.

"I find it hard to believe that those two planes were not being tracked, were not being escorted by other aircraft from either allies or our Air Force," he said. "There's no way in the world that the Secret Service, the White House staff, and the White House military office, were going to let those two planes dangle out there and and and be fending for themselves."
The Pentagon and the Air Force referred questions to the White House.

Trump's move isn't the first time Air Force One aircraft have been put to use to balk potential threats. During President Bill Clinton’s 2000 visit to Pakistan, a marked decoy aircraft arrived first and Secret Service agents disembarked before Clinton landed separately in an unmarked plane.
Military aircraft which reportedly flew President Donald Trump to from Turkey to the United Kingdom. (Pool)
But the reported Turkey operation differs from many past surprise trips, in which a limited press pool traveled with the president and was sworn to secrecy.
Jake Tapper, who traveled with Obama on a secret trip to Afghanistan, said prior White Houses have used deception to protect presidents but that the reported Turkey operation was different.

"Obviously the life of the president is paramount, and previous White Houses have used deception to protect the president’s life. But no officials I’ve spoken to have ever before heard of using an AF1 full of WH staff and journalists as a decoy during an imminent threat," the CNN anchor said.
Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer defended the reported deception as a necessary protective measure if the threat was credible.
