AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
DoorDash Air plans to use company-built drones to deliver eligible food, medicine and everyday essentials. (DoorDash)
DoorDash becomes a certified air carrier

DoorDash announced the FAA certification on July 29, 2026. The company says it is the eighth drone operator to earn this type of federal air carrier certificate. The FAA uses Part 135 certification for companies that carry other people's property for payment. For drones, it provides the regulatory path for commercial package deliveries beyond a pilot's direct line of sight.

Getting certified requires a five-phase FAA review. The agency evaluates the operator's aircraft, maintenance procedures and safety program. Even after earning the certificate, an operator still needs airspace authorization. It may also need exemptions or waivers for flights beyond visual line of sight. State rules and local land-use requirements can also affect where a delivery hub operates. So, DoorDash has cleared a major federal hurdle. Still, each real-world delivery network will require more planning and approval.
Why DoorDash wants to deliver orders by drone

Anyone who has watched a hot meal slowly travel across town can understand the appeal. DoorDash says more than 20% of its orders in 2025 traveled between three and five miles. Those orders took nearly 25% longer than shorter trips, according to the company.

DoorDash blames part of that delay on the challenge of matching a Dasher with a mid-range order. A driver may prefer several shorter deliveries near a busy restaurant area instead of one longer trip. A drone could take the longer order while a Dasher remains close to restaurants. As a result, the customer could get a faster delivery while the driver moves on to another nearby order.

DoorDash estimates that drone deliveries completed during 2025 took an average of about 25 minutes. The company also says some locations in its partner drone pilots saw order volume rise by roughly 30%. That increase continued during the nine weeks after the pilot began. Those are DoorDash's figures, so performance could change by location, weather and the type of order. Still, they help explain why the company wants more control over the aircraft carrying its deliveries.
CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'
DoorDash will continue its partnerships with drone partners like Alphabet's Wing as it designs its own aircraft. (DoorDash)
DoorDash Air will build its own delivery drones
That is the same robotics and autonomy group behind DoorDash's Dot delivery robot.

DoorDash says its drone will be designed and built in the United States. The majority of its components will also come from the U.S., according to the company. DoorDash has not revealed the aircraft's range, payload capacity or final design. A DoorDash spokesperson told CyberGuy that the company plans to share more details about those specifics this fall.
DoorDash drones will work alongside human Dashers

DoorDash says Dashers will continue handling the vast majority of its daily deliveries. That makes sense. A drone cannot walk into an apartment building or carry a large catering order upstairs. It also may struggle with bad weather or a location without a suitable drop zone.
Instead, DoorDash wants its Autonomous Delivery Platform to select the best method for each order. The platform can assign a Dasher. It can also choose an autonomous option such as Dot or a drone.

For example, a small order traveling four miles to a suburban house may fit a drone. A large grocery order going to a high-rise apartment will likely need a person. This approach follows a broader shift across the delivery industry. Uber Eats has also moved toward drone deliveries, while other companies continue testing robots and airborne delivery systems.
What the FAA certification does not guarantee

FAA certification gives DoorDash the legal foundation to operate an air carrier. It does not provide blanket permission to begin unlimited drone flights in every city. DoorDash has not announced its first DoorDash Air markets. The company also has not provided a detailed timeline for deliveries using its in-house aircraft.

In addition, longer autonomous routes may require FAA approval for beyond visual line of sight operations. Local zoning, environmental reviews and community concerns can also shape where hubs are built. Noise could become a major issue. The FAA notes that drone noise may bother a community even when it falls below the level of a significant environmental impact.
Therefore, early service will likely remain limited to carefully selected areas. Suburban neighborhoods with predictable routes and open drop-off spaces may prove easier than dense urban blocks.
JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA
DoorDash says drones will handle select orders while human Dashers continue making most of the company’s deliveries. (DoorDash)
What this means to you

DoorDash drone delivery could shorten the wait for small, urgent orders. Cold medicine could arrive without waiting for a driver to cross town. A nurse finishing a long shift might get a hot meal faster. A forgotten phone charger could reach you before your battery runs out. However, availability will depend heavily on where you live. Your address may need to fall within an eligible drone delivery zone. The order must also meet the aircraft's weight and size limits. DoorDash told CyberGuy that it is testing the aircraft to operate across a wider range of weather conditions and climates. The company said it will pause operations during extreme weather until conditions return to an operable level.

You should also look closely at the final cost. DoorDash has not said whether its new in-house DoorDash Air service will carry a separate fee or change how tipping works. The company also has not explained whether customers will choose between a DoorDash Air drone and a Dasher once the new service launches. DoorDash's current partner-operated program does allow eligible customers to select drone delivery at checkout.

For now, think of DoorDash Air as an important step toward wider service rather than a nationwide launch. The federal certificate gives DoorDash the regulatory foundation to operate its own commercial drone delivery service. However, individual operations may still require airspace authorization and other FAA approvals. The next test will be whether DoorDash can make drone delivery reliable enough for an ordinary Tuesday night dinner. For more background on how companies are already testing airborne orders, check out how drones are changing food delivery.
Kurt's key takeaways

DoorDash has spent years learning how to move orders through streets. Now it wants to control what happens in the sky. FAA certification gives DoorDash Air a serious start. The company has the app, the restaurant relationships and billions of past orders to study. It also knows where deliveries slow down. Still, building a drone is only one piece of the job. DoorDash must prove that its aircraft can operate safely and consistently. It must also keep food intact while avoiding noise problems and neighborhood resistance. Human Dashers are not disappearing. Instead, DoorDash wants drones and robots to handle specific trips that could be faster without a car.

title: Fake party invitation scam can hijack your computer
summary: Fake party invitations trick victims into downloading malware that gives criminals remote access to computers and spreads through contact lists.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You sit down at your computer to clear out your inbox. Then you spot a party invitation from someone you recognize. Maybe it appears to come from a friend. Perhaps the sender belongs to a group you know. Either way, the familiar name makes the message feel safe enough to open.

Inside, everything looks cheerful. There is an envelope graphic, a friendly note and what appears to be an invitation for a wedding or retirement party. However, you cannot see the event details yet. The message tells you to save the invitation or install something to join the guest list.

That request should stop you cold. A legitimate party invitation should not require you to install software before you can see when or where the event takes place. That small download could give a criminal remote access to your computer. Here’s how this fake invitation scam works and what you can do before one click puts your computer and contacts at risk.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA
A fake party invitation can trick recipients into downloading software that gives criminals remote access to a Windows computer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How malicious party invitations reach your inbox

The scam begins with trust. An invitation appears to come from someone whose name you recognize, so you become less suspicious. Criminals may copy the look of a legitimate invitation platform. They can add a colorful envelope, an exclusive-sounding message and a button that promises to reveal the details.

The email has one main purpose: getting you to click. Once you press the invitation, the message sends you to a separate website. That page says a friend sent you something and asks you to download a file to view it.
The request may seem simple. Still, party invitations normally open inside a website or app. They do not need to install a program on your computer.
Why the fake invitation page looks convincing

The landing page may contain a large "Download invitation" button. It may also display a familiar company name inside the web address. However, seeing a trusted brand somewhere in a link proves very little. Criminals can place that name inside a much longer address or add extra letters that make the domain look authentic at a glance.

You need to identify the real domain instead of focusing on the first familiar word you see. The page may also create confusion. It could claim that your invitation is already downloading while another message asks you to click if the download fails. Some versions even include a testimonial from a supposed guest who says opening the invitation was easy.

A review on a private party invitation page should feel strange. Those details are designed to quiet your doubts and push you toward the download button. For more visual breakdowns of scams like this, check out The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com.
What happens after you download the fake invitation

In the example we describe, the website directs you to open the file on a Windows computer. That device-specific request is another major warning sign. Why would a party invitation care which device you use? The malicious file may contain a remote access tool. Businesses use legitimate versions of this software to troubleshoot computers from another location.

Criminals can abuse similar tools to control your system without permission. Once you install the file, an attacker may be able to search your computer or access saved information. The exact damage depends on the program and the permissions it receives. Your email account can become an especially valuable target. It contains personal conversations along with a contact list filled with people who trust you.

The criminals can then send the same fake invitation to your friends and relatives. Those people may open it because the message appears to come from your real account. As a result, one compromised computer can start a chain reaction.
Why these invitation scams keep working

People receive a steady stream of spam, fake alerts and impersonation attempts. Criminals can also use AI tools to create cleaner writing and more realistic designs. That makes the familiar sender name even more powerful.

You may be cautious around a message from a stranger. Yet you might act quickly when the invitation appears to come from someone you know. The scam succeeds when familiarity replaces verification. Email providers and technology companies continue to improve their filters. Even so, dangerous messages still reach real inboxes. That leaves you making the final decision about whether a link deserves your trust.
HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS
Scam emails may appear to come from a trusted contact and use cheerful invitation graphics to make a malicious download seem legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to stay safe from fake party invitation scams
A few precautions can help you recognize a malicious invitation before it compromises your computer or accounts.

Use strong antivirus software and keep it actively running in the background on your devices. Real-time protection can warn you about a dangerous link or block a malicious download before it reaches your computer.

If you clicked the invitation or downloaded a suspicious file, delete the file without opening it and run a full security scan. A scan can help identify unwanted software that may have reached your computer. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated as well. Updates often close weaknesses that criminals try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Stop immediately if an invitation tells you to download or install a program before you can see the event. Real invitation services normally show the details in your browser or inside their official app. You should not need a separate installer. Delete the message instead of trying to see what happens next.

On a computer, place your cursor over a link without pressing it. Your browser or email program should reveal the destination address. Read the entire address carefully. Watch for misspellings, unexpected words or extra letters added around a legitimate company name. A familiar logo does not confirm that the link belongs to the real company.

Avoid using the link inside the email when you have doubts. Instead, type the invitation service's web address into your browser or open its official app. Sign in and look for the invitation there. If it does not appear in your account, the email may be fake.

Reach out through a separate text message or phone call if an invitation feels unusual. Do not reply directly to the suspicious email. A criminal may control the sender's account or may have forged the address. Ask whether the person actually sent the invitation and whether it requires a download.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Legitimate digital invitations should not require users to install software before viewing an event’s date, location or guest information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Your risk is generally lower if you visited the page but did not run anything. Close the browser tab without pressing the download button. If the file has already downloaded, leave it closed and delete it. Opening the file gives the malicious program a chance to run. Never open it simply to find out what it contains.

Use your email provider's Report phishing option before deleting the invitation. Reporting the message can help the provider block similar emails and warn other recipients. You can also block the sender if you do not recognize the address.

A data removal service can help remove your details from many public data broker databases. This may make it harder for scammers to find personal information they can use to make a message feel convincing. However, no service can remove every record. It also cannot prevent a criminal from reaching you through a compromised friend's contact list. Still, reducing your public exposure can give scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email account. This adds another barrier if criminals steal or guess your password. Never approve an unexpected login request. Also, do not share a security code with anyone who contacts you.

If you typed your email address, password or security code into the fake page, use a clean device to change that password immediately. Change it anywhere else you reused it. Then review the account for unfamiliar activity, new recovery information or settings you did not change. Use a password manager to create and store a strong, unique password for every account so one stolen login cannot unlock several services.

Disconnect the computer from the internet if you ran the installer or noticed unexpected remote activity. Next, run a full security scan. You may also need help from a trusted computer professional to confirm that the remote access software is gone. Use a different, clean device to change important passwords. Start with your email account because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Also, review your email account for unfamiliar forwarding rules or active login sessions. Warn your contacts if suspicious messages may have gone out under your name.
Kurt's key takeaways

A party invitation should give you information, not demand access to your computer. Delete the message if it asks you to install anything before revealing the event. Check the full destination of every link. Then contact the supposed sender separately when something feels unusual. If you downloaded a file but did not open it, delete it and run a security scan. If you ran the file, disconnect the computer and secure your accounts from a clean device. Most importantly, pay attention to that moment when something feels off. A few seconds of doubt can stop a criminal from getting inside your computer. Want to see more? Check out The CyberGuy Report podcast.
Should email providers face tougher requirements to stop malicious invitations before they ever reach your inbox? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Man wanted in robbery tied to Penn State student's murder now sought after off-duty cop shootout
summary: U.S. Marshals offer a cash reward for Khadfi Fleming, 19, linked to a Penn State student's robbery case and an aggravated assault on a Philly officer.
story: U.S. Marshals announce the arrest of one 16-year-old suspect in Colorado, connected to the murder of Penn State student Billy Schmidt. Philadelphia police confirm both 16-year-olds will be charged as adults for the June 6 robbery and shooting. Kaiseem Smith, the second suspect, remains a fugitive as authorities issue a wanted poster.

A 19-year-old wanted in the robbery tied to the killing of a Penn State student is now being sought in connection with another violent Philadelphia crime after an off-duty police officer exchanged gunfire with suspected car thieves.

Khadfi Fleming is a person of interest in the Monday aggravated assault of the off-duty officer, according to the U.S. Marshals Service, which is offering an immediate cash reward for information leading to his whereabouts.
The confrontation unfolded early Monday after thieves allegedly targeted the officer's Dodge Charger, Fox 29 Philadelphia reported.
OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN

The U.S. Marshals Service is offering a cash reward for information leading to Khadfi Fleming, 19, who is wanted for robbery and is a person of interest in the Aug. 10 aggravated assault of an off-duty Philadelphia police officer. (U.S. Marshals Service Philadelphia)
The off-duty officer followed the suspects and confronted them, leading to an exchange of gunfire, according to the outlet. No one is believed to have been struck.
The suspects escaped, and investigators later recovered the officer's Charger with a broken window and damage to its steering column, along with numerous 9mm shell casings, Fox 29 reported.
Authorities say the suspects moved to another stolen car – a Lexus that was later found abandoned.
The U.S. Marshals Service has since publicly identified Fleming as a person of interest in the aggravated assault.
MARSHALS NAB TEEN WANTED FOR MURDER OF PENN STATE STUDENT 1,700 MILES FROM CRIME SCENE, 2ND SUSPECT IN CUSTODY

"USMS Philly is offering an immediate cash reward for Khadfi Fleming, 19, wanted for robbery," the agency wrote on X, adding that Fleming is also a "person of interest" in the Monday attack on the off-duty officer.
Fleming has not been charged in connection with the Monday incident.
But authorities were already looking for the 19-year-old before the latest violence.
Fleming is wanted on a robbery charge connected to the June killing of Billy Schmidt, a 22-year-old Penn State student who was shot while walking home from an NBA Finals watch party.
MANHUNT UNDERWAY AFTER COLLEGE STUDENT FATALLY SHOT CHASING ROBBERS WHO ALLEGEDLY STOLE HIS PHONE
Billy Schmidt was shot and killed in Philadelphia while walking home from an NBA Finals watch party on June 6. (Philadelphia Police Department)
Schmidt was just blocks from his South Philadelphia home when he was fatally shot around 1:30 a.m. on June 6.
Surveillance video captured the final moments before the shooting, with Schmidt heard asking for his stolen phone back before a gunshot rang out.
His father, Bill Schmidt, previously described his son as someone who "cared about everybody and never hurt or bothered a soul."
MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR KANSAS CITY SHOOTING SPREE SUSPECT NEAR WORLD CUP VENUE; FBI OFFERING $25K REWARD

Azzubair Outen-Fleming, 16, was arrested in Colorado a month after authorities said he and another teenager, killed Penn State student Billy Schmidt during an armed robbery as he was walking home from an NBA Finals watch party. (U.S. Marshals Service)
"For him to get shot like that is a travesty," he told ABC7.
The killing sparked a search for two 16-year-old murder suspects, including Fleming's younger brother.

U.S. Marshals captured Azzubair Outen-Fleming in Colorado Springs, Colorado, about a month after Schmidt's death. Authorities said the teenager was found at a distant relative's home and initially tried to conceal his identity.
Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said Outen-Fleming would face a murder charge, Fox 29 reported.
NEW YORK STATE POLICE LAUNCH MANHUNT AFTER KILLING, HOUSE FIRE FOR 'ARMED AND DANGEROUS' SUSPECT
The second teen, Kaiseem Smith, surrendered to Philadelphia police.
Schmidt was studying digital journalism and media at Penn State and was expected to graduate in December.
Now, two months after his killing, authorities are seeking the elder Fleming as they investigate whether he was involved in the latest violent encounter.

Anyone with information about Fleming's whereabouts is urged to contact the U.S. Marshals Service at 1-866-865-TIPS (8477).

title: Parents speak out after son with autism, 6, was suspended for biting sandwich into shape of gun
summary: Kristin and Juan "Ricky" Medina told Fox News Digital their son’s autism can make social norms difficult to understand as they push for less severe discipline.
story: In an interview with Fox News Digital, Kristin and Juan "Ricky" Medina are pushing for less severe school discipline after their son, who has autism, was suspended in first grade for biting a sandwich into the shape of a gun.

The parents of a Georgia first-grader with autism are speaking out after their son was suspended for biting his sandwich into the shape of a gun and pointing it at a classmate during lunch, arguing that the school's strict disciplinary policies fail to account for his developmental disabilities.

John Medina, 6, was suspended last March while in first grade at Sarah Harp Elementary School in Fayette County, south of Atlanta. He was diagnosed with level 1 autism at age 4 and later diagnosed with ADHD, conditions his parents say can make it difficult for him to understand social norms.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, parents Kristin and Juan "Ricky" Medina said that John is exceptionally advanced academically, but the school's apparent strict policies and initial lack of developmental assistance have led to roughly 15 suspensions and more than two dozen disciplinary actions since 2023. They added that while some incidents justified escalation, other harmless acts, such as hunting drawings and hand-gun gestures, have also drawn school discipline and scrutiny.

The disciplinary history has ultimately taken a toll on John's self-esteem, especially as he already struggles to make friends and often feels isolated, his parents said. They said their son refers to himself as a "bad kid" because of how he feels he is treated by his peers and the school environment.
10-YEAR-OLD BOY RECOUNTS NEAR-DROWNING AS FAMILY REVEALS FRIENDSHIP WITH CALIFORNIA TEEN LIFEGUARD HERO
Kristin and Ricky Medina pose outdoors with their son, John, in a park.  (Courtesy of the Medina family)

Kristin said she was initially shocked to learn that John had been suspended over the sandwich incident, questioning the school's reported "strike" system, in which minor actions such as making a hand gesture or saying the word "gun" can escalate to suspension.
"It was upsetting for me to hear that it was, that is what he was getting in trouble for," Kristin said.
"I felt like they were cracking down more on small stuff, you know, stuff that maybe he didn't need to be suspended for," Ricky added.

While John has been involved in physical incidents, including pushing another student in PE and hitting a classmate with a branch, his parents said many official disciplinary actions stemmed from what they considered harmless hand gestures. Other standard behaviors, like drawing a pilgrim shooting a turkey for Thanksgiving, also drew intense school scrutiny, they said.

They added that weapon-related topics are specifically not discussed in their home, but said they cannot control the outside influences John encounters. They added that children can naturally develop an imaginative fascination with weapons, but John’s autism makes it more difficult for him to filter his speech in the way other children might.
MONTANA TEEN THROWS LASSO TO MAN IN YELLOWSTONE RIVER IN SPLIT-SECOND RESCUE
The Medina family lives in Fayette County, Georgia, south of Atlanta. (Courtesy of the Medina family)

They also stressed that, because of his autism, traditional punishments are ineffective and could inadvertently reinforce the idea that saying the word "gun" will allow him to leave school when he is having a bad day.
"Instead of singling him out, just make it a teachable moment for him. Teach, ‘Hey, we don't do this in school because of this reason, it's not appropriate,’" Kristin said.

However, the family said they initially faced pushback from the school over developmental accommodations. Kristin said the school initially refused to grant John an Individualized Education Program (IEP), because he was too academically advanced and officials "didn't see" his autism.
According to Kristin, it took about a year and a half, 10 to 12 suspensions and a second evaluation that resulted in an ADHD diagnosis before the school approved his IEP.
Ricky and Kristin Medina stand with their 6-year-old son, John, in front of a diner mural.  (Courtesy of the Medina family)

John’s parents said they worry that repeatedly focusing on what they consider harmless childhood behavior has reinforced a negative self-image and made him increasingly eager to leave school. John is hesitant to attend school because he believes people are "going to laugh at him for making wrong choices," his parents said.
"I just want to see John start to get his self-esteem built up, his confidence built up, friendships built up," Kristin said. "I don't want him to continue to feel singled out."
The parents said John thankfully finished the previous school year strong, reading at a third-grade level and coming just four test points short of qualifying for the gifted and talented program.
The school also appeared to ease up on suspensions recently, particularly after the family hired Donna Reynolds, a special education advocate, to represent them during school meetings.

John is also currently on a behavioral plan that includes an aide during unstructured periods, including lunch, recess and PE. He also spends time in a smaller, calmer classroom setting, where his parents said he performs exceptionally well.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"What I want to see is that there's less severe punishment like suspensions," Ricky said. "And just continue to talk through things so you can have opportunities to learn from things and maybe focus on real serious concerns."

Fox News Digital reached out to Fayette County Public Schools, the school district under which John's school falls, about his situation. The district declined to go into specific details, but encouraged a review of John's "complete disciplinary history and the full context surrounding the situation rather than focusing on one isolated event."

title: Costco employee fatally rammed car into co-worker on motorcycle after seeing hug: DA
summary: Tyler Sorensen allegedly rammed his car into co-worker Jonathon Langdon's motorcycle in an Issaquah Costco parking lot out of jealousy over a hug.
story: Seattle police say a 15-year-old has been charged in connection with food festival shooting that killed three people. Mayor Katie Wilson and police chief Shon Barnes announce a manhunt for a second suspect.

A Costco employee in a Seattle suburb allegedly rammed his car into a co-worker riding a motorcycle, killing him out of anger and jealousy, according to reports citing statements made to investigators.
Tyler Sorensen, 22, is charged with second-degree murder in connection with the July 31 death of 20-year-old Jonathon Langdon in Issaquah.
Sorensen allegedly followed Langdon out of a Costco parking lot before swerving into his lane and striking his motorcycle, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital.
SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH
Security video showing the moments before Tyler Sorensen, 22, allegedly rammed 20-year-old Jonathon Langdon in Issaquah. (King County Prosecuting Attorney's Office)

Langdon was thrown from his motorcycle into a metal signpost, authorities said. Sorensen fled the scene but returned an hour later with a family member to speak with investigators, according to the Issaquah Police Department.

Sorensen told his father that he "did something stupid" and had been in a collision but kept going. Once his father realized that Sorensen had left the scene of an accident, he drove his son back to the collision site an hour after the deadly incident, prosecutors said.

Sorensen allegedly told investigators that he became jealous after seeing Langdon hug a female co-worker whom Sorensen claimed was his girlfriend. After seeing the hug, he texted friends that his "blood is boiling."
SEATTLE POLICE CHIEF SNAPS OVER CHICAGO HOME QUESTIONS, ABSENCE FROM CITY AFTER MASS SHOOTING

Sorensen allegedly told investigators that he and the female co-worker had been in a relationship for about two to three months, which ended in late May. However, she told police that they had never dated and that she only considered him a friend and had repeatedly told him she "needed space" and that he was "crossing boundaries," authorities said.
Sorensen allegedly told law enforcement that his actions were "stupid" and that he only wanted to "spook" Langdon.
A Costco retail location. (iStock)
"Our hearts go out to the family and friends of the victim as they process this tragic loss of life," said Issaquah Police Chief Steve Mylett.

title: NYPD’s legendary ‘Hip-Hop Cop' Derrick Parker, who investigated rap’s biggest stars and murders, dead at 65
summary: Derrick Parker, the NYPD's "Hip-Hop Cop" who investigated cases tied to Tupac Shakur, Notorious B.I.G. and Jam Master Jay, has died at age 65.
story: Former NYPD rap unit investigator Derrick Parker joined 'Fox & Friends' to discuss his reaction to the embattled artist's apology after he took full responsibility for the alleged assault on his former girlfriend caught on surveillance video.
Derrick Parker, the former NYPD detective known as the "Hip-Hop Cop" for his work in the city's rap-related intelligence unit in the 1990s, has died. He was 65.
His brother, Ralph, told Fox News Digital Monday he died unexpectedly on July 24 at a hospital in New York's Nassau County. He did not give a cause.
A funeral is scheduled for Thursday at the J Foster Phillips Funeral Home in Jamaica, New York.

Derrick J. Parker was the former head of the NYPD's rap intelligence unit when the city's hip-hop scene exploded in popularity in the 1990s. His work included monitoring high-profile artists and their entourages as they came and went from the Big Apple. He said he shared his strategies to reduce violence in the music industry in other parts of the country, including in Miami and Atlanta.
TUPAC SHAKUR MURDER SUSPECT TAKES CENTER STAGE AT TRIAL NEARLY 30 YEARS AFTER SHOOTING SHOCKED MUSIC WORLD
Longtime NYPD Detective Derrick Parker pictured in New York in 2024. He was part of an intelligence unit that focused on hip-hop artists and their entourages during the 1990s. (Stefano Giovannini)
He also served as a homicide and cold case detective during a career that spanned more than 20 years and worked alongside the US Marshals, the ATF, the DEA and the FBI, according to his website.

"You have to watch and see who's coming to your city. Who's there and who's what," he told Fox News Digital in a 2024 interview. "We can't track everybody, but when certain people come to the city, you should know who, especially certain people that are on your radar. That's the way I look at it."
Much of the job, he said, involved keeping law enforcement and nightclub management aware of who was going where in order to avoid potential confrontations between rival groups.
CASSIE VENTURA FLED THE UNITED STATES AFTER TESTIFYING AGAINST DIDDY IN SEX CRIMES TRIAL: DOCS
Sean "Diddy" Combs, the Notorious B.I.G. and Lil Kim — three of rap music's biggest '90s stars. (Getty Images)

He played a role in the 1999 investigation into the Club New York shooting where music mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs was charged but later acquitted. Pop superstar Jennifer Lopez was also briefly detained and released.
Parker said his approach to policing the hip-hop world wasn't to come down hard on its stars.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"I was the law, so he was always friendly," he later said of Combs. "I'm never hard on these guys. They know what they get into. They know what trouble they have."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Parker wrote a book about his experiences, "Notorious C.O.P.: The Inside Story of the Tupac, Biggie and Jam Master Jay Investigations from the NYPD's First 'Hip-Hop Cop.'" The book chronicled his involvement in investigations surrounding three of hip-hop's most notorious killings: Tupac Shakur, Christopher Wallace, who performed as the Notorious B.I.G. and Jam Master Jay, the Run-DMC DJ whose real name was Jason Mizell.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Tupac Shakur in Poetic Justice. (Columbia/Kobal / Shutterstock)
It would be decades before Mizell's killers went on trial. Parker was on the witness stand.
After Parker retired from the NYPD in 2002, he worked in security for large events and executive protection applying the same philosophy of knowing who would be going where to avoid conflicts.

He also became a frequent media commentator on high-profile cases involving figures and venues he had encountered during his NYPD career, including Combs' sex-trafficking trial last year and even the wedding between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden.
GOT A TIP?
He had also told Fox News Digital that he hoped to write a follow-up book.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"I want to really tell a big, big story about a lot of stuff," he said.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis enters a courtroom in Clark County District Court for a trial readiness status check at the Regional Justice Center on June 17, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Steve Marcus-Pool/Getty Images)

Days before his death, he said he was closely following the Las Vegas murder case against Duane "Keffe D" Davis, who is charged with playing a role in Tupac Shakur's 1996 murder. Jury selection began Monday.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We were supposed to go out to dinner for my birthday," Ralph Parker told Fox News Digital. "He's like, ‘Oh, we're gonna go out and eat. Your birthday's coming, don't worry about it.’ Well, I won't be able to go eat with him."

title: 2 custodians dead in possible murder-suicide at Chicago elementary school
summary: Two custodians were found dead from gunshot wounds inside Mark Twain Elementary School in Chicago when no students were present in the building.
story: The Chicago Police Department and Mayor Brandon Johnson confirmed one police officer is dead and another was wounded after a prisoner opened fire at a local hospital Saturday. (Credit: WFLD)
Two custodians were found shot to death Monday inside a Chicago elementary school after one of them allegedly killed his co-worker before turning the weapon on himself, according to reports.
A 48-year-old woman and a 63-year-old man were found unresponsive inside Mark Twain Elementary School just after 3:30 p.m., the Chicago Police Department said.
Both were shot once in the head, authorities said. They were taken to local hospitals, where they were pronounced dead.
TWO FOUND SHOT TO DEATH INSIDE CAR ON UNIVERSITY OF CHICAGO CAMPUS: REPORT
The entrance of Mark Twain Elementary School in Chicago. Two custodians were found fatally shot inside the building on Monday, police said. (Google Maps)
An unspecified weapon was found at the scene.
School principal Matthew Moline confirmed the deaths in a letter to parents, WTTW-TV reported. He said shots were fired inside the building at a time when no students were present.
"I am sorry to share that members of our school community were impacted," he wrote.
SEIU Local 73, the union that represents Chicago Public Schools custodial employees, confirmed both unidentified victims worked at the elementary school.
DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE
A custodian shines the walls at a local high school. (MediaNews Group via Getty Images)

"The only facts we know right now are that two families have lost a loved one and our prayers are with their families, and the staff, students, and families at Mark Twain Elementary School," SEIU Local 73 Executive Vice President Trumaine Reeves said in a statement.

The older custodian was upset that he was slated to be transferred from the school, the Chicago Sun-Times reported, citing a police report. He allegedly shot his co-worker before shooting himself, according to the newspaper.

"We know that this news will be deeply concerning to our families and staff," Moline wrote in his letter. "We will work to provide additional information to the school community as the investigation proceeds."
Chicago cops at a crime scene (Getty Images)

story: The apparent malfunction left several workers clinging to the crane before they made their way down. (Macie Norrod via Storyful)
Construction workers clung to a malfunctioning crane Friday as its arm collapsed onto the pool deck of a neighboring luxury high-rise in Miami, video shot by a bystander showed.
The video, recorded by Macie Norrod, showed the crane’s arm flying through the air before crashing through palm trees on an elevated pool area at the One Plaza West Brickell condo building.
Norrod saw the incident unfold from her home office, saying she had been "in shock and disbelief," according to a report from Storyful.
The arm of a construction crane in Miami collapsed Friday onto the pool deck of a neighboring luxury condo high-rise. (Macie Norrod via Storyful)
OFFICIALS INVESTIGATING AFTER DEADLY CRANE COLLAPSE AT INDUSTRIAL SITE NORTH OF BOSTON
"I thought I was about to watch the workers die from being squashed by the weights of the crane," Norrod said.
Her video showed workers in green vests clinging to the upper portion of the structure during the collapse before eventually climbing down ladders to the ground.
The crane, not yet operational, was being assembled that afternoon when it experienced "some kind of failure," Miami Fire Rescue spokesperson Lt. Pete Sanchez told Fox News Digital.
Workers clung to the crane after the arm collapsed. Authorities said the crane was not operational and was being assembled. (Macie Norrod via Storyful)
NEW YORK CITY CONSTRUCTION CRANE CATCHES ON FIRE BEFORE COLLAPSE
After that failure, the arm fell onto the rooftop deck and was partially submerged in the pool, according to a photo shared with Fox News Digital by Miami Fire Rescue.

"Firefighters immediately accessed the pool deck and conducted a thorough search, confirming that no victims were present," Sanchez said. "The pool deck was secured and cordoned off to prevent residents and the public from entering the area while crews ensured the scene remained safe."
A portion of the crane's arm was submerged in the pool, investigators discovered during a search of the area. (Miami Fire-Rescue)

title: Flames shoot from American Airlines flight before emergency landing
summary: Passenger video purportedly showed flames shooting from an American Airlines plane after a bird strike forced an emergency landing.
story: American Airlines Flight 1760 passenger captures scenes onboard aircraft following a bird strike after departure from Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. (Credit: Patrick Gotwalt/Storyful)
A video purportedly captured flames shooting out of an American Airlines flight following a bird strike before the aircraft made an emergency landing at Myrtle Beach International Airport.

The pilot of American Airlines Flight 1760, a Boeing 737-800 heading to Charlotte with 172 people on board, was heard on air traffic control recordings issuing a "mayday" call after the incident Monday morning.
"Mayday, mayday, mayday, we got an engine problem here," the pilot said.
"The engine is backfiring like crazy," another voice was heard saying in a video taken by a passenger on board the plane, which showed flames. "I think she is on fire now."
JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA
Bursts of flames are seen coming from American Airlines Flight 1760 on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. (Patrick Gotwalt/Storyful)

"American Airlines Flight 1760 returned to Myrtle Beach (MYR) shortly after departure due to a maintenance issue. The aircraft landed safely and has been taken out of service to be inspected by our maintenance team," American Airlines told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Our team worked to get customers on their way to Charlotte (CLT) on a replacement aircraft. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding."
American Airlines also said there was no indication of a fire in the plane's engine and there were no reported injuries. It's unclear where the flames originated.

"American Airlines Flight 1760 returned safely to Myrtle Beach International Airport around 8:40 a.m. local time on Monday, Aug. 10, after the crew reported striking a bird while departing," the Federal Aviation Administration told Fox News Digital. "The Boeing 737-800 was headed to Charlotte Douglas International Airport. The FAA will investigate."
In air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC, a worker said a "significant" number of birds were found on the runway and were being removed.

An American Airlines Boeing 737-800 plane, like the one pictured here, made an emergency landing on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, at Myrtle Beach International Airport. (Rodger Mallison/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/MCT/Getty Images)
Data from the website FlightAware shows the plane departed Myrtle Beach at 8:00 a.m. ET before landing about 36 minutes later.
The FAA said on its website that there have been about 292,000 reported wildlife strikes with civil aircraft in the U.S. between 1990 and 2023.

"About 54% of bird strikes occur from July to October which is when young birds recently have fledged from nests and fall migration occurs," it said. "About 62% of bird strikes with civil aircraft occur in day, 8% occur at dawn or dusk, and 30% occur at night."
An American Airlines Boeing 737-800 sits at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Dallas, Texas, on Nov. 23, 2017. (Getty Images)

title: Luigi Mangione judge says jurors will remain anonymous after threats and harassment of witnesses
summary: Prosecutors warn Luigi Mangione's supporters may intimidate witnesses and jurors, urging the judge to limit courtroom access ahead of next month's trial.
story: High-profile trial coverage demands from Luigi Mangione are sparking intense pushback from prosecutors. Criminal defense attorney Josh Ritter warns that the UnitedHealthcare CEO murder suspect is seeking a public platform to send a message. Ritter breaks down the prosecution's concerns regarding potential witness intimidation and jury nullification ahead of courtroom proceedings in New York.

NEW YORK — The judge overseeing the trial of accused assassin Luigi Mangione said jurors will remain anonymous Tuesday after New York City prosecutors warned that the defendant's supporters may intimidate witnesses and jurors during next month's murder trial over the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"The record demonstrates significant pretrial publicity surrounding this case, including extensive media coverage and repeated public demonstrations outside the courthouse," Judge Gregory Carro wrote in an order published Tuesday afternoon. "The People have documented threats, harassment, and exposure of personal information directed at individuals perceived as connected to the case, including witnesses and others. They further cite instances in which individuals identifying themselves as supporters of the defendant engaged in inflammatory and hostile public statements outside the courthouse and announced their intention to attend jury selection to attempt to speak to prospective jurors."

He ordered that jurors' names and addresses secret from everyone but the parties in the case to protect them from harassment and threats, as well as to protect Mangione's right to a fair trial. Prosecutors had requested the move.

"These measures do not close the courtroom, limit public access to the proceedings, or impose any prior restraint on press coverage," he wrote. "They are limited protections directed solely at preventing harassment and preserving the integrity ofthejury process in a high profile matter."
MANGIONE LAWYERS SAY MEDIA LIMITS AT MURDER TRIAL ARE UNCONSTITUTIONAL, FEAR COURT WILL 'HAND-PICK' PRESS
Luigi Mangione attends a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan Criminal Court, in New York City, U.S., August 11, 2026. REUTERS/David Dee Delgado

In a previously sealed court filing opposing the motion, Mangione's defense agreed that jurors' addresses should remain out of the public sphere but argued that prosecutors had failed to show evidence of "an actual threat to the safety or integrity of the jury."

"Rather than alleging that a pending, actual threat exists, as the statute requires, the People instead engage in speculation and conjecture about what could happen in the future," defense attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo wrote on Aug. 5. "However, the statute explicitly requires a threat that exists, not one that might happen in the future. The reality, of course, is that no threat exists. In the absence of a factual showing that an actual threat exists, the statutory predicate has not been satisfied, and the application must be denied."
The judge disagreed.

Prosecutors separately asked the judge in a Monday court filing to limit courtroom access and strictly enforce decorum rules at the high-profile trial, with jury selection scheduled to begin on Sept. 8.

"The media attention surrounding this case — and the efforts of some of defendant’s supporters both to intimidate witnesses and to interfere with the functioning of the jury — will place extraordinary pressure on witnesses and potential jurors alike," Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann wrote in a letter to Judge Gregory Carro Monday evening.

Carro, however, said the court was considering expanding media access not shrinking it and ruled that there would be an overflow room to accommodate reporters who don't fit in the main courtroom, telling prosecutors that it's not his "first rodeo." He said nothing about making the overflow audio only as prosecutors had sought and did not address a defense request to livestream the entire trial.
"There has never been a decision by this court to exclude or limit," Carro said. "There have been discussions on expanding."
And he said concerns from the defense that the Manhattan District Attorney's Office was involved in picking which journalists could attend were without merit.
"I don’t want to hear anymore about this," he told the sides.
Mangione's attorneys spoke only briefly after an appearance in court Tuesday for what was expected to be the final conference before the trial begins.
"I think there should be two overflow rooms — I'll take one," said defense lawyer Marc Agnifilo.
The room is expected to accommodate more than 80 journalists, but Mangione's team has been seeking greater access. Some of his public supporters have obtained city-issued press passes.

At least one pool reporter will have a guaranteed seat in the main courtroom during jury selection, Carro said. There will be less space during that stage of the trial because potential jurors will be taking up seats.
Carro also told the sides to identify any differences they have over the jury questionnaire before it is finalized.

Luigi Mangione talks to one of his lawyers in Manhattan Supreme Court Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026 in Manhattan, New York. Mangione’s trial for the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. (Barry Williams/New York Daily News via Pool)

Prosecutors had also claimed that court officers would face difficulty enforcing courthouse rules in an overflow room if one were made available to accommodate more reporters than can fit in the main courtroom.

"We are particularly concerned about the possibility that a spectator in an overflow courtroom will clandestinely record the proceedings and share any such recordings with others," prosecutors wrote. "That concern will only be heightened if the overflow room includes a video feed as well as an audio feed."
Seidemann recommended that if the judge does approve an overflow room, "it include only an audio feed so as to minimize the potential for witness intimidation and harassment."
Carro warned that anyone who takes a phone out in the courtroom or overflow room would be removed.
Read the prosecution letter:

"The conventional wisdom is that the defense usually doesn't want high-profile cases broadcast. It can put implicit pressure on jurors to return a guilty verdict," Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor, told Fox News Digital last week.
But Mangione's defense team is likely aware that the defendant has a sizable number of supporters and is aiming to leverage that, he said.

"There's upwards of 10 to 20 percent of the people who have been surveyed who believe that even if he did it, it was justified," Rahmani said. "And I think the defense knows this, and they know that more attention creates the possibility of jury nullification, or maybe even an acquittal."
This 2017 file photo of Brian Thompson was released via Businesswire when he was named chief executive officer of UnitedHealthcare Unit in 2017. (Businesswire)

Thompson, a 50-year-old father of two from Minnesota, was walking to a business conference when surveillance video shows a man firing multiple bullets into his back on Dec. 4, 2024 outside a Manhattan hotel.
Police arrested Mangione days later at a McDonald's in Altoona, Pennsylvania.

Luigi Mangione is escorted from an NYPD helicopter in New York City, New York, Thursday, December, 19, 2024. Mangione is the prime suspect in the murder of United Healthcare CEO, Brian Thompson. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

title: Oklahoma victim fights back after teen charged in rapes walks free — as feds could storm in: attorney
summary: Rachel Bussett says one victim's family is pursuing civil litigation after Jesse Mack Butler walked free on 11 counts including rape charges.
story: Rachel Bussett, one victim’s attorney, discussed the planned civil fight and said she hopes federal authorities will storm in to pursue justice against Jesse Butler.

An Oklahoma teenager accused of sexually assaulting and strangling two high school girls walked free without serving a day in prison, spurring public outrage as a victim’s family prepares to fight back.
"We’re moving on to the next phase, which is civil litigation," Rachel Bussett, an attorney representing the family of one girl in the case, told Fox News Digital.

Jesse Mack Butler was initially charged as an adult at 17 with counts including attempted first-degree rape, rape by instrumentation, sexual battery, forcible oral sodomy, and domestic assault and battery by strangulation. But he ultimately received youthful-offender status and pleaded no contest to all 11 counts in August 2025.
OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’

Instead of being sent to prison, he was placed under the supervision of the Oklahoma Office of Juvenile Affairs and ordered to complete a rehabilitation plan. Once Butler reached age 19 at midnight on Aug. 4, the court's jurisdiction lapsed, and the case was dismissed by operation of law.
Jesse Butler pictured in a baseball uniform before the criminal allegations came to light. (Risin Baseball)
For the family she represents, Bussett said, the outcome was painful but hardly unexpected.
"They were sad and upset, obviously, because they didn't want the deal to go through this way, but they weren't surprised," Bussett said. "They knew that it was going to happen from the beginning."
The family may now have two possible paths forward.

title: California sued over policy that could free serial killers as Laci Peterson's friend sounds alarm
summary: A California parole board policy could open reduced sentencing or clemency paths for serial killers and mass shooters serving life without parole.
story: Former Sacramento DA Anne Marie Schubert is spearheading a lawsuit challenging new California Board of Parole Hearings guidelines that she warns will open a pathway to freedom for serial killers, mass shooters and more of the state's criminals.

The family and friends of Laci Peterson are among the advocates of California murder victims opposing a new parole board policy that would open a path to recommend resentencing or clemency for serial killers, mass shooters and other convicts serving sentences of life without parole when it goes into effect later this year.

"We're talking about people that would have been qualified for the death penalty, OK? So they are the worst of the worst," said Anne Marie Schubert, a former Sacramento District Attorney who is now the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF), a nonpartisan, nonprofit group that filed a lawsuit over the new policy.

"We are talking about cop killers. We're talking about baby killers. We had a family at our press conference of a 6-week-old that was tortured to death by her father over a weeklong period of time, all of which, what I understand, was on video — and so you talk about baby killers. We talk about mass shooters, there's a case out of Fresno that happened in the early '90s where a guy killed 10 people and he pled to life without parole. He would potentially be eligible."

David Hill, sitting left, and attorney Philip Moscone in a California courtroom on April 29, 2004. A court order prevented photographs of the suspect's face from being taken. Hill was later convicted of killing San Francisco Police Officer Isaac Espinoza and shooting his partner. (Paul Chinn/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)
Schubert singled out some high-profile prisoners serving life without parole:

Scott Peterson was convicted of killing his pregnant wife Laci and their unborn son after she vanished on Christmas Eve in 2002. Gang member David Hill fatally shot San Francisco Police Officer Isaac Espinoza in 2004 and wounded his partner. Darryl Lamar Collins was 24 when he killed two people in 1995 but was granted early release in 2017 thanks to changes in California's youthful offender parole law — only to kill his girlfriend Fatima Johnson less than a year later. They are among thousands who could potentially benefit from the new regulations, Schubert said.
CALIFORNIA MURDERER WHO SHOT DEPUTY, KILLED CHAPLAIN AT AGE 24 GRANTED 'YOUTH OFFENDER' PAROLE

According to Schubert, the board exceeded its statutory authority by using the bureaucratic rulemaking process to create a resentencing and clemency review system for prisoners sentenced to life without parole, a plan that California's Office of Administrative Law approved on July 9.

"The main primary arguments deal with the fact that one, they don't have the legal authority to do this, that this is an administrative bureaucratic agency that's trying to rewrite the legislature, that they're trying to rewrite sentencing laws that came out of ballot initiatives," she said. "And really, this is a violation of what we call Marsy's Law, which is a constitutional provision that supports the finality of judgments for victims in California."
The CJLF, along with a coalition of victims' families and nonprofit groups, filed the lawsuit in an effort to stop the board's new policy before it goes into effect in October.

After a trial that attracted nationwide attention, California fertilizer salesman Scott Peterson was found guilty on Nov. 12, 2004 in the Christmas Eve 2002 murder of his pregnant wife Laci. A program card from a memorial service for Laci Peterson and her unborn son is shown in this file photo taken May 4, 2003. (REUTERS/Lou Dematteis LD/MR)

"The Board...has taken it upon itself to expand this recommendation authority into a full-blown system of reviews and hearings paralleling and resembling the system of parole hearings — the system that the people of California voted to curb in Marsy’s Law, Proposition 9 of 2008, due to the prolonged suffering it imposes on crime victims and their families," reads the petition, filed in Sacramento's Superior Court on July 15.

"The Board has extended this parallel system to include inmates convicted of first degree murder with special circumstances sentenced to life without parole, despite initiative statutes mandating life without parole as the minimum sentence for this crime and forbidding the striking of special circumstances."
MAN ONCE EYED IN DISAPPEARANCE OF MISSING CALIFORNIA TEEN NOW CHARGED WITH MURDER

Sharon Rocha (C), mother of Laci Peterson, her son Brent Rocha (L) and her husband Ron Grantski (R) arrive at the courthouse in Redwood City on Feb. 17, 2004. Laci Peterson's husband, Scott, has since been convicted of her and the couple's unborn son. (REUTERS/POOL/John Green JDP)

In addition to alleging the new regulations run contrary to California law, the petition raises concerns that the new process would force victims' families to repeatedly relive traumatic cases that were supposed to be over.
CJLF is working with the victims of some of California's most notorious murder cases, including Sharon Rocha, the mother of Laci Peterson.

"My daughter, Laci, was eight months pregnant when she and my unborn grandson, Conner, were murdered," Rocha said in a statement. "Scott Peterson was initially sentenced to death. After his death sentence was overturned, he was resentenced to life without the possibility of parole. Our family believed that sentence would finally bring some measure of certainty. Victims should not have to spend the rest of their lives wondering whether the person responsible will receive another opportunity for release. Justice demands finality."
SCOTT PETERSON'S DEFENSE LOSES BID TO INTRODUCE WITNESS TESTIMONY IN LONG-RUNNING FIGHT TO OVERTURN CONVICTION
READ THE LAWSUIT:

Peterson has maintained his innocence for decades and is still fighting his conviction in court. The California Supreme Court overturned his death sentence but has upheld his murder convictions. Prosecutors have opposed his claims and say the evidence against him is "overwhelming."

When Peterson's death sentence was reduced to life without parole in 2021, Laci's close friend Kim Juarez said she reluctantly accepted it because she believed it still meant he would never walk free.
"The only certainty that we had when Scott was put away was that he wasn't ever going to get out," she told Fox News Digital in a phone interview. "That's what, to me, is aggravating."

Kim Juarez, far left, and Laci Peterson, far right, with friends at a birthday dinner in 2002. Peterson was killed in December of that year, and her husband, Scott, is currently serving life without parole. (Courtesy of Kim Juarez)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? FIND MORE ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Juarez described the last two decades as the repeated removal of scabs as Laci's friends and family have watched appeals, a resentencing and now another potential avenue that could eventually lead to Peterson's freedom.

"In a world where nothing is guaranteed and in something so big, we are guaranteed to never see Laci and Conner again. That's never going to happen," Juarez said. "The person that took her away — we just want to stick to what was handed down to him. This isn't about punishing him further. It's just about sticking to what was handed down to him."
Laci Peterson and Scott Peterson are seen here celebrating the holidays in Modesto, California. (Peterson Family/ZUMA Press Wire)
NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

Juarez described trauma that extended well outside the courtroom and the legal process. Years after Peterson's conviction, she was pregnant with her own first child. But she found herself gripped by the fear that what happened to her friend could happen to her.

"I was about six months pregnant, and I said, 'If you decide that this isn't the life you want, don't kill me. Just let me go,'" she told her husband, a firefighter she'd met while handing out missing person flyers.

Laci Peterson was eight months pregnant on Christmas Eve in 2002, when she went missing from her Modesto home. Peterson was charged with killing her and their unborn son, Conner, when their bodies washed up months later in the San Francisco Bay.

Scott Peterson appears via video call for a status hearing at San Mateo County Superior Court in Redwood City, California, Tuesday, March 12, 2024. (Andy Alfaro/Modesto Bee/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"There was life before this happened and there's life after this happened — this will always be a part of our lives," Juarez said. "Every Christmas, my family decorates a miniature Christmas tree for her."
But Juarez said Scott Peterson continues to cast a shadow over those close to Laci.

"She's never forgotten, and we want to make her the focus of all of these memories, but it's like he's the cloud that hangs over it," Juarez said. "The likelihood of him getting out, I don't know what the likelihood is, but the fact that it's on the table, that it is a possibility, is scary in itself."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The dispute is also playing out against the backdrop of an unsuccessful effort in the California Legislature last year to expand parole eligibility for some younger inmates serving life without parole.

"Last year there was a bill, it was called SB 672, that... tried to achieve a similar goal of letting life without parole out, but they limited that to people under 26," Schubert said. "They could not get that bill through the legislature.... So in lieu of that, they backdoor it, and they go through a bureaucratic process that's not just under 26, it's everybody."
The board, in public filings, countered that there's nothing in existing state law that blocks it from doing so.
GOT A TIP?

"Penal Code sections 1172.1 and 4801 do not exclude individuals sentenced to life without the possibility of parole from consideration by the Board for recommendation of commutation or resentencing," the board wrote in response to a concerned citizen who protested the new policy on inmates serving life without parole.

"Rather, these statutes grant the Board discretion to evaluate these cases and determine whether referral to the sentencing court or the Governor is appropriate. Had the Legislature intended to bar this population from consideration under either statute, it would have done so."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Schubert, however, disagreed with that interpretation.
"The law says in California they can write regulations related to parole," she told Fox News Digital. "That's the word, 'parole.' Well, they don't get parole for life without parole."

Neither the parole board nor the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation responded to a request for comment.

title: Deported child predator who illegally reentered US sentenced to 20 years in federal prison
summary: A deported illegal migrant from Mexico was sentenced to 20 years in prison for child sex crimes and illegal reentry, and will be removed after he finishes his sentence.
story: Former Acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey discusses Juan Arevalo Mendez, a twice-deported illegal immigrant now charged with rape and kidnapping in Fairfax County, VA. Fahey highlights Mendez's extensive criminal history, including assault and drug possession, emphasizing that serious crimes were preventable if Fairfax County had cooperated with ICE to transfer him into federal custody. Mendez has been deported twice.

A Mexican national who had been deported from the U.S. multiple times before illegally reentering the country has been sentenced to 20 years in federal prison for sexually exploiting two minors, according to federal officials.

Erik Santana-Garcia, 34, of Salt Lake City, Utah, was sentenced July 30 to 20 years in federal prison without parole, followed by a lifetime of supervised release, for interstate transportation of a minor with intent to engage in illegal sexual activity, possession of child pornography and illegally reentering the US following a prior deportation, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Missouri.
He pleaded guilty March 3, according to court documents.
ICE LINES UP TO BOOT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD SEX PREDATOR AFTER BOGUS ASYLUM CLAIM, EARLY PRISON RELEASE
Erik Santana-Garcia, 34, of Mexico, was sentenced last month to 20 years in federal prison without parole, followed by a lifetime of supervised release. (ICE)
Santana-Garcia transported a minor across state lines intending to engage in illegal sexual activity with the child, prosecutors said.

He left Utah with the victim on Nov. 10, 2024, and intended to take the child to New York, but Oak Grove, Missouri, police located the pair two days later. Investigators with Homeland Security Investigations later discovered child pornography depicting a second minor on a phone seized from Santana-Garcia at the time of his arrest, prosecutors said.
Erik Santana-Garcia had previously been deported from the U.S. on multiple occasions. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Santana-Garcia had previously been deported and removed from the U.S. multiple times, most recently on March 6, 2019, according to prosecutors.

"Now, Erik Santana-Garcia’s going to spend the next 20 years in a federal prison because ICE HSI Kansas City, ICE HSI Salt Lake City, ICE HSI Billings and local police from Oak Grove, Missouri, nabbed him," Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote on X.

title: Florida woman accused of faking cancer to scam hundreds out of $40K, police say
summary: A Florida woman was arrested after she allegedly scammed more than 200 people out of $40,000 with a fake cancer diagnosis. GoFundMe says it refunded the money.
story: Aimee Bock, the mastermind behind the 'Feeding Our Future' fraud scheme, received a 41.5-year prison sentence from a Minnesota judge. The scheme involved the theft of nearly $250 million in COVID funding meant to feed hungry children. Bock's defense argued many actors were outside her control, while prosecutors highlighted the lasting damage and erosion of public trust caused by her crimes.
A Florida woman was arrested after authorities said she falsely claimed to have cancer and scammed more than 200 people out of more than $40,000 to pay off personal debts.

Maribeth Ellen Jones, 51, of Bonita Springs, has been charged with grand theft between $20,000 and $100,000. She turned herself in at the Naples Jail Center this week after detectives obtained a warrant for her arrest on the second-degree felony charge, according to the Collier County Sheriff’s Office.

Jones, who worked as an activities' director in the community, allegedly told residents between 2022 and 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing treatment, leading more than 200 people to donate to her because they believed she needed help.
OHIO BROTHERS WHO POSED AS MIDDLE EASTERN ROYALTY RECEIVE LENGTHY SENTENCE FOR $21M FRAUD SCHEME
Maribeth Ellen Jones, 51, of Bonita Springs, has been charged with grand theft between $20,000 and $100,000. (Collier County Sheriff's Office)
Detectives said she even pretended her condition was worsening and had community members cut her hair to make it appear she was preparing to undergo chemotherapy.
Community members created a GoFundMe page for Jones that was linked to her personal bank account, according to the sheriff's office. They also gave her cash and personal checks.
WHAT SCAMMERS DO THE WEEK YOUR SPOUSE DIES
Jones had been the beneficiary of two previous GoFundMe campaigns in which she also claimed to have cancer, the sheriff's office said.
Detectives said the woman had community members cut her hair to keep up the appearance and make it seem like she was preparing for chemotherapy. (Collier County Sheriff's Office)
"GoFundMe has zero tolerance for the misuse of our platform and anyone who seeks to take advantage of the generosity of others," a GoFundMe spokesperson told Fox 13.

More than $41,000 was refunded to donors on the platform through GoFundMe’s Giving Guarantee, which offers a full refund in the rare case something isn’t right," the spokesperson continued.

Detectives discovered that Maribeth Ellen Jones lied about having cancer and used the money to pay her personal debts. (Collier County Sheriff's Office)
She is accused of defrauding 238 Naples residents out of more than $40,000.

"This is an appalling case because it exploited the kindness and generosity of people who truly wanted to help someone they believed was fighting for her life," Sheriff Kevin Rambosk said in a statement.
